cases.name: The Orchard Golf & Country Club, Inc., et al. v. Yu and Yuhico
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On May 28, 2000, members Ernesto Yu and Manuel Yuhico wanted to play golf at the Orchard Golf & Country Club as a pair, but the club's "no twosome" policy barred groups of fewer than three from teeing off on weekend mornings. When the assistant golf director, Francis Montallana, refused to let them play, Yu shouted invectives at him and the two teed off anyway, without permission and without the required tee time slip. After asking for their written comments, the board suspended them for three months. After much litigation over injunctions, the Regional Trial Court of Imus declared the suspension void and awarded each of them ₱2,000,000 moral damages, ₱2,000,000 exemplary damages, attorney's fees and costs; ₱9,200,000 was paid under a writ of execution. The club filed a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review under Rule 43 (as required for intra-corporate cases by A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC), then asked the Court of Appeals for time to file the petition. The Court of Appeals first granted the extension, then reversed itself.
cases.issue: (1) Should the Court of Appeals have allowed the late petition for review? (2) Were Yu and Yuhico entitled to damages for their suspension?
cases.ruling: The Court granted the petition, dismissed the complaints and ordered Yu and Yuhico to return the ₱9,200,000. (1) The rules on the period to appeal are generally inviolable, but may be relaxed to serve substantial justice, especially where the appeal appears meritorious or there are compelling reasons; here the delay was only seven days, the club candidly admitted its mistake, A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC itself allows extensions, and there was no material prejudice. (2) On the merits, the members admitted violating the club's rules, were given notice and opportunity to be heard, and were validly suspended under the by-laws. Their claimed damages were supported only by self-serving declarations. Any damage was damnum absque injuria: injury is the illegal invasion of a legal right, damage is the resulting loss, and damages are the compensation; there must be both a legal wrong and resulting damage. One who makes use of his own legal right does no injury (qui jure suo utitur nullum damnum facit), and the mental anguish, if any, was self-inflicted.
cases.keyDoctrine: Damages are the recompense or compensation awarded for the damage suffered; damage is the loss, hurt or harm resulting from the injury; injury is the illegal invasion of a legal right. To recover damages there must be both a right of action for a legal wrong inflicted by the defendant and damage resulting from it (damnum et injuria). Damage without injury (damnum absque injuria) is not compensable, and one who makes use of his own legal right does no injury. Procedural rules on appeal periods may be relaxed to serve substantial justice.

cases.name: People v. Muyco
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On the night of May 13, 1995, cousins Jesus and Arnulfo Muyco were drinking with Romeo Boteja, Jr., 19, and Romeo's uncle Ernesto under a mango tree in Cabatuan, Iloilo. Arnulfo suddenly grabbed Romeo's hands and Jesus stabbed him below the collarbone, killing him. Ernesto, frozen with shock, later fled. Only Jesus was caught. He raised alibi, saying he was in Passi, Iloilo, some 50 kilometers away. The trial court convicted him of murder, sentenced him to reclusion perpetua, and ordered him to pay ₱30,000 death indemnity and ₱27,000 funeral expenses, but awarded nothing for loss of earning capacity although the victim's mother testified that he earned ₱1,600 a month as a farm laborer.
cases.issue: (1) Was the conviction for murder proper? (2) Are the heirs entitled to damages for the victim's loss of earning capacity, and how much?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the conviction with modifications. The eyewitness's failure to react was understandable, since people react differently to startling events, and minor discrepancies strengthen rather than destroy credibility. Alibi failed against positive identification, especially as it was not shown to be physically impossible for the accused to be at the scene. Treachery was present. On damages, the death indemnity was increased to ₱50,000, and the Court awarded loss of earning capacity: following People v. Dizon, documentary evidence is the rule, but testimony suffices when the victim was self-employed or a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage. Using the formula 2/3 (80 − age at death) × (gross annual income − 80% of gross annual income), the heirs of the 19-year-old victim were awarded ₱156,172.80.
cases.keyDoctrine: Lost earnings are computed as: net earning capacity = 2/3 × (80 − age at time of death) × (gross annual income − living expenses of 80% of gross annual income). Documentary evidence is generally required to prove loss of earning capacity, but testimony suffices when the victim was self-employed or a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage. Alibi must show physical impossibility of being at the crime scene.

cases.name: Victory Liner, Inc. v. Gammad, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On March 14, 1996, a Victory Liner bus bound for Tuguegarao, running at high speed, fell into a ravine in Nueva Vizcaya, killing passenger Marie Grace Pagulayan-Gammad, a 39-year-old Section Chief of the BIR. Her husband and children sued for damages for breach of contract of carriage. Victory Liner's counsel failed to appear at hearings, so it was deemed to have waived cross-examination and the presentation of its evidence. The trial court awarded actual damages, death indemnity, moral and exemplary damages lumped together, compensatory damages for loss of earning capacity, and attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals modified the amounts. Victory Liner argued that its counsel's gross negligence denied it due process, and that the damages were baseless.
cases.issue: (1) Was Victory Liner denied due process by its counsel's negligence? (2) Is it liable for breach of contract of carriage? (3) Were the damages proper?
cases.ruling: The Court partly granted the petition. (1) The negligence of counsel binds the client, except where reckless or gross negligence deprives the client of due process; here counsel filed an answer, a pre-trial brief and a timely appeal, and Victory Liner itself was negligent. (2) A common carrier is presumed at fault when a passenger dies, and the presumption is overcome only by proof of extraordinary diligence, which was not shown. (3) Under Article 1764 in relation to Article 2206, the heirs are entitled to death indemnity (₱50,000), indemnity for loss of earning capacity, and moral damages. But the award for loss of earning capacity was deleted: documentary evidence is required, and the deceased, a BIR section chief, did not fall under the exceptions for low-wage workers; ₱500,000 temperate damages were awarded instead under Article 2224, since loss was shown but not its amount. Moral and exemplary damages cannot be lumped together, having different jural foundations; ₱100,000 each was awarded. Actual damages were reduced to the ₱78,160 supported by official receipts. Attorney's fees of 10% were allowed since exemplary damages were awarded, and interest was imposed following Eastern Shipping Lines.
cases.keyDoctrine: In the death of a passenger, the carrier is liable for death indemnity, loss of earning capacity and moral damages (Arts. 1764 and 2206). Loss of earning capacity needs documentary proof, except for self-employed or daily-wage workers earning below the minimum wage; when loss is shown but its amount cannot be proved, temperate damages may be awarded (Art. 2224). Actual damages require competent proof such as official receipts. Moral and exemplary damages have different bases and must be determined separately.

cases.name: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On March 17, 1991, in Gumaca, Quezon, a bus of Philippine Hawk Corporation driven by Margarito Avila hit a motorcycle carrying Silvino Tan and his wife Vivian Tan Lee, and a jeep parked on the roadside. Silvino died; Vivian was injured. Vivian sued the company and the driver for damages based on quasi-delict. The trial court found that the driver, who saw the motorcycle ahead, did not slow down but veered to the left lane, and held him guilty of simple negligence; the company was held solidarily liable for failing to exercise the diligence of a good father of a family in selecting and supervising him. Silvino, who operated a gasoline station, earned about ₱1,000,000 a year, shown by a certificate of creditable income tax withheld. The Court of Appeals affirmed and added temperate damages for the motorcycle, moral damages for Vivian's injuries and civil indemnity, though Vivian had not appealed.
cases.issue: (1) Was the driver negligent, and is the company liable? (2) Could the Court of Appeals award damages that Vivian did not appeal for? (3) Were the damages properly computed?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition with modifications. Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence; the driver saw the motorcycle but did not slow down and veered left. When an employee's negligence causes damage, the employer is presumed negligent in selecting or supervising him and must overcome that by convincing proof; the company's tests covered only driving ability and fitness, and it did not know of the driver's prior sideswiping incidents. Under Section 8, Rule 51, an appellate court may review matters not assigned as errors if necessary for a just decision, so the added damages were proper. Indemnity under Article 2206 is for loss of capacity to earn, computed on net earnings: with documentary proof of a ₱1,000,000 gross annual income, and absent other evidence, necessary business expenses were pegged at 80% and living expenses at 50% of the net, giving ₱1,000,000 for the 65-year-old deceased. Actual damages were limited to receipted amounts (₱127,192.85); temperate damages of ₱10,000 were proper for the motorcycle, since only a job estimate was presented; moral damages for the injuries were reduced to ₱30,000; and ₱50,000 civil indemnity was affirmed.
cases.keyDoctrine: Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence. An employee's negligence raises a presumption that the employer failed in the selection or supervision of employees. Indemnity for loss of earning capacity (Art. 2206) compensates loss of capacity to earn and is computed on net earnings: life expectancy of 2/3 x (80 - age at death) multiplied by the gross annual income less necessary expenses, less living expenses. Actual damages need receipts; a mere estimate may justify temperate damages. An appellate court may consider errors not assigned when necessary for a just decision.

cases.name: People v. Asilan
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On March 27, 2006, in Sta. Mesa, Manila, PO1 Randy Adovas, a 29-year-old police officer in uniform, was about to handcuff a man when Joseph Asilan came from behind and stabbed him in the back several times; the man being arrested then took the officer's gun and shot him. Adovas died. Two eyewitnesses identified Asilan, who was arrested near the scene. Charged with direct assault with murder, he was convicted of murder qualified by treachery and ordered to pay actual damages, moral damages and civil indemnity; the Court of Appeals affirmed. Asilan attacked the witnesses' credibility, argued that treachery was not shown and was not properly alleged, and that he could only be guilty of homicide. The widow had testified, with documentary proof, that her husband earned ₱8,605 a month.
cases.issue: (1) Was Asilan's guilt for murder proved? (2) What damages are due to the heirs, including loss of earning capacity?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the conviction for murder and modified the damages. The trial court's assessment of credibility stands; minor inconsistencies enhance credibility; there is no standard reaction to a shocking event; and flight indicates guilt but its converse does not prove innocence. Treachery was present, since the officer was stabbed from behind without warning, and it was alleged in the Information; objections to the Information's sufficiency were in any case waived. Civil indemnity was increased to ₱75,000 and moral damages to ₱50,000, exemplary damages of ₱30,000 were added under Article 2230 because of treachery, and actual damages were fixed at the ₱80,224 shown by receipts. Under Article 2206, the lower courts failed to award loss of earning capacity; computing life expectancy as 2/3 (80 − 29) = 34 years and net income as gross annual income (₱103,260) less 50% living expenses, the Court awarded ₱1,755,420, with 6% interest on all damages from finality.
cases.keyDoctrine: Under Article 2206, the defendant is liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, assessed and awarded in every case unless the deceased had no earning capacity due to a permanent disability not caused by the defendant. The factors are the number of years (life expectancy = 2/3 × (80 − age at death)) and the rate of loss (net income, which is gross income less living expenses). Exemplary damages may be awarded under Article 2230 when the crime is committed with an aggravating circumstance such as treachery.

cases.name: Quirante, et al. v. Intermediate Appellate Court, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Atty. John Quirante represented Dr. Indalecio Casasola in a suit against a building contractor and its surety, PHILAMGEN, and won a judgment for actual, moral and exemplary damages, attorney's fees of ₱30,000 and the ₱120,000 surety bond. While PHILAMGEN's challenge to the judgment was pending in the Supreme Court, Dr. Casasola died. Atty. Quirante then moved in the same case for confirmation of his attorney's fees, claiming an oral agreement with the late Dr. Casasola, allegedly confirmed in writing by the widow and two daughters, under which he would get ₱30,000 if the surety bond was recovered, and any award above the bond would be divided equally among the heirs, himself and Atty. Dante Cruz. The trial court confirmed the fees; the Intermediate Appellate Court set aside the confirmation as premature and held that it could not bind heirs who did not sign.
cases.issue: Was the trial court's confirmation of the attorney's fees proper?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the Intermediate Appellate Court, with an observation. Counsel may claim attorney's fees either in the very action in which the services were rendered or in a separate action; claiming them in the same action is proper, since the right is an incident of the case and the court is familiar with the lawyer's services, and it avoids multiplicity of suits. The fees claimed here, based on a contract for professional services, differ from attorney's fees as damages under Article 2208, which are awarded to the litigant, not to counsel. But the confirmation was premature: the main case was not yet final, and an attorney's fee cannot be determined until the main litigation is decided and something has been recovered from which the fee is to be paid, especially as the agreement was contingent. The Court rejected, however, the appellate court's holding that the confirmation could not affect non-signatory heirs, since that too should be determined by the trial court after the case is adjudicated.
cases.keyDoctrine: Attorney's fees as damages under Article 2208 are awarded to the litigant, who is the judgment creditor, while attorney's fees for professional services are owed by the client to counsel under their contract. Counsel's claim for fees may be made in the same action or in a separate action, but a fee contingent on recovery cannot be determined until the main litigation has been decided and something has been recovered from which the fee is to be paid.

cases.name: Philippine National Bank v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: A government check for ₱97,650 issued by the Ministry of Education and Culture, payable to F. Abante Marketing and drawn against the Philippine National Bank (PNB), was deposited with Capitol City Development Bank, which sent it through the Philippine Bank of Communications (PBCom) for clearing. PNB cleared the check, but more than two months later returned it and debited PBCom's account, claiming a material alteration of the check's serial number. PBCom debited Capitol's account, but Capitol could no longer debit the payee, which had already withdrawn the money. Capitol sued PBCom, which filed a third-party complaint against PNB. The trial court ordered reimbursement with 12% interest and ₱10,000 attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals ordered PNB to honor the check with interest and to pay the attorney's fees.
cases.issue: (1) Is the alteration of a check's serial number a material alteration? (2) Should the uncorroborated certification of the Ministry be given weight? (3) Was the award of attorney's fees proper?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the Court of Appeals except for the attorney's fees, which it deleted. An alteration is material if it alters the effect of the instrument, that is, if it changes the items required to be stated under Section 1 of the Negotiable Instruments Law. A check's serial number is not one of them: the change did not alter the relations of the parties, the drawer, the drawee, the payee or the amount, and the issuing agency was clearly printed on the check. Being an innocent alteration, it gave PNB no right to dishonor the check. The Ministry's certification deserved no weight because its signatory was not presented to identify it. As to attorney's fees, neither lower court explained the award: the discretion to award attorney's fees under Article 2208 demands factual, legal and equitable justification; the reason must be stated in the text of the decision, not only in the dispositive portion, since the award is the exception rather than the rule.
cases.keyDoctrine: The award of attorney's fees under Article 2208 is the exception, not the rule; it demands factual, legal and equitable justification, and the reason must be stated in the text of the decision. An award stated only in the dispositive portion is disallowed. A material alteration is one that changes the items required to be stated under Section 1 of the Negotiable Instruments Law; changing a check's serial number is not material.

cases.name: Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Two fiber drums of riboflavin were shipped from Japan to Manila on a vessel of Eastern Shipping Lines. On arrival, one drum was found damaged; it then passed through the arrastre operator and the customs broker, and when it reached the consignee, one drum had spillage and adulterated contents. The insurer paid the consignee ₱19,032.95 and, as subrogee, sued the carrier, the arrastre operator and the broker. The trial court held them jointly and severally liable, with legal interest of 12% a year from the filing of the complaint; the Court of Appeals affirmed. The carrier questioned its solidary liability and argued that the interest should run only from the trial court's decision and at 6%, since the claim was unliquidated.
cases.issue: (1) Is the carrier liable for the damage, solidarily with the arrastre operator and the broker? (2) From when does legal interest run on an award for loss or damage, and at what rate?
cases.ruling: The petition was partly granted. When goods arrive damaged, the carrier is presumed at fault, and since it failed to rebut the presumption, its liability was inevitable whether or not others were solidarily liable with it. On interest, the Court reconciled its earlier rulings into rules of thumb: (1) for a loan or forbearance of money, the stipulated interest applies, the interest due itself earns legal interest from judicial demand, and absent stipulation the rate is 12% a year from default (judicial or extrajudicial demand); (2) for other obligations, interest on damages may be imposed at the court's discretion at 6% a year, but not on unliquidated claims until the demand can be established with reasonable certainty: from demand if then reasonably certain, otherwise from the court's judgment, always on the amount finally adjudged; (3) once a money judgment becomes final and executory, the rate is 12% a year until satisfied, that period being equivalent to a forbearance of credit. Applying these, interest was set at 6% from the trial court's decision and 12% from finality.
cases.keyDoctrine: Interest as actual and compensatory damages: for a loan or forbearance of money, the stipulated rate (in writing), or absent stipulation the legal rate from judicial or extrajudicial demand; for other obligations, 6% at the court's discretion, running from demand if the claim is then reasonably certain, or else from the judgment; and from the finality of a money judgment, interest until satisfaction because that period is equivalent to a forbearance of credit. Interest due earns legal interest from judicial demand (Art. 2212). The 12% rates applied in this case were later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013 (BSP Circular No. 799, Nacar v. Gallery Frames); check the current rate.

cases.name: Estores v. Spouses Supangan
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In 1993, Hermojina Estores agreed in a Conditional Deed of Sale to sell a lot in Naic, Cavite to the spouses Supangan for ₱4.7 million. The contract required her to secure a DAR clearance, move a house off the lot and complete the documents, and gave the buyers the right to demand the return of their down payment if she failed to complete the documents. After almost seven years and ₱3.5 million in payments, she had still not complied. On September 27, 2000, the spouses demanded the return of the ₱3.5 million; she acknowledged it and promised to return it, but did not. In the suit for sum of money, she agreed to return the principal but refused to pay interest, since the contract did not provide for it. The trial court imposed 6% interest and attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals set the 6% to run from the demand and reduced the attorney's fees to ₱100,000.
cases.issue: (1) May interest be imposed though the contract does not stipulate it, and at what rate? (2) Are attorney's fees warranted, and in what amount?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition but modified the award. Interest may be imposed even without stipulation: under Article 2210, interest may in the court's discretion be allowed on damages for breach of contract, and the seller, who used the money and failed to return it, was in default from the demand on September 27, 2000. The rate is 12%, because the transaction was a forbearance of money: the phrase "forbearance of money, goods or credits" has a meaning separate from a loan and covers arrangements where a person acquiesces to the temporary use of his money pending the happening of certain events or the fulfillment of conditions. The buyers parted with their money before the conditions were fulfilled, and the seller's unwarranted withholding of it amounts to an involuntary loan. Eastern Shipping and Reformina involved torts, with no forbearance and damages not reasonably certain at demand. The 12% runs from the demand until full satisfaction. Attorney's fees were warranted because the buyers were compelled to litigate, but were reduced to ₱50,000, since they must always be reasonable.
cases.keyDoctrine: Interest may be awarded on damages for breach of contract even without a stipulation (Art. 2210), from default upon demand. "Forbearance of money, goods or credits" is distinct from a loan: it covers arrangements where a person acquiesces to the temporary use of his money pending the happening of events or the fulfillment of conditions; the unwarranted withholding of money that should be returned is a forbearance, an involuntary loan. Attorney's fees under Art. 2208 must always be reasonable. (The 12% rate then applied to forbearances was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013; check the current rate.)

cases.name: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Lamberto Chua and Jacinto Sunga formed a partnership in 1977 to market liquefied petroleum gas under the name Shellite, registered as Jacinto's sole proprietorship. After Jacinto died, his widow Cecilia and daughter Lilibeth Sunga-Chan continued the business without Chua's consent and ignored his demands for accounting and winding up. Chua sued and won: a final judgment ordered an accounting, the return of his one-half share of the partnership assets, unreceived profits of ₱35,000 a month "with legal rate of interest until fully paid", and damages and fees; it became final on December 20, 2001. In execution, the trial court approved Chua's computation of ₱8,733,644.75, which added 12% interest to his share of the assets and to the profits. Lilibeth's property was levied and sold to Chua for ₱8 million.
cases.issue: (1) Was the interest added to Chua's claims proper, and at what rates? (2) Is the petitioners' liability solidary? (3) May the absolute community property of Lilibeth and her husband answer for the judgment?
cases.ruling: The petition was partly granted. Applying the Eastern Shipping rules, the unreceived profits earn 6% from the trial court's decision (October 7, 1997) to its finality (December 20, 2001), and then, with the added interest, 12% from finality until paid, as the award is by then equivalent to a forbearance of credit; the goodwill value and the damages and fees earn 12% from finality. But Chua's one-half share of the partnership assets was an unliquidated claim that earns no interest until reasonably determined: the norm is "reasonably determinable", not determinable by mathematical computation. Since the judgment itself required an accounting and inventory, his share became liquidated only when the trial court approved the accounting, so no interest attaches to it. Chua's claim was reduced to ₱5,529,392.52, and he must pay the excess of his ₱8 million bid. The obligation is solidary because the acts complained of were not severable, the duty to account was indivisible, and the petitioners resisted a legitimate claim in bad faith; and the absolute community may answer for debts contracted by one spouse to the extent the family benefited.
cases.keyDoctrine: Interest does not run on an unliquidated claim until it is reasonably determinable, which is not the same as determinable by mathematical computation; a share that can be fixed only after an accounting becomes liquidated only when the accounting is approved. Under the Eastern Shipping rules, an award not involving a loan or forbearance earns 6% from the judgment, and from finality the award (with the interest added) earns the forbearance rate until satisfied. (The 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013; check the current rate.)

cases.name: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: John Anthony de Camilis, on a pilgrimage in Europe with Air France tickets, was refused entry to Moscow for lack of a transit visa. He claimed that Air France agents then rudely denied his requests, reported him as a security threat (leading to police interrogations and the lifting of his flight coupons), refused to honor his confirmed flight from Rome to Paris, failed to check in his baggage so that he missed his connection, did not give the promised motel pass, and told him his confirmed flight to Manila was overbooked. He sued for breach of contract of carriage. The trial court awarded actual, moral and exemplary damages and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals held that the passenger, not the airline, was responsible for the travel documents, but found the airline in bad faith for the poor service, verbal abuse and lack of respect by its agents; it reduced the actual and exemplary damages and imposed 6% interest from the extrajudicial demand, and 12% from finality.
cases.issue: (1) Can the Supreme Court review the award of damages and attorney's fees? (2) From when does the legal interest on the damages run?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition. Whether the passenger was entitled to damages and attorney's fees requires a review of the evidence, a question of fact; a Rule 45 petition is limited to questions of law, and none of the exceptions applied. Both lower courts laid down the factual and legal bases for their awards. On interest, following Eastern Shipping Lines, the 6% legal interest runs not from the extrajudicial demand but from April 25, 2007, when the trial court rendered its judgment, since that is when the quantification of damages may be deemed reasonably ascertained; from the finality of the decision, 12% applies until full satisfaction, on all sums awarded.
cases.keyDoctrine: For damages that cannot be established with reasonable certainty when demanded (such as moral and exemplary damages for breach of contract of carriage), the 6% legal interest runs from the date of the trial court's judgment, when the quantification of damages may be deemed reasonably ascertained, not from the extrajudicial demand; from finality, the higher rate applies until satisfaction. (The 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013; check the current rate.) A Rule 45 petition raises only questions of law.

cases.name: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Veronica Padillo bought a lot and building in Lucena City covered by TCT No. T-9863, but Tomas Averia, Jr., who claimed the same property under an unregistered contract to sell and occupied it, refused to turn it over and filed several suits over it. In a registration case (M.C. No. 374-82), Padillo was declared the sole owner, a ruling affirmed up to the Supreme Court. Meanwhile, she had filed a separate action for declaratory relief and damages; the Court of Appeals, in a final decision in CA-G.R. SP No. 15356, ordered that action merely suspended, not dismissed, pending the registration case. The trial court later awarded Padillo ₱150,000 a year in unrealized income, ₱107,000 attorney's fees plus ₱1,000 per appearance and ₱10,000 litigation expenses, ₱50,000 moral and ₱20,000 exemplary damages. The Court of Appeals reversed on the ground of res judicata.
cases.issue: (1) Was the action for damages barred by res judicata? (2) Were the damages and attorney's fees awarded by the trial court proper?
cases.ruling: The Court granted the petition but reduced the awards. All the requisites of res judicata (bar by prior judgment) were present, but the Court of Appeals' final decision ordering the mere suspension of the damages suit had become the law of the case between the parties, even if erroneous, so Padillo could not be faulted for pursuing it. On damages: the claimed income of ₱150,000 a year was conjectural and speculative, since actual damages must be proved and cannot be presumed; she was entitled only to the unrealized rentals Averia admitted (₱800 a month), or ₱97,600 for the period he occupied the property, with legal interest from finality. Moral and exemplary damages were deleted: filing suits does not by itself show malice or bad faith, the law does not impose a penalty on the right to litigate, and the anxiety of being a party to a suit is not the kind that warrants moral damages. Attorney's fees, the exception and not the rule, were reduced to a reasonable ₱25,000, since they are not meant to enrich the winning party.
cases.keyDoctrine: Actual damages must be proved and cannot be presumed; testimony on expected income that is vague and unspecified is too speculative. No moral damages for filing suits without malice or bad faith, since no penalty is put on the right to litigate. Attorney's fees as damages (extraordinary concept, paid by the loser to the winner, Art. 2208) differ from attorney's fees in the ordinary concept (compensation paid by the client to his lawyer); they are the exception, must be justified and reasonable, and are not meant to enrich the winning party. The law of the case binds the same parties in the same case even if erroneous.

cases.name: Batong Buhay Gold Mines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Francisco Aguac sold his 62,495 shares in Batong Buhay Gold Mines to Incorporated Mining Corporation without his wife's consent. The wife wrote the company asking it to withhold the transfer, since the shares were conjugal property, and the company held back the transfer for fear of being held liable to her. Incorporated Mining sued to compel the transfer and for damages. The trial court ordered the transfer by preliminary mandatory injunction, later made permanent, but awarded no damages. On appeal, the Court of Appeals added an award of ₱5,625.55, the profit the buyer could have made had the shares been transferred when demanded, since the price of the shares had risen and later fallen.
cases.issue: May damages for unrealized profits be awarded without proof that the claimant would have sold the shares and made the profit?
cases.ruling: No. The Court set aside the Court of Appeals and reinstated the trial court's decision. The stipulation of facts did not show that the buyer intended to sell, or would have sold, the shares on specific dates. Although the shares rose and later fell in value, whatever profits could have been made were purely speculative, since it was difficult to predict the rise and fall of their value with any certainty, and speculative damages cannot be recovered. The buyer could just as well have refused to sell and waited for further increases.
cases.keyDoctrine: Unrealized profits (lucro cesante) must be duly established; the claimant must prove that it was in fact damaged by the defendant's act. Speculative damages cannot be recovered: a mere rise in the market price of shares does not prove a lost profit without proof that the claimant would have sold them.

cases.name: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In 1959, Lianga Bay Logging, a log producer, appointed General Enterprises as distributor of part of its log production to Korea and Europe for two years, for a 13% commission. The producer bound itself to make at least 2,000,000 board feet a month available for export from September 1959. The contract allowed suspension only for listed causes, such as fire, flood, strikes, government orders and similar causes beyond a party's control. After a few months, the producer stopped supplying logs, citing barter restrictions, machinery breakdowns, the Margin Law, a demand to renegotiate prices and its plan to build a veneer plant, and it sold logs to other buyers. The distributor sued for breach. The trial court awarded ₱400,000 actual damages, ₱100,000 exemplary damages and ₱400,000 attorney's fees and expenses of litigation.
cases.issue: (1) Was the producer justified in suspending the contract? (2) Were the damages properly awarded?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed with a modification. The contract was valid and had a cause. The demand to renegotiate prices and the veneer plant were not among the stipulated causes of suspension; and even if the barter restrictions, breakdowns and the Margin Law were fortuitous, they did not make it impossible for the producer to comply, since it kept producing logs and selling them to others. A fortuitous event does not necessarily extinguish an obligation unless it makes normal fulfillment impossible. Under Article 2200, indemnity covers not only the loss suffered but also the profits the creditor fails to obtain (lucrum cessans). From the commission the distributor actually earned per board foot on earlier shipments, its lost commission over the 17 remaining months was estimated at ₱365,350.40, so the ₱400,000 award was a reasonable estimate, not speculative. Exemplary damages were reduced to ₱50,000, since the producer's misstatements, though reprehensible, were not wanton or malevolent; the attorney's fees were affirmed under Article 2208.
cases.keyDoctrine: Under Article 2200, indemnification for damages comprehends not only the value of the loss suffered (daño emergente) but also the profits the creditor fails to obtain (lucrum cessans), provided they can be determined with reasonable certainty, as by projecting the claimant's past earnings under the same contract. A fortuitous event does not extinguish an obligation unless it makes normal fulfillment impossible. Exemplary damages require wanton, oppressive or malevolent conduct (Art. 2232).

cases.name: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: A passenger bus of Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, driven by Freddie Suelto, suddenly swerved to the right on Kamias Road, Quezon City, and struck the terrace of Erlinda Valdellon's commercial apartment. Valdellon had an engineer estimate the repairs at ₱171,088.46 and presented a receipt for ₱35,000 for repair work; the engineer did not testify. The defense's architect put the repair cost at ₱55,000. Suelto claimed he swerved to avoid a jeepney that intruded into his lane, but his account in court differed from his counter-affidavit. In a joint trial of the criminal and civil cases, Suelto was convicted of reckless imprudence resulting in damage to property and sentenced to one year; he and the bus company were ordered to pay ₱150,000 actual damages, ₱20,000 compensatory and exemplary damages and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals reduced the actual damages to ₱100,000.
cases.issue: (1) Was Suelto negligent, or did the sudden emergency rule apply? (2) Was the award of actual damages proved? (3) Was the one-year prison term proper?
cases.ruling: The petition was partly granted. Suelto was negligent: he admitted swerving and hitting the terrace, a driver violating a traffic regulation is presumed negligent (Art. 2185), the heavy damage showed he was speeding, his accounts were inconsistent, and the sudden emergency rule does not apply where the defense is not proved. On damages, actual damages under Article 2199 cover the loss of what one has (daño emergente) and the failure to receive a benefit (lucro cesante), but they are not presumed: the claimant must prove the actual loss with a reasonable degree of certainty, on competent proof and the best evidence obtainable. A claimant's bare testimony must be viewed with caution, and an estimate of the repair cost does not suffice. Neither lower court stated the basis of its award; since the defense's own evidence showed ₱55,000, that amount was awarded, with ₱20,000 exemplary damages. Because the offense resulted only in damage to property, Article 365 calls for a fine, not imprisonment, so Suelto was fined ₱55,000.
cases.keyDoctrine: Actual damages (Art. 2199) are not presumed; the claimant must prove the actual amount of loss with a reasonable degree of certainty, on competent proof and the best evidence obtainable, pointing to specific facts that afford a basis for measuring them. An estimate of the cost of repairs, without testimony to support it, does not suffice, and a claimant's bare self-serving testimony must be admitted with extreme caution. The sudden emergency rule does not excuse one whose own negligence created the emergency, and it must be proved by the one invoking it.

cases.name: People v. Jugueta
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: At night on June 6, 2002, in Atimonan, Quezon, Ireneo Jugueta and two companions stripped off the sack wall of Norberto Divina's one-room nipa hut, where his family lay down to sleep, and fired at them. Two of his daughters, aged 13 and 3½, were killed; Norberto, his wife and two other daughters survived. Jugueta was convicted of double murder and multiple attempted murder; the Court of Appeals affirmed. On appeal, the Supreme Court used the case to restate in detail the damages to be awarded in criminal cases.
cases.issue: (1) Was Jugueta's guilt proved, and what penalties apply? (2) What damages are due, and what are the standard amounts for crimes where the imposable penalty is reclusion perpetua to death?
cases.ruling: The conviction was affirmed with modifications. With the aggravating circumstance of dwelling, the imposable penalty for each murder was death, reduced to reclusion perpetua without parole under R.A. 9346. The Court explained the kinds of damages: civil indemnity ex delicto, equivalent to actual or compensatory damages, which is not a penalty and has a minimum (₱3,000 under Art. 2206) but no ceiling; moral damages, compensatory in nature, requiring injury from a case under Arts. 2219 or 2220; exemplary damages under Arts. 2229-2230, due for any aggravating circumstance, ordinary or qualifying, even if not alleged in the Information but proved, or for highly reprehensible conduct; and temperate damages. The basis is the penalty imposable by law for the crime, not the penalty actually imposed. It set standard amounts: for murder where the penalty would be death but is reduced to reclusion perpetua, ₱100,000 each as civil indemnity, moral and exemplary damages; for reclusion perpetua only, ₱75,000 each; for homicide, ₱50,000 civil indemnity and ₱50,000 moral damages; and ₱50,000 temperate damages when no proof of burial or funeral expenses is presented. All amounts earn 6% interest from finality.
cases.keyDoctrine: In crimes, the damages are civil indemnity (compensatory, not a penalty; a floor but no ceiling), moral damages (compensatory), exemplary damages (for an aggravating circumstance, ordinary or qualifying, proved at trial even if not alleged, or for highly reprehensible conduct), and actual or temperate damages. The amounts follow the penalty imposable by law for the crime, not the penalty actually imposed. Murder punishable by death but reduced to reclusion perpetua: ₱100,000 each; reclusion perpetua only: ₱75,000 each; homicide: ₱50,000 civil indemnity and ₱50,000 moral damages; temperate damages of ₱50,000 when no burial expenses are proved.

cases.name: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Dario Nacar won a case for illegal dismissal. The Labor Arbiter's 1998 decision awarded him backwages and separation pay, computed only up to the date of that decision, ₱158,919.92. The employer appealed up to the Supreme Court and lost; the judgment became final on May 27, 2002. In execution, Nacar asked that his backwages and separation pay be computed up to the finality of the judgment, with interest. The Labor Arbiter, the NLRC and the Court of Appeals refused, holding that the final 1998 decision could no longer be altered, and limited him to the balance of the original amount.
cases.issue: (1) May the monetary awards be recomputed up to the finality of the judgment without violating the immutability of judgments? (2) What legal interest applies to the awards, in light of BSP-MB Circular No. 799?
cases.ruling: The petition was granted. A decision in an illegal dismissal case has two parts: the finding of illegality and its monetary consequences, which are final, and the computation, which is time-bound and may be recomputed. Recomputation up to finality is part of the law (Art. 279, Labor Code) read into the decision and does not violate the immutability of judgments; the employer ran that risk by appealing. On interest, BSP-MB Circular No. 799, effective July 1, 2013, lowered the legal rate for loans or forbearance of money, goods or credits and the rate allowed in judgments, absent stipulation, from 12% to 6% a year, applied prospectively only. The Court modified the Eastern Shipping guidelines accordingly: 6% from default for loans or forbearance without stipulation; 6% at the court's discretion for other obligations, from demand or judgment depending on certainty; and 6% from finality until satisfaction. Judgments final before July 1, 2013 are not disturbed. Nacar was awarded backwages and separation pay up to May 27, 2002, with 12% interest from May 27, 2002 to June 30, 2013 and 6% from July 1, 2013.
cases.keyDoctrine: From July 1, 2013 (BSP-MB Circular No. 799), absent stipulation, the legal interest for loans or forbearance of money, goods or credits and the rate allowed in judgments is 6% a year, applied prospectively; 12% applies only until June 30, 2013. The modified Eastern Shipping guidelines: (1) loan or forbearance, no stipulation: 6% from judicial or extrajudicial demand; interest due earns legal interest from judicial demand; (2) other obligations: 6% at the court's discretion, from demand if reasonably certain, otherwise from judgment, on the amount finally adjudged; (3) from finality of a money judgment until satisfaction: 6%. Judgments final before July 1, 2013 are not disturbed.

cases.name: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In 2007, Lara's Gifts & Decors bought industrial and construction materials worth ₱1,263,104.22 from Midtown Industrial Sales on a 60-day credit term; the sales invoices stated that 24% interest a year would be charged on overdue accounts. Its postdated checks, and the replacement checks, bounced. Midtown made an extrajudicial demand on January 22, 2008 and sued on February 5, 2008. Lara's Gifts admitted the purchases but claimed the materials were substandard. The trial court ordered it to pay the principal with 24% interest from judicial demand until full payment, and ₱50,000 attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals affirmed.
cases.issue: (1) Were the sales invoices admissible and the claim proved? (2) Is the 24% stipulated interest valid, and does it apply until full payment or only until finality of judgment? (3) What interest applies to the interest due?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed with modification. Lara's Gifts did not specifically deny under oath the genuineness and due execution of the invoices, so they were deemed admitted; it failed to prove that the materials were substandard. The 24% interest stated in the invoices was valid and binding on an established company that had long dealt with Midtown. The stipulated interest, unless excessive or unconscionable, is the law between the parties and applies until full payment; the legal interest applies only in the absence of stipulated interest (Arts. 2209, 1159, 1956). There is no compounding unless expressly agreed or mandated by law. The Court distinguished Article 2209 (loans or forbearance, mandatory interest) from Articles 2210-2211 (other obligations, discretionary interest), held that P.D. 116 amended the legal rate in Article 2209, and further modified the Eastern Shipping and Nacar guidelines. It ordered 24% interest from the extrajudicial demand until full payment, legal interest under Article 2212 on the accrued interest from judicial demand (12% to June 30, 2013, then 6%), and 6% on the attorney's fees from finality. On reconsideration, in a Resolution of September 20, 2022, the Court modified this Decision: it held the contract a sale of goods on credit, not a loan or forbearance, restated the guidelines, and deleted the award of legal interest on the 24% interest.
cases.keyDoctrine: A stipulated interest rate, unless excessive or unconscionable, is the law between the parties and applies until full payment; legal interest applies only in the absence of stipulated interest. Interest is not compounded unless expressly stipulated or mandated by law. Article 2209 (obligations to pay a sum of money: interest is mandatory) differs from Articles 2210-2211 (other obligations: interest is discretionary). The genuineness and due execution of an actionable document are deemed admitted unless specifically denied under oath. Note: modified on reconsideration by the Resolution of September 20, 2022.

cases.name: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In its August 28, 2019 Decision, the Court ordered Lara's Gifts & Decors to pay Midtown Industrial Sales the ₱1,263,104.22 price of materials bought on a 60-day credit term, with the 24% annual interest stated in the sales invoices from the extrajudicial demand until full payment, plus legal interest on the accrued 24% interest from judicial demand, and attorney's fees with interest. Lara's Gifts moved for reconsideration, repeating its earlier arguments and claiming that the legal interest on the 24% compensatory interest was excessive. Midtown itself had never appealed the trial court's judgment, which awarded only the principal with 24% interest and attorney's fees.
cases.issue: Was the imposition of legal interest on the 24% compensatory interest proper?
cases.ruling: The motion was partly granted. The Court explained that interest is of two kinds: conventional interest, the agreed price for the use of money, which must be expressly stipulated in writing; and compensatory interest, the indemnity for delay in paying a sum of money, which is allowed by law even without a promise and may be stipulated through a penal clause. The Eastern Shipping and Nacar rules govern only compensatory interest. Stipulated rates, conventional or compensatory, are subject to the unconscionability standard; a stipulated rate more than twice the prevailing legal rate is suspect, and the creditor must show it is required by market conditions. But that standard does not apply to interest on interest under Article 2212, which is fixed by law. The Court restated the guidelines for loans or forbearance and for other obligations, liquidated or unliquidated. Applying them, it held the transaction a sale of goods on credit, not a loan or forbearance, and the 24% a compensatory interest under Article 2209. Although Article 2212 could apply, the award of legal interest on the 24% interest was deleted, because Midtown did not appeal and the trial court's judgment had become final as to it, so granting more on Lara's Gifts' appeal was ultra vires.
cases.keyDoctrine: Conventional interest (the price for the use of money, which must be expressly stipulated in writing) differs from compensatory interest (indemnity for delay, allowed by law, or stipulated as a penalty); the Eastern Shipping and Nacar rules govern compensatory interest. Stipulated rates may be reduced if unconscionable; a rate more than twice the prevailing legal rate is suspect, and the creditor must justify it. Interest on interest under Article 2212 is fixed by law and is not subject to the unconscionability standard. A party who did not appeal cannot obtain affirmative relief greater than the judgment on the other party's appeal.

cases.name: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Simex International, a food exporter that bought most of its products on credit, deposited ₱100,000 in its checking account with Traders Royal Bank, but the bank failed to credit the deposit. Eight checks Simex issued to suppliers and others were dishonored for insufficient funds. Suppliers sent demand letters threatening prosecution, withheld deliveries, and one canceled Simex's credit line. The bank corrected the error only on June 17, 1981, about a week after Simex complained and 23 days after the deposit, without explaining the error. Simex sued for moral and exemplary damages. The trial court found the bank negligent but awarded only ₱20,000 nominal damages and attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that bad faith, the essential ingredient of moral damages, was not proved.
cases.issue: Is Simex entitled to moral and exemplary damages for the bank's negligence?
cases.ruling: Yes. The bank's initial carelessness, aggravated by its lack of promptness in repairing the error, was gross negligence if not wanton bad faith. Simex's credit line was canceled, its orders held, its business declined and its reputation tarnished. Moral damages compensate, not penalize; their amount need not be proved with exactness, since under Article 2216 no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary, and the amount is left to the court's discretion. A corporation is as a rule not entitled to moral damages, since it cannot feel physical suffering or mental anguish, except where its good reputation is debased, resulting in social humiliation, as here. Nominal damages (Art. 2221) vindicate a right, not indemnify a loss, so since a loss was shown, moral damages of ₱20,000 were awarded in their place. Because a bank, as a business affected with public interest, must treat its depositors' accounts with meticulous care given their fiduciary relationship, its ineptness was wanton under Article 2232, and ₱50,000 exemplary damages were imposed.
cases.keyDoctrine: Moral damages compensate, not penalize; no proof of pecuniary loss is needed (Art. 2216), and the amount is left to the court's discretion. A corporation is generally not entitled to moral damages, except where its good reputation is debased, resulting in social humiliation. Nominal damages vindicate a violated right and are not proper where a loss is shown. A bank, being impressed with public interest and in a fiduciary relationship with its depositors, must treat their accounts with meticulous care; gross negligence in handling them may warrant moral and exemplary damages.

cases.name: Makabali, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Georgina Makabali, a new medical graduate, and her sister Lourdes, a schoolteacher, bought a Hong Kong package tour from Baron Travel Corporation, which assured them of a tour group, a tour guide, a send-off at the airport and a booking at the President Hotel. None of it happened: no group or representative met them, the supposed tour guide turned out to be a stranger traveling on his own, nobody met them in Hong Kong, and the hotel had no booking. They tagged along with another tour group, paid for their own meals while others had prepaid ones, and lived on sidewalk hot dogs and fruit to save their limited funds. Only on the fourth day of the five-day tour did Baron arrange to pay their bills, and it ignored their complaint on their return. They sued for ₱30,000 moral and ₱6,000 exemplary damages; the trial court awarded ₱500, and the Court of Appeals ₱5,000 as moral and exemplary damages and ₱1,000 attorney's fees.
cases.issue: Are the petitioners entitled to more than ₱5,000 in moral and exemplary damages?
cases.ruling: Yes. There is no hard and fast rule for a fair amount of moral damages; each case depends on its own circumstances. Moral damages (Art. 2217) are incapable of pecuniary estimation; exemplary damages (Art. 2229), though not recoverable as a matter of right and needing no proof, require the plaintiff first to show entitlement to moral, temperate or compensatory damages. The two have different natures and purposes, so separate awards are proper. The claimant must prove the factual basis of the damages and its causal connection to the defendant's acts, and moral damages must be specifically prayed for. Moral damages are not meant to enrich, but to restore the spiritual status quo ante, and must be proportionate to the suffering. Given the petitioners' social standing, their humiliation and anxiety, and the travel agency's wanton disregard of their rights, ₱5,000 was minimal; but since their complaint limited the claim to ₱35,000, the award was raised to ₱35,000 in moral and exemplary damages and ₱5,000 attorney's fees.
cases.keyDoctrine: Moral damages (Art. 2217) are incapable of pecuniary estimation, but the claimant must prove their factual basis and causal connection to the defendant's acts, and they must be specifically prayed for. They are not meant to enrich, but to restore the spiritual status quo ante, proportionate to the suffering. Exemplary damages are not a matter of right and need not be proved, but the plaintiff must first show entitlement to moral, temperate or compensatory damages. Moral and exemplary damages differ in nature and purpose and are awarded separately. The award may not exceed what the complaint prayed for.

cases.name: Raagas, et al. v. Traya, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: The spouses Raagas sued the owners and the driver of a truck that ran over and killed their three-year-old son in MacArthur, Leyte, claiming actual damages of ₱10,000, moral, nominal and corrective damages, and attorney's fees. In their answer, the defendants denied reckless driving, claimed the child ran into the truck, invoked due diligence in selecting and supervising the driver, and stated that they had no knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to the damages alleged. On the plaintiffs' motion, the trial court rendered judgment on the pleadings, reasoning that the defendants had not denied that the truck lacked a current registration plate, and awarded ₱10,000 for the death, ₱2,000 moral damages, ₱1,000 actual damages and attorney's fees.
cases.issue: Was the judgment on the pleadings proper?
cases.ruling: No. The judgment was set aside and the case remanded for trial. The defendants' averment that they had no knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to the damages, with their claim that the death was due to an unforeseen event or the fault of the child or his parents, tendered a valid issue. Even if the amounts of damages alleged in a complaint are not specifically denied, the damages are not deemed admitted. Actual damages must be proved; a court cannot rely on speculation, conjecture or guesswork as to their fact and amount. And although an allegation is not necessary for moral damages, the claimant must still satisfactorily prove the factual basis of the damage and its causal relation to the defendant's acts. A full-blown trial was needed.
cases.keyDoctrine: Damages are not deemed admitted even if the amounts alleged in the complaint are not specifically denied; an answer stating lack of knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief tenders a valid issue. Actual damages must be proved and cannot rest on speculation, conjecture or guesswork. For moral damages, the claimant must satisfactorily prove the existence of the factual basis of the damage and its causal relation to the defendant's acts. So a claim for damages generally cannot be decided by judgment on the pleadings.

cases.name: San Miguel Brewery, Inc. v. Magno
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: San Miguel Brewery stopped paying Butuan City's taxes on its sale of beer and soft drinks. After repeated demands, the City Treasurer, Francisco Magno, with the Mayor's approval, issued a warrant of distraint and levy under a city ordinance and seized two of the company's delivery trucks. The company sued Magno in his personal capacity for the trucks' release and damages, alleging the seizure was without authority and for reasons unknown to it, although it had been told in writing which ordinance he relied on. Magno counterclaimed for ₱40,000 moral and ₱10,000 exemplary damages and attorney's fees for the shock and humiliation of being sued, but presented no evidence. The trial court dismissed the complaint and awarded Magno ₱2,000 damages and ₱1,000 attorney's fees.
cases.issue: (1) Is the City Treasurer personally liable for damages? (2) Was the award of damages to the City Treasurer on his counterclaim proper?
cases.ruling: The decision was modified. Magno issued the warrant in his capacity as City Treasurer, under an ordinance authorizing it, and was not shown to have acted in bad faith; a public officer merely performing a duty enjoined by law cannot be made to answer personally for damages. The validity of the ordinance could not be raised for the first time on appeal or collaterally. On the counterclaim, moral damages require pleading and proof of moral suffering, mental anguish, fright and the like; though no proof of pecuniary loss is needed (Art. 2216), the claimant must satisfactorily prove the factual basis of the damages (Art. 2217) and its causal connection to the defendant's acts. Since Magno presented no evidence, the ₱2,000 damages were set aside. Nor could it be exemplary damages: a complaint found unmeritorious, or filed against the wrong party, does not justify a penalty on the right to litigate. But since he was sued personally for acts done in his official duty and had to hire counsel, attorney's fees of ₱2,000 and ₱100 nominal damages were just and equitable.
cases.keyDoctrine: Moral damages require pleading and proof of moral suffering, mental anguish, fright and the like; no proof of pecuniary loss is needed, but the factual basis of the damages and its causal connection to the defendant's acts must be satisfactorily proved. Filing an unmeritorious suit, or suing the wrong party, does not by itself justify moral or exemplary damages, since no penalty should be placed on the right to litigate. A public officer who acts in good faith in performing a duty enjoined by law is not personally liable for damages.

cases.name: Tulfo v. People, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In four columns in the tabloid Remate in 1999, columnist Erwin Tulfo accused Atty. Carlos "Ding" So of the Bureau of Customs of corruption and called him insulting names. Tulfo admitted he did not know Atty. So, relied only on one unnamed source, and did no further research. Tulfo and the tabloid's managing editor, national editor, city editor and publishing company president were convicted of four counts of libel and ordered to pay, jointly and severally, ₱800,000 actual damages, ₱1,000,000 moral damages and ₱500,000 exemplary damages. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Before the Supreme Court (in G.R. Nos. 161032 and 161176), Tulfo invoked qualified privilege, and the editors and publisher claimed they had no participation in the articles.
cases.issue: (1) Are the petitioners guilty of libel? (2) Were the damages properly awarded?
cases.ruling: The petitions were dismissed, with modifications. The qualified privilege defense was raised only on appeal, and Tulfo did not exercise press freedom responsibly: he relied on an unnamed source without verification. Under Article 360 of the Revised Penal Code, the editors and publisher are equally liable with the author. As first-time offenders, the penalty was reduced to a fine of ₱6,000 for each count. On damages, actual damages require proof of pecuniary loss (Art. 2199); none was shown, so the ₱800,000 was deleted. Moral damages compensate injuries such as besmirched reputation and wounded feelings; they require an injury that sprang from a case in Articles 2219 or 2220, with a causal relation between the act and the injury. Libel falls squarely under Article 2219(7), and moral damages may be awarded even without actual damages; the Court noted the impact of the libel on the victim's family, so the ₱1,000,000 moral damages stood. Exemplary damages were deleted because no aggravating circumstance attended the crime (Art. 2230).
cases.keyDoctrine: Moral damages may be recovered in cases of libel, slander or any other form of defamation (Art. 2219(7)), and may be awarded even in the absence of actual or compensatory damages. They require that (1) injury was suffered and (2) it sprang from a case in Articles 2219 or 2220, with the act as the proximate cause of the injury. Actual damages require proof of pecuniary loss (Art. 2199). In crimes, exemplary damages require an aggravating circumstance (Art. 2230).

cases.name: Guilatco v. City of Dagupan, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In 1978, Florentina Guilatco, a court interpreter, fell into an open manhole on a sidewalk of Perez Boulevard in Dagupan City, a national road, while about to board a tricycle; the hole was only partly covered by a concrete flower pot. Her right leg was fractured; she was hospitalized, operated on, used crutches for a long time, could not work for a year, and changed from a jovial person to a depressed one. The City Engineer, who was also the ex-officio Highway Engineer, admitted that he supervised the maintenance of the manholes through maintenance personnel detailed to the city. The trial court ordered the city to pay actual damages, ₱150,000 moral damages, ₱50,000 exemplary damages and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the city had no control or supervision over the national road.
cases.issue: (1) Is the city liable under Article 2189 for an injury on a national road? (2) Were the damages properly awarded?
cases.ruling: The trial court's decision was reinstated with reduced amounts. Under Article 2189, provinces, cities and municipalities are liable for death or injuries caused by the defective condition of roads, streets and other public works under their control or supervision; the road need not belong to them. The city charter gave the city supervision over the sidewalk, exercised through the City Engineer, whose salary came mainly from the city and who directed the maintenance personnel. Actual damages for medical expenses were limited to the ₱8,053.65 proved, since a court cannot rely on speculation or guesswork. Moral damages may be awarded without proof of pecuniary loss; the Court listed as considerations that the defendant's acts be the proximate cause, that there be satisfactory proof of the factual basis, and that the case be one enumerated in the Civil Code. Her physical suffering and mental anguish were proved, but ₱150,000 was excessive since her handicap was not permanent; it was reduced to ₱20,000. Exemplary damages were proper as a warning to cities to cover open manholes, but reduced to ₱10,000. Execution pending appeal had been premature.
cases.keyDoctrine: Under Article 2189, a province, city or municipality is liable for injuries caused by the defective condition of roads, streets, bridges, public buildings and other public works under its control or supervision, even if it does not own them. Actual damages are limited to the amount proved. Moral damages need no proof of pecuniary loss, but the defendant's act must be the proximate cause, the factual basis must be satisfactorily proved, and the case must be one enumerated in the Civil Code; the amount must not be excessive.

cases.name: Filinvest Credit Corporation v. Mendez
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Ivan Mendez bought a Ford Cortina on installment, secured by a promissory note and chattel mortgage assigned to Filinvest Credit Corporation. He missed the February, March and April 1976 installments; the check he gave to cover them bounced, and Filinvest sued for replevin and the balance under the acceleration clause. The check later cleared on redeposit, but the court's seizure order was carried out and the car was taken from Mendez's house. Filinvest released the car after he paid the April to June installments and ₱1,894.80 repossession expenses, and it moved to dismiss its case. Mendez then sued Filinvest, claiming the seizure was illegal and that he was humiliated before a visitor and the people at a seminar. The trial court ordered Filinvest to return the repossession expenses and to pay ₱80,000 moral damages and attorney's fees; the appellate court affirmed.
cases.issue: Is Mendez entitled to the return of the repossession expenses, moral damages and attorney's fees?
cases.ruling: No; the complaint was dismissed. A check produces the effect of payment only when cashed (Art. 1249), so the bounced check did not cure the default, and Filinvest had a valid cause of action when it sued. The repossession expenses were for Mendez's account, since he should have surrendered the car upon valid demand. There was no basis for attorney's fees: they are improper on the sole basis of an adverse decision or where the party acted in good faith. Moral damages cannot be awarded in the absence of a wrongful act or omission, fraud or bad faith; when an action is filed in good faith there should be no penalty on the right to litigate, and error alone is not a ground for moral damages. Filinvest's willingness to release the car on payment of only the overdue installments and its voluntary dismissal of its case showed a lack of fraud or bad faith, and the car was in fact seized at Mendez's residence, not before his visitor.
cases.keyDoctrine: Moral damages cannot be awarded in the absence of a wrongful act or omission, or of fraud or bad faith; the exercise of a right within legal bounds, and an action filed in good faith, do not give rise to moral damages, since there should be no penalty on the right to litigate, and error alone is not a ground for them. Attorney's fees are not awarded on the sole basis of an adverse decision. A check produces the effect of payment only when cashed (Art. 1249).

cases.name: Lopez, et al. v. Pan American World Airways
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Then Senate President Pro Tempore Fernando Lopez, his wife, his daughter and his son-in-law had confirmed first-class reservations on Pan Am's Tokyo-San Francisco flight of May 24, 1960 and paid for first-class tickets. A Pan Am employee had mistakenly cancelled their reservations a month earlier; the airline's reservations supervisor learned of it but deliberately withheld the information, hoping for last-minute cancellations, and tickets marked "OK" were issued. In Tokyo, Pan Am refused them first-class seats, and because of pressing engagements they traveled tourist class under protest; Mrs. Lopez, who had been ill, suffered physical discomfort on the 13-hour trip. The employee who made the error was later given a salary increase. The trial court awarded ₱150,000 moral damages, ₱25,000 exemplary damages and attorney's fees.
cases.issue: (1) Did Pan Am breach its contracts in bad faith? (2) What damages are due?
cases.ruling: The judgment was modified, increasing the awards. Pan Am's own evidence showed that, after cancelling the reservations by mistake, it deliberately withheld the cancellation and let the passengers believe their reservations stood; this willful non-disclosure, not the error itself, caused the breach, and it is bad faith, meaning a breach of a known duty through some motive of interest or ill will. Even granting the mistakes, there was negligence so gross and reckless as to amount to malice or bad faith. Moral damages are recoverable in breach of contract where the defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith (Art. 2220); the passengers suffered social humiliation, wounded feelings, serious anxiety and mental anguish, since it is humiliating to be compelled to travel tourist class despite first-class tickets. Considering their standing, the Court awarded ₱200,000 moral damages (₱100,000 to the Senator, ₱50,000 to Mrs. Lopez, ₱25,000 each to the Montelibanos), ₱75,000 exemplary damages to deter similar breaches, 6% interest, and ₱50,000 attorney's fees under the written contract.
cases.keyDoctrine: Moral damages are recoverable in breach of contract where the defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith (Art. 2220); bad faith is a breach of a known duty through some motive of interest or ill will, and gross and reckless negligence may amount to bad faith. Exemplary damages may be added where the defendant acted in a wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive or malevolent manner (Arts. 2229, 2232). The amount of moral damages may consider the social, official and financial standing of the offended parties and the business and financial position of the offender.

cases.name: Gutierrez v. Villegas, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Adela Santos Gutierrez, a niece and one of the heirs of Irene Santos, signed a Tagalog deed selling her share in the estate to her sister Rizalina Santos Rivera for ₱50,000, payable in two installments, and a manifestation informing the probate court of the sale. She later sued to annul the sale for fraud and mistake, claiming she thought she was signing a loan document, could not read it without her eyeglasses, and was misled about the estate's value; alternatively, she sought rescission of the sale as a partition for lesion. The widower Jose D. Villegas and Rizalina counterclaimed for ₱200,000 moral and exemplary damages and ₱50,000 attorney's fees for the allegedly malicious suit. The trial court dismissed both the complaint and the counterclaim, and both sides appealed.
cases.issue: (1) Was the plaintiff's consent vitiated by fraud or mistake, or the sale rescissible for lesion? (2) Are the defendants entitled to damages and attorney's fees on their counterclaim?
cases.ruling: The decision was affirmed. Fraud may be proved by circumstantial evidence but is not to be lightly inferred; the plaintiff's uncorroborated testimony did not overcome the presumption of good faith and regularity, and her own conduct (securing a residence certificate, accepting the first installment) belied her claim. The price was not grossly inadequate, and even if the sale were deemed a partition under Article 1082, the lesion was less than the one-fourth required by Article 1098. On the counterclaim, damages and attorney's fees are primarily in the trial court's discretion, which found no facts to support them. The allegations of fraud in the complaint were privileged; failure to seek an amicable settlement among relatives under Article 222 had not been pleaded; there was no proof of mental suffering on which to base moral damages; and the absence of moral, temperate or compensatory damages blocks the grant of exemplary damages (Art. 2234).
cases.keyDoctrine: Moral damages need proof of mental suffering; without it, none can be awarded. Exemplary damages cannot be granted in the absence of moral, temperate or compensatory damages (Art. 2234). Allegations in a complaint are privileged, so filing a suit that fails does not by itself support a counterclaim for damages. Fraud is not lightly inferred and must overcome the presumption of good faith. A partition may be rescinded for lesion only if an heir receives less, by at least one-fourth, than his share (Art. 1098).

cases.name: Ramos, et al. v. Ramos, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Martin Ramos left a large landed estate in Negros Occidental, settled in an intestate proceeding that ended in 1913–1914 with a court-approved partition in which his natural children received only cash, while the legitimate children took the lands. In 1957, more than forty years later, some of the natural children and their heirs sued the heirs of a legitimate son for reconveyance of their shares, claiming the lands were held in trust for them and that the partition was unfair and irregular. The defendants pleaded res judicata and prescription and counterclaimed for ₱50,000 moral damages and attorney's fees, claiming the suit was baseless and filed in bad faith. The trial court dismissed the complaint on the ground of res judicata but did not act on the counterclaim; both sides appealed.
cases.issue: (1) Is the action for reconveyance barred? (2) Are the defendants entitled to moral damages, attorney's fees and exemplary damages on their counterclaim?
cases.ruling: The judgment was affirmed, and the counterclaim dismissed. No express trust was proved, and an action to enforce an implied (resulting or constructive) trust may be barred by prescription and laches; the action, filed forty years after it accrued, was barred by prescription and res judicata, since the final decree of distribution vests title. On the counterclaim, moral damages may be recovered only in the cases listed in Articles 2219 and 2220 (and 1764 and 2206) or analogous cases; this litigation was not one of them, and the worries and anxiety of a defendant in a suit not maliciously instituted are not the moral damages the law contemplates. The adverse result of an action does not make it wrongful, for no penalty should be placed on the right to litigate. Attorney's fees are recoverable only in the cases in Article 2208; the plaintiffs honestly believed they had a good cause of action and acted in good faith, so neither paragraph 4 (clearly unfounded suit) nor paragraph 11 applied. Exemplary damages, raised only on appeal, could not be granted since no compensatory or moral damages were awarded.
cases.keyDoctrine: Moral damages may be recovered only in the cases enumerated in Articles 2219 and 2220 (and 1764 and 2206) or analogous cases; the worries and anxiety of a defendant in a suit not maliciously instituted are not compensable. The adverse result of an action does not per se make it wrongful; no penalty on the right to litigate. Attorney's fees need a specific ground under Article 2208, and an adverse decision does not ipso facto justify them. Exemplary damages require an award of compensatory or moral damages. An action to enforce an implied trust may be barred by prescription and laches.

cases.name: Galang v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Beatriz Galang and Rodrigo Quinit, both of age and from Sison, Pangasinan, were engaged, though Rodrigo's parents opposed the marriage. From April 27 to May 9, 1955, they lived as husband and wife in a house at Colorado Falls, Tuba, Mountain Province; then Rodrigo left and never returned. Galang sued Rodrigo and his father for breach of promise to marry, claiming the father had arranged the marriage and then had his son taken away. The trial court ordered both defendants to pay actual damages of ₱275, ₱5,000 moral damages and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals found her evidence on the father's role not credible, absolved the father, and, as to Rodrigo, eliminated the moral damages and attorney's fees.
cases.issue: (1) May the Supreme Court review the Court of Appeals' findings on credibility? (2) Are moral damages recoverable for breach of promise to marry?
cases.ruling: The decision of the Court of Appeals was affirmed. Its findings on the credibility of the evidence are beyond the Supreme Court's power of review on appeal by certiorari and are conclusive. On moral damages, the claim that moral damages for breach of promise to marry are collectible had already been settled against the plaintiff in Hermosisima v. Court of Appeals (L-14628, September 30, 1960).
cases.keyDoctrine: A breach of promise to marry is not, by itself, a ground for moral damages; the question was settled in Hermosisima v. Court of Appeals. Findings of the Court of Appeals on the credibility of evidence are conclusive on the Supreme Court on appeal by certiorari.

cases.name: Mercado, et al. v. Lira, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In 1951, a bus of the Laguna Transportation Company, owned and operated by Gonzalo Mercado and others, blew a tire while overspeeding near Calamba, Laguna, and fell into a ravine. Among the passengers, Ramon Lira, Jr., 24, was killed and Nita Lira was injured. His parents and Nita Lira sued the operators. After the Court of Appeals' rulings, the parents were awarded damages for the death, loss of earning capacity, ₱4,000 moral damages for mental anguish and ₱4,000 attorney's fees; Nita Lira's moral damages for her injuries were eliminated. The operators (G.R. Nos. L-13328-29) argued that the moral damages to the parents should be reduced to a nominal ₱500, and Nita Lira (G.R. No. L-13358) argued that her case was analogous to a quasi-delict causing physical injuries under Article 2219.
cases.issue: (1) Was the ₱4,000 moral damages to the parents of the deceased passenger proper? (2) Is an injured passenger entitled to moral damages for breach of contract of carriage through the carrier's negligence?
cases.ruling: The Court of Appeals was affirmed.
