questions.prompt: In Eastern Shipping Lines v. Court of Appeals, why does interest run from the finality of a judgment awarding a sum of money until its satisfaction?

choices.A: Because that interim period is deemed equivalent to a forbearance of credit.
choices.B: Because the judgment debtor is presumed to be in bad faith.
choices.C: Because the parties are deemed to have agreed to it.
choices.D: Because it is a penalty for appealing the case.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said legal interest applies "from such finality until its satisfaction, this interim period being deemed to be by then an equivalent to a forbearance of credit." **B, C and D are wrong:** none is the reason given. **Bar trap:** this rule applies whether the obligation was a loan (rule 1) or not (rule 2). The 12% rate then used was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013; check the current rate.

source.caseTitle: Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, the rules of thumb on interest (rule II.3)
source.excerpt: 3. When the judgment of the court awarding a sum of money becomes final and executory, the rate of legal interest, whether the case falls under paragraph 1 or paragraph 2, above, shall be 12% per annum from such finality until its satisfaction, this interim period being deemed to be by then an equivalent to a forbearance of credit.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Eastern Shipping Lines v. Court of Appeals, the Court noted a consistent holding in earlier cases on the Central Bank Circular imposing 12% interest. To what did that circular apply?

choices.A: To all monetary judgments, whatever the cause of action.
choices.B: Only to loans or forbearance of money, goods or credits, and to judgments involving them.
choices.C: Only to actions for damages arising from quasi-delicts.
choices.D: Only to expropriation cases.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court observed "a consistent holding that the Central Bank Circular imposing the 12% interest per annum applies only to loans or forbearance of money, goods or credits, as well as to judgments involving such loan or forbearance," while the Civil Code's 6% governs indemnities for damage from breach or delay in obligations in general. **A is wrong:** other monetary judgments were outside it. **C and D are wrong:** damages for quasi-delicts and just compensation in expropriation (National Power Corporation v. Angas) took the 6% rate. **Bar trap:** classify the obligation first: loan or forbearance, or damages.

source.caseTitle: Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, reconciliation of earlier rulings (the first group of cases)
source.excerpt: It is easily discernible in these cases that there has been a consistent holding that the Central Bank Circular imposing the 12% interest per annum applies only to loans or forbearance of money, goods or credits, as well as to judgments involving such loan or forbearance of money, goods or credits, and that the 6% interest under the Civil Code governs when the transaction involves the payment of indemnities in the concept of damage arising from the breach or a delay in the performance of obligations in general.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: How did the Court modify the interest award in Eastern Shipping Lines v. Court of Appeals?

choices.A: 12% from the filing of the complaint until fully paid.
choices.B: 6% from the filing of the complaint until fully paid.
choices.C: No interest at all, since the claim was unliquidated.
choices.D: 6% from the trial court's decision, and 12% from the finality of the Supreme Court's decision until payment.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court held that "the legal interest to be paid is SIX PERCENT (6%) on the amount due computed from the decision, dated 03 February 1988, of the court a quo," and that "[a] TWELVE PERCENT (12%) interest, in lieu of SIX PERCENT (6%), shall be imposed on such amount upon finality of this decision until the payment thereof." **A is the lower courts' award, which was modified. B is wrong:** the claim was unliquidated, so interest ran from the judgment, not the complaint. **C is wrong:** interest runs once the amount is reasonably certain. **Bar trap:** two periods, two rates.

source.caseTitle: Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, the disposition
source.excerpt: WHEREFORE, the petition is partly GRANTED. The appealed decision is AFFIRMED with the MODIFICATION that the legal interest to be paid is SIX PERCENT (6%) on the amount due computed from the decision, dated 03 February 1988, of the court a quo. A TWELVE PERCENT (12%) interest, in lieu of SIX PERCENT (6%), shall be imposed on such amount upon finality of this decision until the payment thereof.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: S agreed to sell a lot to B in a conditional sale. B paid ₱2 million in advance, but S never fulfilled the conditions she undertook. The contract provided only that the down payment would be returned if S failed, and said nothing about interest. After B's written demand, S still kept the money. B sues for the ₱2 million plus 12% interest. S argues that (1) no interest is due since none was stipulated, and (2) at most 6% applies because the contract is a sale, not a loan. Rule on S's arguments, citing Estores v. Spouses Supangan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Both arguments fail. Interest may be imposed without a stipulation, and the rate is that for a forbearance of money (12% when Estores was decided), running from B's demand until full payment.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Estores v. Spouses Supangan, the Court held that under Article 2210, interest may in the court's discretion be allowed upon damages awarded for breach of contract, and the seller was in default from the date of demand. On the rate, the phrase "forbearance of money, goods or credits" has a meaning separate from a loan: it refers to arrangements other than loans where a person acquiesces to the temporary use of his money pending the happening of certain events or the fulfillment of conditions. The buyers parted with their money before the conditions were fulfilled, and the seller's unwarranted withholding of it amounts to a forbearance of money, an involuntary loan, so the rate applicable to a loan applies.
suggestedAnswer.application: B parted with the ₱2 million before S fulfilled the conditions, allowing her the use of it. When the conditions failed and S kept the money despite demand, B was deprived of its use. B is entitled to the return of the principal and to compensation for its use, at the forbearance rate, from the demand.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Interest is due at the forbearance rate from demand. **Bar trap:** a contract that is not a loan can still involve a forbearance of money; do not stop at the name of the contract. Note also that the 12% rate applied in Estores was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013 (BSP Circular No. 799, Nacar v. Gallery Frames); check the current rate.

keyPoints: Interest may be awarded on damages for breach of contract without stipulation (Art. 2210)
Default from the date of demand
Forbearance has a meaning separate from a loan
Forbearance: acquiescing to the temporary use of one's money pending events or conditions
Unwarranted withholding of the money = forbearance, an involuntary loan; the loan rate applies
The 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013

source.caseTitle: Estores v. Spouses Supangan
source.part: Our Ruling, interest at 12% (forbearance of money)
source.excerpt: We sustain the ruling of both the RTC and the CA that it is proper to impose interest notwithstanding the absence of stipulation in the contract. Article 2210 of the Civil Code expressly provides that "[i]nterest may, in the discretion of the court, be allowed upon damages awarded for breach of contract." … We believe however, that the phrase "forbearance of money, goods or credits" is meant to have a separate meaning from a loan, otherwise there would have been no need to add that phrase as a loan is already sufficiently defined in the Civil Code. Forbearance of money, goods or credits should therefore refer to arrangements other than loan agreements, where a person acquiesces to the temporary use of his money, goods or credits pending happening of certain events or fulfillment of certain conditions. In this case, the respondent-spouses parted with their money even before the conditions were fulfilled. They have therefore allowed or granted forbearance to the seller (petitioner) to use their money pending fulfillment of the conditions. They were deprived of the use of their money for the period pending fulfillment of the conditions and when those conditions were breached, they are entitled not only to the return of the principal amount paid, but also to compensation for the use of their money. And the compensation for the use of their money, absent any stipulation, should be the same rate of legal interest applicable to a loan since the use or deprivation of funds is similar to a loan. Petitioner’s unwarranted withholding of the money which rightfully pertains to respondent-spouses amounts to forbearance of money which can be considered as an involuntary loan. Thus, the applicable rate of interest is 12% per annum.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Counsel for a seller who failed to return a buyer's advance payment argues that, under Eastern Shipping Lines v. Court of Appeals, the 6% rate for obligations other than loans applies, and that interest should run only from the judgment. How did the Court in Estores v. Spouses Supangan answer this, and from when did it reckon the interest?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court distinguished Eastern Shipping and Reformina: both were torts cases with no forbearance of money, and the damages claimed could not be established with reasonable certainty when the claim was made. In Estores, there was a forbearance, and the amount (₱3.5 million) and the date of demand were certain, so interest at the forbearance rate ran from the demand until full satisfaction.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Estores v. Spouses Supangan: "Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals and its predecessor case, Reformina v. Tongol both involved torts cases and hence, there was no forbearance of money, goods, or credits. Further, the amount claimed (i.e., damages) could not be established with reasonable certainty at the time the claim was made." Since the date of demand, September 27, 2000, was satisfactorily established during trial, the 12% rate was reckoned from that date until the principal and interest are fully satisfied.
suggestedAnswer.application: The seller's counsel treats every non-loan obligation as falling under the 6% rule. But the obligation to return a definite sum withheld after demand is a forbearance, and the amount was known from the start, so there is no reason to wait for the judgment.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Interest at the forbearance rate from the date of demand. **Bar trap:** interest runs from the judgment only for claims that were not reasonably certain at demand, as in torts; a fixed sum withheld after demand earns interest from the demand.

keyPoints: Eastern Shipping and Reformina were torts cases: no forbearance of money
In those cases, the damages were not reasonably certain when claimed
Here the amount was fixed and the date of demand established at trial
Interest ran from the demand (September 27, 2000) until full satisfaction

source.caseTitle: Estores v. Spouses Supangan
source.part: Our Ruling, distinguishing Eastern Shipping Lines
source.excerpt: Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals and its predecessor case, Reformina v. Tongol both involved torts cases and hence, there was no forbearance of money, goods, or credits. Further, the amount claimed (i.e., damages) could not be established with reasonable certainty at the time the claim was made. Hence, we arrived at a different ruling in those cases. Since the date of demand which is September 27, 2000 was satisfactorily established during trial, then the interest rate of 12% should be reckoned from said date of demand until the principal amount and the interest thereon is fully satisfied.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A buyer forced to sue to recover the advance payment that a defaulting seller refused to return asks for attorney's fees of ₱50,000 plus 20% of whatever is recovered. The seller argues that no attorney's fees are due because the buyer did not win everything it asked for. Are attorney's fees warranted? In what amount? Explain, citing Estores v. Spouses Supangan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, attorney's fees are warranted because the buyer was compelled to litigate to protect its interest, but the award must be reasonable; in Estores the Court fixed it at ₱50,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, attorney's fees may be recovered (2) when the defendant's act or omission has compelled the plaintiff to litigate or to incur expenses to protect his interest, and (11) in any other case where the court deems it just and equitable; in all cases, they must be reasonable. In Estores, the spouses were forced to litigate to recover their money, so they were entitled to attorney's fees, but the Court found ₱50,000 more appropriate, in line with the policy that the award must always be reasonable. The trial court's ₱50,000 plus 20% of the recoverable amount had been found excessive and reduced to ₱100,000 by the Court of Appeals, then further reduced.
suggestedAnswer.application: The seller's refusal to return the money despite demand compelled the buyer to sue. That the buyer did not obtain every amount it asked for does not remove the ground under Article 2208. But the 20% add-on would be excessive.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Attorney's fees of a reasonable amount (₱50,000 in Estores). **Bar trap:** the fact that a party was compelled to litigate justifies the award, but never an unreasonable amount; the court may reduce it.

keyPoints: Art. 2208(2): the defendant's act compelled the plaintiff to litigate to protect his interest
Art. 2208(11): when just and equitable
In all cases, attorney's fees must be reasonable
₱50,000 plus 20% was excessive; reduced to ₱100,000 by the CA, then to ₱50,000

source.caseTitle: Estores v. Spouses Supangan
source.part: Our Ruling, attorney's fees
source.excerpt: In all cases, the attorney’s fees and expenses of litigation must be reasonable. Considering the circumstances of the instant case, we find respondent-spouses entitled to recover attorney’s fees. There is no doubt that they were forced to litigate to protect their interest, i.e., to recover their money. However, we find the amount of ₱50,000.00 more appropriate in line with the policy enunciated in Article 2208 of the Civil Code that the award of attorney’s fees must always be reasonable.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under Estores v. Spouses Supangan, what provision allows a court to impose interest on damages for breach of contract even if the contract is silent on interest?

choices.A: Article 1956 of the Civil Code.
choices.B: Article 2213 of the Civil Code.
choices.C: Article 2208 of the Civil Code.
choices.D: Article 2210 of the Civil Code.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court said: "Article 2210 of the Civil Code expressly provides that '[i]nterest may, in the discretion of the court, be allowed upon damages awarded for breach of contract.'" **A is wrong:** Article 1956 requires a written stipulation for conventional interest, not for interest as damages. **B is wrong:** Article 2213 bars interest on unliquidated claims until reasonably certain. **C is wrong:** Article 2208 governs attorney's fees. **Bar trap:** "no interest without a written stipulation" refers to conventional interest only.

choices.B: loan agreements only, where the debtor is given a period to pay.
choices.C: any obligation to pay damages arising from a quasi-delict.
choices.D: the creditor's waiver of interest.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A final judgment ordered the defendants to render an accounting and inventory of a partnership's assets and to deliver to the plaintiff his one-half share. In execution, the plaintiff added 12% interest on his share of the assets from the time the business closed, arguing that his claim was liquidated because it could be determined by mathematical computation. The court of appeals agreed. Is the plaintiff's claim correct? Explain, citing Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The share in the partnership assets was an unliquidated claim that earns no interest until reasonably determined, and it became liquidated only when the trial court approved the accounting.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Sunga-Chan v. CA, the Court agreed that the partner's share and interest in the assets "partake of an unliquidated claim which, until reasonably determined, shall not earn interest for him." The legal norm for interest to accrue is "reasonably determinable," not determinable by mathematical computation, as the Court of Appeals had declared. The judgment's own directive to render an accounting, inventory and appraisal recognized that the exact share could not be determined with reasonable precision without that process; a liquidated claim cannot validly be asserted without accounting.
suggestedAnswer.application: The plaintiff's share could be fixed only after the inventory and accounting. It became liquidated only upon the trial court's approval of the accounting report, after the computation was submitted, so no interest could be added to it.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: No interest on the share of the assets. **Bar trap:** "capable of mathematical computation" is not the test; the test is whether the amount is reasonably determinable, and an amount that needs an accounting is not.

keyPoints: No interest on an unliquidated claim until reasonably determined (Art. 2213)
The norm is "reasonably determinable", not "determinable by mathematical computation"
The judgment's order to account shows the share could not be fixed without accounting
A liquidated claim cannot be asserted without accounting
The share became liquidated only when the accounting was approved

source.caseTitle: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, first issue (interest on the share of the partnership assets)
source.excerpt: Anent the impasse over the partnership assets, we are inclined to agree with petitioners’ assertion that Chua’s share and interest on such assets partake of an unliquidated claim which, until reasonably determined, shall not earn interest for him. As may be noted, the legal norm for interest to accrue is "reasonably determinable," not, as Chua suggested and the CA declared, determinable by mathematical computation. The Court has certainly not lost sight of the fact that the October 7, 1997 RTC decision clearly directed petitioners to render an accounting, inventory, and appraisal of the partnership assets and then to wind up the partnership affairs by restituting and delivering to Chua his one-half share of the accounted partnership assets. The directive itself is a recognition that the exact share and interest of Chua over the partnership cannot be determined with reasonable precision without going through with the inventory and accounting process. In fine, a liquidated claim cannot validly be asserted without accounting. In net effect, Chua’s interest and share over the partnership asset, exclusive of the goodwill, assumed the nature of a liquidated claim only after the trial court, through its November 6, 2002 resolution, approved the assets inventory and accounting report on such assets.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A trial court's judgment, rendered on March 1, 2010, ordered the defendants to pay the plaintiff his unreceived profits from a partnership business, a fixed amount per month, "with legal rate of interest until fully paid." The judgment became final on March 1, 2012, but the defendants did not pay. Following the approach in Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals, what interest should the profits earn, and for which periods?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The profits should earn 6% a year from the date of the trial court's decision (March 1, 2010) until it became final (March 1, 2012); after that, the total profits with the added interest should earn the forbearance rate (12% in Sunga-Chan) from finality until fully paid.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Sunga-Chan v. CA, applying the Eastern Shipping rules, the Court held that the award of earned but unremitted profits "must earn interest at 6% per annum reckoned from October 7, 1997, the rendition date of the RTC decision, until December 20, 2001, when the said decision became final and executory. Thereafter, the total of the monthly profits inclusive of the add on 6% interest shall earn 12% per annum reckoned from December 20, 2001 until fully paid, as the award for that item is considered to be, by then, equivalent to a forbearance of credit."
suggestedAnswer.application: The profits award does not arise from a loan or forbearance, so the 6% rate under Article 2209 applies until finality. Once the judgment is final and unpaid, the period is treated as a forbearance of credit, and the base for the higher rate includes the 6% interest already earned.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: 6% from the decision to finality; then the forbearance rate on profits plus interest until paid. **Bar trap:** after finality, the higher rate applies to the total, including the 6% interest already accrued. Note that the 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013 (BSP Circular No. 799, Nacar v. Gallery Frames), so the rate for the period after finality must be checked against the current rule.

keyPoints: Profits award: not a loan or forbearance, so 6% (Art. 2209)
6% from the trial court's decision until finality
From finality: 12% on the profits plus the 6% interest added
After finality the award is equivalent to a forbearance of credit
The 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013

source.caseTitle: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, first issue (interest on the unreceived profits)
source.excerpt: Guided by the foregoing rules, the award to Chua of the amount representing earned but unremitted profits, i.e.. PhP 35,000 monthly, from January 1988 until May 30, 1992, must earn interest at 6% per annum reckoned from October 7, 1997, the rendition date of the RTC decision, until December 20, 2001, when the said decision became final and executory. Thereafter, the total of the monthly profits inclusive of the add on 6% interest shall earn 12% per annum reckoned from December 20, 2001 until fully paid, as the award for that item is considered to be, by then, equivalent to a forbearance of credit. Likewise, the PhP 250,000 award, representing the goodwill value of the business, the award of PhP 50,000 for moral and exemplary damages, PhP 25,000 attorney’s fee, and PhP 25,000 litigation fee shall earn 12% per annum from December 20, 2001 until fully paid.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: After their father's death, a widow and her daughter continued a partnership business against the surviving partner's will and refused to account. Held liable to him, they argue that their liability is only joint, so the sheriff could not levy on the daughter's absolute community property with her husband for the whole judgment. Are they correct? Explain, citing Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Their obligation is solidary, and the daughter's absolute community property may answer for it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Sunga-Chan v. CA, the Court held the obligation solidary because (1) continuing the business against the partner's will gave rise to a solidary obligation, the acts not being severable, a case where the nature of the obligation requires solidarity under Article 1207; (2) the duty to remit his share proceeds from the indivisible obligation to account; and (3) the obligation to pay damages and fees is solidary, the petitioners having resisted in bad faith a legitimate claim. The community property is not exempt from execution, and under Article 94 of the Family Code the absolute community is liable for debts contracted by either spouse without the other's consent to the extent the family benefited; the daughter's use of the business assets may reasonably be considered to have been for her and her husband's benefit.
suggestedAnswer.application: It is impossible to draw the line where one petitioner's liability ends and the other's begins, or to quantify how much each misappropriated. The levy on the daughter's community property for the whole obligation was valid.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Solidary liability; the community property answers. **Bar trap:** solidarity is not presumed (Art. 1207), but it exists when the law or the nature of the obligation requires it, as here.

keyPoints: Solidarity only when the obligation states it, or the law or nature of the obligation requires it (Art. 1207)
The acts complained of were not severable; the duty to account was indivisible
Bad-faith resistance to a legitimate claim: damages and fees solidary
Community property not exempt from execution
Art. 94, Family Code: the community answers to the extent the family benefited

source.caseTitle: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, second and third issues (solidary liability, community property)
source.excerpt: For one, the complaint of Chua for winding up of partnership affairs, accounting, appraisal, and recovery of shares and damages is clearly a suit to enforce a solidary or joint and several obligation on the part of petitioners. As it were, the continuance of the business and management of Shellite by petitioners against the will of Chua gave rise to a solidary obligation, the acts complained of not being severable in nature. Indeed, it is well-nigh impossible to draw the line between when the liability of one petitioner ends and the liability of the other starts. In this kind of situation, the law itself imposes solidary obligation. … For the other, the duty of petitioners to remit to Chua his half interest and share of the total partnership assets proceeds from petitioners’ indivisible obligation to render an accounting and inventory of such assets. The need for the imposition of a solidary liability becomes all the more pronounced considering the impossibility of quantifying how much of the partnership assets or profits was misappropriated by each petitioner. And for a third, petitioners’ obligation for the payment of damages and attorney’s and litigation fees ought to be solidary in nature, they having resisted in bad faith a legitimate claim and thus compelled Chua to litigate. … Absent any indication otherwise, the use and appropriation by petitioner Sunga-Chan of the assets of Shellite even after the business was discontinued on May 30, 1992 may reasonably be considered to have been used for her and her husband’s benefit.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals, what is the legal norm for interest to accrue on a claim?

choices.A: The claim must be determinable by mathematical computation.
choices.B: The claim must be stated in the complaint.
choices.C: The claim must be reasonably determinable.
choices.D: The claim must be supported by an official receipt.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said: "the legal norm for interest to accrue is 'reasonably determinable,' not, as Chua suggested and the CA declared, determinable by mathematical computation." **A is wrong:** that is the test the Court rejected. **B and D are wrong:** neither is the norm. **Bar trap:** almost anything can be computed once figures are known; the question is whether the amount was reasonably determinable at the time.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Why did the Court in Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals refuse to disturb the ₱250,000 award for the partner's share in the goodwill?

choices.A: Because the parties, by their own judicial admissions, agreed on that monetary value.
choices.B: Because goodwill is never subject to proof.
choices.C: Because the amount was computed by a certified public accountant.
choices.D: Because goodwill earns no interest.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court noted that "the parties, by their own judicial admissions, agreed on the monetary value, i.e., PhP 250,000, of this item," so the petitioners contradicted themselves in calling it baseless. **B is wrong:** no such rule was stated. **C is wrong:** that was not the reason. **D is wrong:** the goodwill award earned 12% from finality. **Bar trap:** a party cannot dispute an amount it admitted in its own pleadings or reports.

source.caseTitle: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, first issue (the goodwill)
source.excerpt: From the foregoing submitted valuation reports, there can be no dispute about the goodwill earned thru the years by Shellite. In fact, the parties, by their own judicial admissions, agreed on the monetary value, i.e., PhP 250,000, of this item. Clearly then, petitioners contradict themselves when they say that such amount of goodwill is without basis.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: As restated in Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals, which provision governs interest on indemnities in the concept of damages arising from default in the performance of obligations in general, not involving a loan or forbearance?

choices.A: Article 2209 of the Civil Code, prescribing a yearly 6% interest.
choices.B: Central Bank Circular No. 416, prescribing 12%.
choices.C: Article 1956 of the Civil Code.
choices.D: Article 2208 of the Civil Code.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said that for "transactions involving payment of indemnities in the concept of damages arising from default in the performance of obligations in general and/or for money judgment not involving a loan or forbearance of money, goods, or credit, the governing provision is Art. 2209 of the Civil Code prescribing a yearly 6% interest." **B is wrong:** the circular applied to loans and forbearances. **C is wrong:** Article 1956 concerns stipulated interest. **D is wrong:** Article 2208 concerns attorney's fees. **Bar trap:** classify the obligation before picking the rate.

source.caseTitle: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, first issue (the rates under Reformina)
source.excerpt: And for transactions involving payment of indemnities in the concept of damages arising from default in the performance of obligations in general and/or for money judgment not involving a loan or forbearance of money, goods, or credit, the governing provision is Art. 2209 of the Civil Code prescribing a yearly 6% interest.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals, the property of the judgment debtor was sold at auction to the judgment creditor for ₱8 million, but the Court reduced his legitimate claim to ₱5,529,392.52. What did the Court order?

choices.A: The auction sale was annulled.
choices.B: The excess was forfeited in favor of the State.
choices.C: Subject to the creditor's payment of the excess (₱2,470,607.48) to the debtor, the confirmation of the sale and the writ of possession were affirmed.
choices.D: The creditor kept the property without paying anything more.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said that "Chua owes petitioner Sunga-Chan the amount of PhP 2,470,607.48, representing the excess of the purchase price over his legitimate claims," and affirmed the confirmation of the final deed of sale and the writ of possession "subject to the payment by Chua" of that amount. **A is wrong:** the levy and sale were valid. **B and D are wrong:** the excess belongs to the debtor. **Bar trap:** a creditor who bids more than his claim must pay the difference.

source.caseTitle: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, the disposition

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A passenger sent an airline an extrajudicial demand on August 1, 2003 for damages for breach of contract of carriage. The trial court, in its judgment of April 25, 2007, awarded him actual damages, ₱1 million moral damages, exemplary damages and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals imposed 6% legal interest from the date of the extrajudicial demand. The airline argues that interest should run only from the trial court's judgment. Is the airline correct? Explain, citing Air France v. De Camilis.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. The 6% legal interest runs from April 25, 2007, the date of the trial court's judgment, not from the extrajudicial demand; from the finality of the decision, the higher rate applies until full satisfaction.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Air France v. De Camilis, the Court applied Eastern Shipping Lines: for an obligation not constituting a loan or forbearance, no interest is adjudged on unliquidated claims or damages except when or until the demand can be established with reasonable certainty; when such certainty cannot be established at the time of demand, interest runs only from the date of the judgment. The Court held that the interest "shall be reckoned from April 25, 2007 when the RTC rendered its judgment, not from the time of respondent's extrajudicial demand. This must be so as it was at the time the RTC rendered its judgment that the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained."
suggestedAnswer.application: The passenger's claims for moral and exemplary damages and attorney's fees could not be fixed with reasonable certainty when he made his demand; their amounts were set only when the trial court decided. So interest runs from that judgment, on all sums awarded.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The airline is correct on the starting date. **Bar trap:** the date of the extrajudicial demand applies only when the amount was already reasonably certain then; damages left to the court's discretion become certain only on judgment. Note too that the 12% rate after finality was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013; check the current rate.

keyPoints: Breach of contract of carriage: not a loan or forbearance, so 6%
No interest on unliquidated damages until they can be established with reasonable certainty
Here the damages were reasonably ascertained only when the trial court rendered judgment
Interest runs from the trial court's judgment, not from the extrajudicial demand
From finality, the higher rate until full satisfaction, on all sums awarded

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, discussion of the legal interest
source.excerpt: Pursuant to this ruling, the legal interest is 6% p.a. and it shall be reckoned from April 25, 2007 when the RTC rendered its judgment, not from the time of respondent’s extrajudicial demand. This must be so as it was at the time the RTC rendered its judgment that the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained. Then, from the time this decision becomes final and executory, the interest rate shall be 12% p.a. until full satisfaction.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A passenger was refused entry at a transit stop because he did not have the required transit visa. He sues the airline, claiming that its agents should have told him about the visa. The evidence also shows that, afterwards, the airline's agents rudely refused his requests, falsely reported him as a security threat, refused to honor his confirmed flights and treated him with verbal abuse. Is the airline liable? Explain, citing Air France v. De Camilis.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The airline is not liable for the refused entry, because the passenger is responsible for having the correct travel documents; but it is liable for damages for the bad-faith treatment by its agents.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Air France v. De Camilis, the Court of Appeals ruled that it was the passenger, and not the airline, who was responsible for having the correct travel documents, but that this did not absolve the airline from liability for damages. It found that the airline's agents "repeatedly subjected respondent to very poor service, verbal abuse and abject lack of respect and consideration," so the airline was guilty of bad faith. It therefore charged the passenger with his expenses for the Moscow leg, but held the airline liable for his expenses from the false security-threat report to the dishonored Paris-Manila reservation, and affirmed moral damages and attorney's fees. The Supreme Court denied the airline's petition.
suggestedAnswer.application: The missing visa is the passenger's own fault, so his losses from being refused entry are his. But the later abuse by the airline's agents is the airline's breach, committed in bad faith, and supports actual damages for the expenses it caused, as well as moral and exemplary damages.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Liable, but only for the consequences of its agents' bad faith. **Bar trap:** the passenger's fault on one point does not excuse the carrier's separate bad-faith acts; separate the losses by cause.

keyPoints: The passenger is responsible for having the correct travel documents
That did not absolve the airline from liability for damages
Very poor service, verbal abuse and lack of respect by its agents = bad faith
Actual damages limited to expenses caused by the airline's acts; the Moscow leg borne by the passenger
Moral damages and attorney's fees affirmed

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, statement of the Court of Appeals' ruling on liability
source.excerpt: The CA ruled that it was respondent (as passenger), and not AF, who was responsible for having the correct travel documents. However, the appellate court stated that this fact did not absolve AF from liability for damages. The CA agreed with the findings of fact of the RTC that AF’s agents and representatives repeatedly subjected respondent to very poor service, verbal abuse and abject lack of respect and consideration. As such, AF was guilty of bad faith for which respondent ought to be compensated. The appellate court affirmed the award of ₱1 million moral damages and ₱300,000 attorney’s fees. However, it reduced the actual damages to US$906 (or its peso equivalent). According to the CA, this amount represented the expenses respondent incurred from the time he was unable to join his group in Rome (due to the unfounded "communiqué" of Ms. Soeyesol that he was a security threat) up to the time his flight reservation from Paris to Manila was dishonored for which he was forced to stay in Paris for two additional days. The appellate court pointed out that, on the other hand, respondent’s expenses for the Moscow leg of the trip must be borne by him as AF could not be faulted when he was refused entry to Moscow for lack of a transit visa.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Losing on appeal, an airline files a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45, arguing that the passenger's injury was not clearly established and that the moral and exemplary damages and attorney's fees awarded are exorbitant. Will the Supreme Court review the awards? Explain, citing Air France v. De Camilis.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Whether the passenger is entitled to the damages and attorney's fees requires a review of the evidence, which is a question of fact outside a Rule 45 petition, absent any of the recognized exceptions.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Air France v. De Camilis, the Court held that the issue of entitlement to damages and attorney's fees "entails a resort to the parties' respective evidence," so the airline was asking the Court to consider a question of fact. The jurisdiction of the Court in a Rule 45 petition is limited to questions of law, save for certain exceptions, none of which was present. Both the trial court and the Court of Appeals had properly laid down the factual and legal bases for their decisions.
suggestedAnswer.application: The airline's attack on whether the injury was proved, and on the amounts, depends on weighing the evidence. Since the lower courts stated the factual and legal bases of the awards and no exception applies, the Court would not disturb them.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The petition fails on this point; only the interest was clarified. **Bar trap:** a Rule 45 petition cannot be used to re-weigh the evidence on damages; the lower courts' stated bases also distinguish this from an unexplained award of attorney's fees.

keyPoints: Entitlement to damages and attorney's fees requires a resort to the evidence: a question of fact
Rule 45 is limited to questions of law, save for certain exceptions
No exception was present
The lower courts laid down the factual and legal bases for their awards

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, discussion of the entitlement to damages
source.excerpt: Preliminarily, on the issue pertaining to whether or not respondent was entitled to damages and attorney’s fees, the same entails a resort to the parties’ respective evidence. Thus, AF is clearly asking us to consider a question of fact. Time and again, we have held that the jurisdiction of this Court in a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 is limited only to questions of law, save for certain exceptions, none of which are present in this case. Both the RTC and the CA have competently ruled on the issue of respondent’s entitlement to damages and attorney’s fees as they properly laid down both the factual and legal bases for their respective decisions. We see no reason to disturb their findings.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Air France v. De Camilis, why did the Court reckon the 6% legal interest from the date of the trial court's judgment instead of the extrajudicial demand?

choices.A: Because the passenger made no extrajudicial demand.
choices.B: Because it was at the time the trial court rendered judgment that the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained.
choices.C: Because interest on damages for breach of contract always runs from the filing of the complaint.
choices.D: Because the obligation was a forbearance of money.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court said the interest runs from the trial court's judgment, "not from the time of respondent's extrajudicial demand. This must be so as it was at the time the RTC rendered its judgment that the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained." **A is wrong:** there was an extrajudicial demand (August 1, 2003). **C is wrong:** there is no such rule. **D is wrong:** a breach of contract of carriage is not a forbearance, which is why 6% applied. **Bar trap:** the answer turns on when the amount became reasonably certain.

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, discussion of the legal interest
source.excerpt: Pursuant to this ruling, the legal interest is 6% p.a. and it shall be reckoned from April 25, 2007 when the RTC rendered its judgment, not from the time of respondent’s extrajudicial demand. This must be so as it was at the time the RTC rendered its judgment that the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Air France v. De Camilis, who was held responsible for having the correct travel documents, such as a transit visa?

choices.A: The airline, as the common carrier.
choices.B: The airline's agent in Paris.
choices.C: The passenger.
choices.D: The tour organizer of the pilgrimage.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court of Appeals "ruled that it was respondent (as passenger), and not AF, who was responsible for having the correct travel documents," so his expenses for the Moscow leg were his own. **A and B are wrong:** the airline could not be faulted for his refused entry. **D is wrong:** no such ruling was made. **Bar trap:** this did not absolve the airline from damages for its agents' bad faith.

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, statement of the Court of Appeals' ruling on liability
source.excerpt: The CA ruled that it was respondent (as passenger), and not AF, who was responsible for having the correct travel documents. However, the appellate court stated that this fact did not absolve AF from liability for damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Air France v. De Camilis, the airline was found guilty of bad faith because

choices.A: it failed to inform the passenger of the need for a transit visa.
choices.B: its agents and representatives repeatedly subjected the passenger to very poor service, verbal abuse and abject lack of respect and consideration.
choices.C: it charged the passenger for excess baggage.
choices.D: its flight was delayed by bad weather.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court of Appeals agreed with the trial court that the airline's "agents and representatives repeatedly subjected respondent to very poor service, verbal abuse and abject lack of respect and consideration. As such, AF was guilty of bad faith." **A is wrong:** the passenger was responsible for his travel documents. **C and D are wrong:** neither was in the case. **Bar trap:** bad faith here came from the agents' treatment of the passenger, not from the visa problem.

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, statement of the Court of Appeals' ruling on liability
source.excerpt: The CA agreed with the findings of fact of the RTC that AF’s agents and representatives repeatedly subjected respondent to very poor service, verbal abuse and abject lack of respect and consideration. As such, AF was guilty of bad faith for which respondent ought to be compensated.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Air France v. De Camilis, which expenses were covered by the award of actual damages of US$906?

choices.A: All of the passenger's expenses for the whole pilgrimage.
choices.B: Only his expenses for the Moscow leg of the trip.
choices.C: The expenses from the time he could not join his group in Rome, because of the unfounded report that he was a security threat, until his Paris-Manila reservation was dishonored and he had to stay two more days in Paris.
choices.D: Only the cost of his ticket.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court of Appeals reduced the actual damages to US$906, representing "the expenses respondent incurred from the time he was unable to join his group in Rome (due to the unfounded 'communiqué' of Ms. Soeyesol that he was a security threat) up to the time his flight reservation from Paris to Manila was dishonored." **A is wrong:** the award was limited to losses the airline caused. **B is wrong:** the Moscow expenses were borne by him. **D is wrong:** the ticket was not the measure. **Bar trap:** actual damages cover only the loss caused by the defendant's breach.

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, statement of the Court of Appeals' ruling on actual damages
source.excerpt: However, it reduced the actual damages to US$906 (or its peso equivalent). According to the CA, this amount represented the expenses respondent incurred from the time he was unable to join his group in Rome (due to the unfounded "communiqué" of Ms. Soeyesol that he was a security threat) up to the time his flight reservation from Paris to Manila was dishonored for which he was forced to stay in Paris for two additional days.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What did the Court order in Air France v. De Camilis?

choices.A: Legal interest of 6% a year from the trial court's decision of April 25, 2007, and 12% from finality of the Supreme Court's decision, on all sums awarded until full satisfaction.
choices.B: Legal interest of 6% a year from the extrajudicial demand until full payment.
choices.C: Legal interest of 12% a year from the filing of the complaint.
choices.D: No interest at all, since the damages were unliquidated.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court affirmed the Court of Appeals and ordered the airline to "PAY legal interest of 6% p.a. from the date of promulgation of the decision dated April 25, 2007 of the Regional Trial Court ... and 12% p.a. from the time the decision of this Court attains finality, on all sums awarded until their full satisfaction." **B is wrong:** that was the Court of Appeals' reckoning, which the Court corrected. **C is wrong:** neither the rate nor the date applied. **D is wrong:** unliquidated damages earn interest once reasonably ascertained, at the latest from the judgment. **Bar trap:** two periods, two rates (the 12% was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013).

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, the disposition
source.excerpt: Petitioner is ordered to PAY legal interest of 6% p.a. from the date of promulgation of the decision dated April 25, 2007 of the Regional Trial Court, Branch 59, Makati City and 12% p.a. from the time the decision of this Court attains finality, on all sums awarded until their full satisfaction.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish attorney's fees in their ordinary concept from attorney's fees in their extraordinary concept. In a suit where the plaintiff wins, may the court award her attorney's fees of ₱107,000 plus ₱1,000 per appearance and ₱10,000 litigation expenses simply because she prevailed? Explain, citing Padillo v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: In the ordinary concept, attorney's fees are the reasonable compensation a client pays his lawyer for legal services. In the extraordinary concept, they are awarded by the court as indemnity for damages, paid by the losing party to the prevailing party. They are not awarded every time a party wins, and an excessive award will be reduced.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Padillo v. CA, the Court held that the award of attorney's fees is the exception rather than the general rule; counsel's fees are not awarded every time a party prevails, because no premium should be placed on the right to litigate. Attorney's fees as part of damages are awarded only in the instances in Article 2208; the court must make findings of fact and law that bring the case within the exception, and in all cases the fees must be reasonable. They are not meant to enrich the winning party at the expense of the losing litigant.
suggestedAnswer.application: Winning the case is not enough. Even where the court finds it just and equitable to award attorney's fees, the amount must be reasonable. In Padillo, the Court found ₱107,000 plus ₱1,000 per appearance and ₱10,000 litigation expenses unreasonable and excessive, and reduced it to ₱25,000.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Not simply because she prevailed; and the amount awarded must be reasonable. **Bar trap:** the extraordinary concept goes to the litigant as damages and is the exception; the ordinary concept is between lawyer and client.

keyPoints: Ordinary concept: reasonable compensation paid by the client to the lawyer
Extraordinary concept: indemnity for damages paid by the losing party to the prevailing party
The exception, not the rule; not awarded every time a party prevails
Only in the cases in Art. 2208, with findings of fact and law; always reasonable
Not meant to enrich the winning party; reduced to ₱25,000 in Padillo

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of attorney's fees
source.excerpt: With respect to attorney's fees, the award thereof is the exception rather than the general rule; counsel's fees are not awarded every time a party prevails in a suit because of the policy that no premium should be placed on the right to litigate. Attorney's fees as part of damages are not the same as attorney's fees in the concept of the amount paid to a lawyer. In the ordinary sense, attorney's fees represent the reasonable compensation paid to a lawyer by his client for the legal services he has rendered to the latter, while in its extraordinary concept, they may be awarded by the court as indemnity for damages to be paid by the losing party to the prevailing party. Attorney's fees as part of damages is awarded only in the instances specified in Article 2208 of the Civil Code. As such, it is necessary for the court to make findings of facts and law that would bring the case within the exception and justify the grant of such award, and in all cases it must be reasonable. … Attorney's fees as part of damages is not meant to enrich the winning party at the expense of the losing litigant. Thus, it should be reasonably reduced to Twenty-Five Thousand Pesos (P25,000.00).

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: An owner kept out of her commercial lot and building for ten years testified that she could have earned ₱150,000 a year from it, and that the occupant had made millions from it, but gave no details on how such income could be earned. The occupant admitted that he had been paying the former owner a monthly rental of ₱800. How much should the owner recover as actual damages for the lost income? Explain, citing Padillo v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: She should recover only the unrealized rentals at the admitted rate of ₱800 a month for the period of occupancy, not the claimed ₱150,000 a year.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Padillo v. CA, the Court held the claimed ₱150,000 yearly income "highly conjectural and speculative," since the owner did not detail how such income could be derived from the property. Actual, compensatory and consequential damages must be proved and cannot be presumed; if the proof is flimsy and insufficient, no damages will be allowed. The only unrealized income she was entitled to was the monthly rental the occupant admitted, ₱800 a month, for the period he occupied the property.
suggestedAnswer.application: Her bare testimony is too vague and unspecified to support ₱150,000 a year. But the occupant's own admission of the ₱800 monthly rental is competent proof of the loss. In Padillo, that came to ₱97,600 for January 1982 to February 1992, with legal interest from the finality of the decision.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Only the admitted rentals, with legal interest from finality. **Bar trap:** actual damages are never presumed; a claimant's estimate without supporting details fails, but an admitted figure can still support a smaller award.

keyPoints: Actual damages must be proved and cannot be presumed
Vague, unspecified testimony on expected income is conjectural and speculative
Flimsy or insufficient proof: no damages allowed
The admitted rental (₱800 a month) is the measure of the lost income
₱97,600 for the period of occupancy, with legal interest from finality

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the unrealized income
source.excerpt: Concerning the alleged forgone income of One Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (P150,000.00) per year since 1982 as testified on by petitioner as the income she could have realized had possession of the property not been withheld from her by respondent Averia, we consider such amount of expected profit highly conjectural and speculative. With an allegation that respondent made millions for the improper use and exploitation of the property, petitioner's testimony regarding the matter of unrealized income is sadly lacking of the requisite details on how such huge amount of income could be made possible. Petitioner did not detail out how such huge amount of income could have been derived from the use of the disputed lot and building. Well-entrenched is the doctrine that actual, compensatory and consequential damages must be proved, and cannot be presumed. If the proof adduced thereon is flimsy and insufficient, as in this case, no damages will be allowed. Verily, the testimonial evidence on alleged unrealized income earlier referred to is not enough to warrant the award of damages. It is too vague and unspecified to induce faith and reliance. The only amount of unrealized income petitioner should be entitled to is the unrealized monthly rentals which respondent Averia admits to be in the amount of Eight Hundred Pesos (P800.00) a month

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In an earlier certiorari case between the same parties, the Court of Appeals, instead of dismissing the plaintiff's damages suit for litis pendentia, ordered it merely suspended until a related registration case was finished. No appeal was taken, and that ruling became final. After the plaintiff won the damages suit, the Court of Appeals reversed it on the ground of res judicata, since the requisites were present. Was the reversal correct? Distinguish the law of the case from res judicata, citing Padillo v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Although all the requisites of res judicata were present, the final ruling ordering only the suspension of the damages suit had become the law of the case between the parties, even if erroneous, so the plaintiff could not be faulted for continuing with it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Padillo v. CA, the Court explained that the law of the case means that whatever is once irrevocably established as the controlling legal rule or decision between the same parties in the same case continues to be the law of the case, whether correct or not, so long as the facts remain the same. It differs from res judicata: the law of the case does not have the finality of res judicata and applies only to that one case, whereas res judicata forecloses parties or privies in one case by what has been done in another case. Since no appeal was taken from the decision ordering suspension instead of dismissal, it became final and may no longer be disturbed.
suggestedAnswer.application: The final ruling of the Court of Appeals, in the same litigation between the same parties, allowed the damages suit to proceed after the registration case. The plaintiff yielded to it in good faith, so the later reversal on the ground of res judicata was wrong.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The reversal was incorrect. **Bar trap:** the presence of all four requisites of res judicata does not end the inquiry; a final, even erroneous, ruling in the same case binds the parties as the law of the case.

keyPoints: Law of the case: what is irrevocably established between the same parties in the same case stays the law of the case, even if wrong
It applies only to that one case and lacks the finality of res judicata
Res judicata binds parties in one case by what was done in another case
The unappealed ruling ordering suspension became final and binding
The plaintiff could not be faulted for pursuing her claim in good faith

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of res judicata and the law of the case
source.excerpt: However, a different conclusion is warranted under the principle of law of the case. Law of the case has been defined as the opinion delivered on a former appeal. More specifically, it means that whatever is once irrevocably established as the controlling legal rule or decision between the same parties in the same case continues to be the law of the case, whether correct on general principles or not, so long as the facts on which such decision was predicated continue to be the facts of the case before the court. … The appellate court apparently overlooked the significance of this principle called the law of the case which is totally different from the concept of res judicata. Law of the case does not have the finality of the doctrine of res judicata, and applies only to that one case, whereas res judicata forecloses parties or privies in one case by what has been done in another case. … Thus, even if erroneous, the ruling of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 15356 has become the law of the case as between herein petitioner Padillo and respondent Averia, and may no longer be disturbed or modified.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under Padillo v. Court of Appeals, attorney's fees in their extraordinary concept refer to

choices.A: the reasonable compensation paid by a client to his lawyer for legal services.
choices.B: the docket fees paid to the court.
choices.C: an indemnity for damages awarded by the court, to be paid by the losing party to the prevailing party.
choices.D: the lawyer's contingent fee agreed upon in writing.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said that "in its extraordinary concept, they may be awarded by the court as indemnity for damages to be paid by the losing party to the prevailing party." **A is wrong:** that is the ordinary concept. **B is wrong:** docket fees are judicial costs. **D is wrong:** a contingent fee is part of the lawyer-client contract (the ordinary concept). **Bar trap:** the two concepts have different payors and payees.

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of attorney's fees
source.excerpt: In the ordinary sense, attorney's fees represent the reasonable compensation paid to a lawyer by his client for the legal services he has rendered to the latter, while in its extraordinary concept, they may be awarded by the court as indemnity for damages to be paid by the losing party to the prevailing party.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Padillo v. Court of Appeals, why are counsel's fees not awarded every time a party prevails in a suit?

choices.A: Because of the policy that no premium should be placed on the right to litigate.
choices.B: Because attorney's fees are always paid by the client.
choices.C: Because the Rules of Court prohibit them.
choices.D: Because they can be awarded only in criminal cases.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said: "counsel's fees are not awarded every time a party prevails in a suit because of the policy that no premium should be placed on the right to litigate." **B is wrong:** in the extraordinary concept the losing party pays. **C and D are wrong:** Article 2208 allows them in the cases it lists, civil ones included. **Bar trap:** the award is the exception, not the rule.

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of attorney's fees
source.excerpt: With respect to attorney's fees, the award thereof is the exception rather than the general rule; counsel's fees are not awarded every time a party prevails in a suit because of the policy that no premium should be placed on the right to litigate.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A defendant filed a separate suit over the same property while a related case was pending; the suit was dismissed. Under Padillo v. Court of Appeals, does that alone justify moral damages against him?

choices.A: Yes, because every dismissed suit is presumed malicious.
choices.B: Yes, because the plaintiff suffered anxiety from the litigation.
choices.C: Yes, if the plaintiff hired a lawyer.
choices.D: No, because the law could not have meant to impose a penalty on the right to litigate; error alone is not a ground for moral damages.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court held that filing a suit that was later dismissed "does not per se make such actions or appeals wrongful," since "[t]he law could not have meant to impose a penalty on the right to litigate," and "error alone is not a ground for moral damages." **A is wrong:** malice or bad faith is not presumed. **B is wrong:** the anxiety usually caused to a party hauled into court is not the kind that warrants moral damages. **C is wrong:** hiring a lawyer is irrelevant. **Bar trap:** moral damages for litigation need malice or bad faith.

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral and exemplary damages
source.excerpt: That respondent Averia instituted a separate suit which was subsequently dismissed and all actions or appeals taken by respondent Averia relative to M.C. No. 374-82 does not per se make such actions or appeals wrongful and subject respondent Averia to payment of moral damages. The law could not have meant to impose a penalty on the right to litigate. Such right is so precious that moral damages may not be charged on those who may exercise it erroneously. One may have erred, but error alone is not a ground for moral damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Padillo v. Court of Appeals, which of the following is NOT a requisite of res judicata as a bar by prior judgment?

choices.A: The former judgment must be final.
choices.B: Both actions must have been filed in the same court.
choices.C: It must be a judgment or order on the merits.
choices.D: There must be identity of parties, subject matter and cause of action.

questions.explanation: **B is correct**, because it is not a requisite. The four requisites listed are: (1) the former judgment must be final; (2) it must have been rendered by a court having jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties; (3) it must be a judgment or order on the merits; and (4) identity of parties, subject matter and cause of action. **A, C and D are wrong:** each is a requisite. **Bar trap:** jurisdiction of the first court is required, not that the second case be in the same court.

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of res judicata
source.excerpt: 1. The former judgment must be final; 2. It must have been rendered by a court having jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties; 3. It must be a judgment or order on the merits; and 4. There must be between the first and second action identity of parties, identity of subject matter, and identity of cause of action.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What did the Court finally award in Padillo v. Court of Appeals?

choices.A: ₱150,000 a year in unrealized income, moral and exemplary damages, and ₱107,000 attorney's fees.
choices.B: Nothing, because the claim was barred by res judicata.
choices.C: ₱97,600 as unrealized rentals with legal interest from the finality of the decision until fully paid, and ₱25,000 attorney's fees.
choices.D: ₱97,600 as unrealized rentals with interest from 1982, plus ₱50,000 moral damages.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court ordered the respondent to pay "(a) Ninety-Seven Thousand Six Hundred Pesos (P97,600.00) as unrealized rentals which shall earn interest at the legal rate from the finality of the this decision until fully paid, and (b) Twenty-Five Thousand Pesos (P25,000.00) as attorney's fees." **A is the trial court's award, which was reduced. B is wrong:** the law of the case allowed the claim. **D is wrong:** interest runs from finality, and moral damages were deleted. **Bar trap:** a winning party may still receive far less than the trial court gave.

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, the disposition
source.excerpt: WHEREFORE, the instant petition is GRANTED. The Decision of the Court of Appeals dated November 22, 1994 in CA-G.R. CV No. 40142 is REVERSED and SET ASIDE and another in its stead is hereby rendered ORDERING respondent Tomas Averia, Jr., to pay petitioner Veronica Padillo the amounts of (a) Ninety-Seven Thousand Six Hundred Pesos (P97,600.00) as unrealized rentals which shall earn interest at the legal rate from the finality of the this decision until fully paid, and (b) Twenty-Five Thousand Pesos (P25,000.00) as attorney's fees.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: X Corp. bought shares of a mining company and asked the company to register the transfer. The company delayed for several months. During the delay, the market price of the shares rose sharply, then fell to below the purchase price. After the transfer was finally made, X Corp. sued for the profit it says it would have made had it been able to sell at the peak. The parties' stipulation of facts says nothing about any plan of X Corp. to sell. Should the claim be granted? Explain, citing Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The claimed profit is speculative and cannot be recovered.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. CA, the Court held that a claim for unrealized profit must be duly and sufficiently established; the claimant must prove that it was in fact damaged by the defendant's act or omission. Where nothing shows that the claimant intended to sell, or would have sold, the shares on specified dates, whatever profits could have been made are purely speculative, since the rise and fall of share prices cannot be predicted with certainty, and speculative damages cannot be recovered.
suggestedAnswer.application: X Corp. shows only that the price went up and later down. Nothing shows it would have sold at the peak; it could equally have held the shares and waited for further increases. The supposed profit is a guess, not a proved loss.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The claim should be denied. **Bar trap:** a market rise alone does not prove lucro cesante; the claimant must prove that it would actually have earned the profit.

keyPoints: Unrealized profit (lucro cesante) must be duly and sufficiently established
The claimant must prove it was in fact damaged by the defendant's act
No showing that it intended to sell, or would have sold, on specified dates
Share prices rise and fall unpredictably: the profit is purely speculative
Speculative damages cannot be recovered

source.caseTitle: Batong Buhay Gold Mines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (unrealized profits)
source.excerpt: Petitioner company also alleges that the claim for unrealized profit must be duly and sufficiently established, that is, that the claimant must submit proof that it was in fact damaged because of petitioner's act or omission. The stipulation of facts of the parties does not at all show that private respondent intended to sell, or would sell or would have sold the stocks in question on specified dates. While it is true that shares of stock may go up or down in value (as in fact the concerned shares here really rose from fifteen (15) centavos to twenty three or twenty four (23/24) centavos per share and then fell to about two (2) centavos per share, still whatever profits could have been made are purely SPECULATIVE, for it was difficult to predict with any decree of certainty the rise and fall in the value of the shares. Thus this Court has ruled that speculative damages cannot be recovered.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Counsel for a buyer of shares argues: "Had the company transferred the shares when we demanded, we would have sold them and made a profit of ₱5,600. Its refusal deprived us of that profit, so it must pay." How did the Supreme Court answer this argument in Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court rejected it: it is easy to say after the fact that the buyer would have sold and made a profit, but it is equally possible that the buyer's officials would have refused to sell and waited for further increases in value.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. CA, the Court said that "human nature, being what it is, private respondent's officials could also have refused to sell and instead wait for expected further increases in value." Because the profit depended on a decision to sell that was never shown, it was speculative, and speculative damages cannot be recovered.
suggestedAnswer.application: The argument assumes the very fact that had to be proved: that the buyer would have sold at the right time. Without proof, the claimed ₱5,600 is hindsight, not a loss caused by the refusal.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Court set aside the award and reinstated the trial court's decision, which granted no damages. **Bar trap:** hindsight about what a claimant could have done is not proof of what it would have done.

keyPoints: The claimed profit assumes the buyer would have sold at the right time
The buyer's officials could equally have refused to sell and waited
Hindsight is not proof of a loss
The award was set aside and the trial court's decision reinstated

source.caseTitle: Batong Buhay Gold Mines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (human nature)
source.excerpt: It is easy to say now that had private respondent gained legal title to the shares, it could have sold the same and reaped a profit of P5,624.95 but it could not do so because of petitioner's refusal to transfer the stocks in the former's name at the time demand was made, but then it is also true that human nature, being what it is, private respondent's officials could also have refused to sell and instead wait for expected further increases in value. … WHEREFORE, the assailed decision and resolutions of the Court of Appeals are hereby SET ASIDE, and a new one is hereby rendered REINSTATING the decision of the trial court.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals, why did the company refuse to register the transfer of the shares, how did the trial court and the Court of Appeals rule, and what did the Supreme Court finally decide?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The company withheld the transfer because the seller's wife wrote to it that the shares were conjugal property sold without her consent, and it feared being held liable to her. The trial court ordered the transfer (by a preliminary mandatory injunction made permanent) but awarded no damages; the Court of Appeals added ₱5,625.55 as unrealized profit with legal interest. The Supreme Court set aside the Court of Appeals and reinstated the trial court's decision.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. CA, the company justified its refusal by its apprehension of liability for damages under Article 173 of the Civil Code. The Court held that the unrealized profit awarded by the Court of Appeals was purely speculative and that speculative damages cannot be recovered.
suggestedAnswer.application: The buyer received the shares through the injunction, so the only question was damages for the delay. Because the claimed profit was not proved, nothing was due beyond the transfer itself.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The transfer stood, but no damages were due. **Bar trap:** winning the main relief does not mean an award of damages follows; each item of actual damages must be proved.

keyPoints: The wife claimed the shares were conjugal and sold without her consent
The company feared liability (Art. 173, Civil Code)
Trial court: transfer ordered, no damages
Court of Appeals: added ₱5,625.55 unrealized profit
Supreme Court: award set aside; trial court reinstated

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals, what must a claimant prove to recover unrealized profit?

choices.A: That the market price of the property rose during the delay.
choices.B: That it was in fact damaged because of the defendant's act or omission.
choices.C: That the defendant acted in bad faith.
choices.D: Nothing, since unrealized profits are presumed.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The claim "for unrealized profit must be duly and sufficiently established, that is, that the claimant must submit proof that it was in fact damaged because of petitioner's act or omission," a position the Court upheld. **A is wrong:** a price rise alone was held insufficient. **C is wrong:** bad faith was not the issue. **D is wrong:** damages are not presumed. **Bar trap:** proof of a market movement is not proof of a lost profit.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals, the shares rose from 15 centavos to about 23 or 24 centavos, then fell to about 2 centavos. How did the Court classify the profits the buyer could have made?

choices.A: Purely speculative, since the rise and fall of share prices could not be predicted with certainty.
choices.B: Temperate damages, since some loss was suffered.
choices.C: Liquidated damages, since the price was known.
choices.D: Actual damages, proved by the market quotations.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said that "whatever profits could have been made are purely SPECULATIVE, for it was difficult to predict with any decree of certainty the rise and fall in the value of the shares," and that "speculative damages cannot be recovered." **B, C and D are wrong:** the Court awarded nothing, since no loss was shown. **Bar trap:** a known price history does not make a profit certain when the decision to sell is uncertain.

source.caseTitle: Batong Buhay Gold Mines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (unrealized profits)
source.excerpt: While it is true that shares of stock may go up or down in value (as in fact the concerned shares here really rose from fifteen (15) centavos to twenty three or twenty four (23/24) centavos per share and then fell to about two (2) centavos per share, still whatever profits could have been made are purely SPECULATIVE, for it was difficult to predict with any decree of certainty the rise and fall in the value of the shares. Thus this Court has ruled that speculative damages cannot be recovered.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals, what was missing from the parties' stipulation of facts that defeated the claim for unrealized profit?

choices.A: Proof of the purchase price of the shares.
choices.B: Proof of the date of the demand for transfer.
choices.C: Any showing that the buyer intended to sell, or would have sold, the shares on specified dates.
choices.D: Proof that the seller's wife consented to the sale.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court noted that "[t]he stipulation of facts of the parties does not at all show that private respondent intended to sell, or would sell or would have sold the stocks in question on specified dates." **A and B are wrong:** these were in the record. **D is wrong:** the wife's consent bore on the transfer, not on the damages. **Bar trap:** identify the missing link between the defendant's act and the claimed loss.
