questions.prompt: What was the disposition in Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals?

choices.A: The Court of Appeals' award of ₱5,625.55 was affirmed.
choices.B: The case was remanded for a new trial on the newly discovered evidence.
choices.C: The award was reduced to nominal damages.
choices.D: The Court of Appeals' decision was set aside and the trial court's decision, which awarded no damages, was reinstated.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court ruled: "the assailed decision and resolutions of the Court of Appeals are hereby SET ASIDE, and a new one is hereby rendered REINSTATING the decision of the trial court." **A is wrong:** the award was speculative. **B is wrong:** the Court found no need to discuss the second issue. **C is wrong:** no nominal damages were awarded. **Bar trap:** a failed claim for actual damages does not automatically become a different kind of damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: P, a producer, appointed D as its exclusive export distributor for two years, for a commission on every shipment. After seven months, P stopped delivering in breach of the contract, and D sued for the commissions it would have earned for the remaining 17 months. P argues that D cannot recover because it did not prove any actual unfilled sale, any ready buyer or the price such buyers would pay. D proves the volume it shipped and the commissions it earned before the breach. Is D entitled to recover its unearned commissions? Explain, citing General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Lost profits (lucrum cessans) are recoverable under Article 2200, and D's unearned commissions can be estimated with reasonable certainty from what it earned under the same contract before the breach.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, the Court held that under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, indemnification for damages comprehends not only the value of the loss suffered but also the profits the creditor fails to obtain, so lucrum cessans is a basis for indemnification. The question is whether the creditor failed to make profits because of the breach and whether there is basis for determining such profits with reasonable certainty. Since the distributor had been earning commissions whenever logs were delivered, it was reasonable to expect it would have continued earning in the same manner, and the commission was not difficult to estimate.
suggestedAnswer.application: From D's earnings per unit on past shipments multiplied by the volume P was bound to deliver for the remaining months, the lost commission can be computed. In the case itself, the Court computed ₱365,350.40 and held the ₱400,000 award "not speculative, but based on reasonable estimate."
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: D may recover its unearned commissions. **Bar trap:** compare Batong Buhay v. CA, where a profit depending on an unproved decision to sell was speculative; here the profit rests on a contract and an established earning record.

keyPoints: Art. 2200: damages include the loss suffered and the profits the creditor fails to obtain
Lucrum cessans is a basis for indemnification
Test: profits lost because of the breach, and a basis to determine them with reasonable certainty
Estimate from past commissions per unit times the volume due for the remaining term
The award was a reasonable estimate, not speculative

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the sixth issue (actual damages)
source.excerpt: This argument must be overruled in the light of the law and evidence on the latter. Under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, indemnification for damages comprehends not only the value of the loss suffered but also at of the profits which the creditor fails to obtain. In other words, lucrum cessans is also a basis for indemnification. The question then that arises is: Has appellee failed to make profits because of appellant's breach of contract, and in the affirmative, is there here basis for determining with reasonable certainty such unearned profits? … Had appellant continued to deliver the logs as it was bound to pursuant to the agreement it is reasonable to expect that it would have continued earning its commission in much the same manner as it used to in connection with the previous shipments of logs, which clearly indicates that it failed to earn the commissions it should earn during this period of time. And this commission is not difficult to estimate. … The award therefore, made by the court a quo of the amount of P400,000.00 as compensatory damages is not speculative, but based on reasonable estimate.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A supply contract allows a party to suspend performance only for listed causes such as fire, flood, strikes, government orders and similar causes beyond its control. The supplier suspends deliveries, citing (a) a demand to renegotiate prices, (b) its plan to build its own processing plant, and (c) new government restrictions and machinery breakdowns. It continued producing and sold its output to other buyers. Was the suspension justified? Explain, citing General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Grounds (a) and (b) are not among the stipulated causes of suspension, and ground (c), even if fortuitous, did not make it impossible for the supplier to perform.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, the Court held that the demand for renegotiation of prices and the establishment of a veneer plant "are not among the various causes of suspension enumerated" in the contract, so suspension on those grounds was not justified. As to the barter restrictions, breakdowns and the Margin Law, even assuming they were fortuitous, they did not cause such a reduction in production as to make compliance impossible; a fortuitous event does not necessarily extinguish an obligation, as it must be of such a character as to render it impossible for the obligor to fulfill it in a normal manner.
suggestedAnswer.application: The supplier kept producing and sold its output to others, which shows it could have delivered. Its own business plans are not grounds the contract recognizes.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The suspension was a breach, and damages are due. **Bar trap:** labeling an event "fortuitous" is not enough; the obligor must show that the event made normal performance impossible.

keyPoints: Suspension is allowed only for the causes the contract lists
Price renegotiation and a new plant were not listed causes
A fortuitous event must make normal fulfillment impossible to excuse performance
The supplier kept producing and sold to others: no impossibility
The unjustified suspension was a breach

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the second issue (suspension and fortuitous events)
source.excerpt: Even assuming that the restrictions imposed by the government on barter, the breakdown of machineries and the inability to secure spare parts, replacements and wire ropes, as well as the passage of the Margin Law, have the nature of fortuitous events, yet it cannot be said that they had caused such a reduction in appellant's production of logs that made it impossible for it to comply wholly, or even partly, with its commitment with appellee. The rule is that even the happening of a fortuitous event in itself does not necessarily extinguish an obligation for, as this Court has said, the fortuitous event must be of such a character as to render it impossible for the obligor to fulfill his obligation in a normal manner (Lassam v. Smith, 45 Phil. 990). … One of the causes for the suspension of the agreement alleged by appellant was the demand for the renegotiation of prices provided in paragraph 2 of the agreement. Another reason advanced is the establishment of a veneer plant for the purpose of increasing the log production. But these two matters are not among the various causes of suspension enumerated in paragraph 8 of the agreement. The suspension, therefore, of the contract on these causes is not justified.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A party that breached a distribution contract tried to justify its breach with misstatements and half-truths by one of its officers. The trial court awarded the other party ₱100,000 exemplary damages. Should the award be sustained in full? Explain, citing General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Not in full. The award should be reduced, since the breaching party did not act in a wanton, oppressive or malevolent manner; in the case, the Court reduced it to ₱50,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, the Court found the ₱100,000 exemplary damages "somewhat excessive," since the producer, in suspending the contract, "has not acted in a wanton, oppressive or malevolent manner to deserve such a heavy punishment within the purview of the law (Article 2232, new Civil Code)." Its officer's misstatements or half-truths, though reprehensible, were not a wanton or malevolent perversion of the truth, so ₱50,000 was a reasonable exemplary penalty. The attorney's fees were affirmed under Article 2208, considering the importance of the litigation and the time and effort involved.
suggestedAnswer.application: Misstatements meant to justify a breach are blameworthy but fall short of the wanton or malevolent conduct that would warrant a heavy exemplary award in a contract case.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The exemplary damages should be mitigated. **Bar trap:** in contracts, exemplary damages depend on wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive or malevolent conduct (Art. 2232); a reprehensible but not malevolent act justifies only a reduced award.

keyPoints: Exemplary damages in contracts: wanton, oppressive or malevolent conduct (Art. 2232)
Misstatements and half-truths were reprehensible but not wanton or malevolent
₱100,000 was excessive; reduced to ₱50,000
Attorney's fees affirmed under Art. 2208 given the importance of the case and the effort

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the sixth issue (exemplary damages and attorney's fees)
source.excerpt: We believes however, that the amount of P100,000.00 awarded to appellee as exemplary damages is somewhat excessive it appearing that appellant is suspending the operation of the contract has not acted in a wanton, oppressive or malevolent manner to deserve such a heavy punishment within the purview of the law (Article 2232, new Civil Code). The most that can be said is that appellant, to suit its purpose, has availed to certain misstatements or half truths as reflected in the declarations of Mr. Dempsey, one of its high officials, in an attempt to justify its desistance from the contract. While this is reprehensible, it is not a wanton or malevolent perversion of the truth. Hence, the award should be mitigated and in our opinion the amount of P50,000.00 is a reasonable exemplary penalty. We also find reasonable the amount awarded by the court a quo as attorney's fees considering the importance of this litigation and the amount of time and effort therein involved. This is justified under Article 2208 of the Civil Code.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, as applied in General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, indemnification for damages comprehends

choices.A: only the value of the loss suffered.
choices.B: only the profits the creditor fails to obtain.
choices.C: not only the value of the loss suffered but also the profits which the creditor fails to obtain.
choices.D: only damages that were foreseen at the time the contract was made, excluding profits.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said: "Under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, indemnification for damages comprehends not only the value of the loss suffered but also at of the profits which the creditor fails to obtain. In other words, lucrum cessans is also a basis for indemnification." **A and B are wrong:** each states only half the rule. **D is wrong:** Article 2200 expressly covers unrealized profits. **Bar trap:** the two components are daño emergente (loss suffered) and lucro cesante (profits lost).

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the sixth issue (actual damages)
source.excerpt: Under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, indemnification for damages comprehends not only the value of the loss suffered but also at of the profits which the creditor fails to obtain. In other words, lucrum cessans is also a basis for indemnification.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, how did the Court determine the distributor's lost commissions?

choices.A: By the distributor's own estimate of its expected profits.
choices.B: By multiplying the volume the producer was bound to deliver in the remaining 17 months by the commission per board foot the distributor actually earned on earlier shipments.
choices.C: By awarding nominal damages, since lost profits are inherently speculative.
choices.D: By the market value of the logs the producer sold to other buyers.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court took the 34 million board feet due for the remaining 17 months and the commission of ₱.0107456 per board foot earned on earlier shipments, arriving at ₱365,350.40 as "the lucrum cessans that should accrue to appellee." **A is wrong:** the estimate was based on actual past earnings. **C is wrong:** the award was held not speculative. **D is wrong:** not the measure used. **Bar trap:** reasonable certainty, not absolute certainty, is enough for lost profits.

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the sixth issue (actual damages)
source.excerpt: Thus, during the seventeen remaining months of the contract, at the rate of at least 2,000,000 board feet, appellant should have delivered thirty-four million board feet. If we take the number of board feet delivered during the months prior to the interruption, namely, 7,405,861 board feet, and the commission received by appellee thereon, which amounts to P79,580,82, we would have that appellee received a commission of P.0107456 per board feet. Multiplying 34 million board feet by P.0107456, the product is P365,350.40, which represents the lucrum cessans that should accrue to appellee.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, the Court defined the cause of a contract as

choices.A: the essential reason which moves the contracting parties to enter into it.
choices.B: the motive of each party, whatever it may be.
choices.C: the object of the contract.
choices.D: the consent of the parties.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said: "The cause of a contract is the essential reason which moves the contracting parties to enter into it," or "the immediate, direct and proximate reason which justifies the creation of an obligation thru the will of the contracting parties." For the producer, it was the distribution of its logs; for the distributor, the sale of the logs for a commission. **B is wrong:** motives are distinct from cause. **C and D are wrong:** object and consent are different requisites. **Bar trap:** a side promise not in the contract was not its cause.

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (cause of the contract)
source.excerpt: The cause of a contract is the essential reason which moves the contracting parties to enter into it (8 Manresa., 5th edition, p. 450). In other words, the cause is the immediate, direct and proximate reason which justifies the creation of an obligation thru the will of the contracting parties (3 Castan, 4th edition, p. 347).

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A bus crashed into the terrace of O's building. To prove her actual damages, O presented (a) a written cost estimate of ₱171,000 prepared by an engineer who never testified, (b) a receipt of ₱35,000 for repair work, and (c) her own testimony that the damage was severe. The bus owner's architect testified that repairs would cost ₱55,000. The trial court awarded ₱150,000 without explaining how it arrived at that figure. Is the award correct? What amount should be awarded? Explain, citing Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The ₱150,000 award has no factual basis. Actual damages must be proved with a reasonable degree of certainty, and the evidence supports only ₱55,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Marikina Auto Line v. People, the Court held that actual damages are not presumed: the claimant must prove the actual amount of loss with a reasonable degree of certainty premised upon competent proof and on the best evidence obtainable, pointing out specific facts that afford a basis for measuring them; they cannot rest on surmises or conjectures. A claimant's bare testimonial assertions should be admitted with extreme caution and buttressed by independent evidence, and an estimate of the damage cost will not suffice.
suggestedAnswer.application: The engineer's estimate is unsupported since he did not testify; O's own testimony is self-interested. Neither the trial court nor the Court of Appeals stated the basis of its award. In the case, the Court awarded ₱55,000, the amount shown by the defendants' own evidence.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The award should be reduced to ₱55,000. **Bar trap:** a repair estimate or a court's unexplained figure is not proof of actual loss; look for competent evidence of the actual amount.

keyPoints: Actual damages are not presumed
Prove the actual loss with reasonable certainty, on competent proof and the best evidence obtainable
Point out specific facts that afford a basis for measuring the damages
Bare self-serving testimony: admit with extreme caution; an estimate will not suffice
Award based on the defense's own evidence: ₱55,000

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the second issue (actual damages)
source.excerpt: The burden of proof is on the party who would be defeated if no evidence would be presented on either side. The burden is to establish one’s case by a preponderance of evidence which means that the evidence, as a whole, adduced by one side, is superior to that of the other. Actual damages are not presumed. The claimant must prove the actual amount of loss with a reasonable degree of certainty premised upon competent proof and on the best evidence obtainable. Specific facts that could afford a basis for measuring whatever compensatory or actual damages are borne must be pointed out. Actual damages cannot be anchored on mere surmises, speculations or conjectures. … While claimants’ bare testimonial assertions in support of their claims for damages should not be discarded altogether, however, the same should be admitted with extreme caution. Their testimonies should be viewed in light of claimants’ self-interest, hence, should not be taken as gospel truth. Such assertion should be buttressed by independent evidence. … An estimate of the damage cost will not suffice: … We note, however, that petitioners adduced evidence that, in their view, the cost of the damage to the terrace of private respondent would amount to P55,000.00. Accordingly, private respondent is entitled to P55,000.00 actual damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Charged with reckless imprudence resulting in damage to property, a bus driver who swerved into a building invokes the sudden emergency rule, claiming he had to avoid a jeepney that intruded into his lane. In his counter-affidavit, however, he said he swerved because the jeepney ahead suddenly stopped. Photographs show heavy damage to the building. Will the defense prosper? Explain, citing Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The sudden emergency rule was not proved, and the evidence shows the driver's own negligence.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Marikina Auto Line v. People, the Court quoted the sudden emergency rule: one who suddenly finds himself in a place of danger and must act without time to consider the best means to avoid it is not guilty of negligence if he fails to adopt what later appears a better method, "unless the emergency in which he finds himself is brought about by his own negligence." The burden was on the driver to prove that he acted in an emergency. Under Article 2185, a person driving a motor vehicle is presumed negligent if at the time of the mishap he was violating a traffic regulation; by his own admission, the driver violated the Land Transportation and Traffic Code when he suddenly swerved to the right.
suggestedAnswer.application: The heavy damage showed a strong impact and a speeding bus; had he not been speeding, he could have stopped. His conflicting statements destroyed his credibility. And if the jeepney were really to blame, he could have filed a third-party complaint against its driver and owner.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The defense fails, and the driver is liable. **Bar trap:** the sudden emergency rule does not protect one whose own negligence (here, speeding) created the emergency, and the one invoking it must prove it.

keyPoints: Sudden emergency rule: no negligence for failing to choose the best means in a sudden danger
Not if the emergency was brought about by one's own negligence
The one invoking it bears the burden of proof
Presumption of negligence when violating a traffic regulation (Art. 2185)
Heavy damage showed speeding; inconsistent statements destroyed credibility

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (sudden emergency rule)
source.excerpt: It was the burden of petitioners herein to prove petitioner Suelto’s defense that he acted on an emergency, that is, he had to swerve the bus to the right to avoid colliding with a passenger jeep coming from EDSA that had overtaken another vehicle and intruded into the lane of the bus. The sudden emergency rule was enunciated by this Court in Gan v. Court of Appeals, thus: [O]ne who suddenly finds himself in a place of danger, and is required to act without time to consider the best means that may be adopted to avoid the impending danger, is not guilty of negligence if he fails to adopt what subsequently and upon reflection may appear to have been a better method unless the emergency in which he finds himself is brought about by his own negligence. … In relation thereto, Article 2185 of the New Civil Code provides that "unless there is proof to the contrary, it is presumed that a person driving a motor vehicle has been negligent, if at the time of mishap, he was violating any traffic regulation." By his own admission, petitioner Suelto violated the Land Transportation and Traffic Code when he suddenly swerved the bus to the right, thereby causing damage to the property of private respondent.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A driver is convicted of reckless imprudence that resulted only in damage to another's property worth ₱55,000. The trial court sentenced him to a straight term of one year of imprisonment. Is the penalty correct? Explain, citing Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. When reckless imprudence results only in damage to property, the penalty under Article 365 of the Revised Penal Code is a fine, not imprisonment.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Marikina Auto Line v. People, the Court held that under the third paragraph of Article 365, "[w]hen the execution of the act covered by this article shall have only resulted in damage to the property of another, the offender shall be punished by a fine ranging from an amount equal to the value of said damages to three times such value, but which shall in no case be less than 25 pesos."
suggestedAnswer.application: Since the only damage was to the terrace, worth ₱55,000, the driver should be fined. In the case, the Court sentenced him to a fine of ₱55,000 with subsidiary imprisonment in case of insolvency.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The prison term should be replaced by a fine. **Bar trap:** the penalty for imprudence resulting only in damage to property is a fine measured by the value of the damage, from once to three times that value.

keyPoints: Art. 365, third paragraph: damage to property only = a fine
Fine from the value of the damage to three times that value, not less than ₱25
A straight prison term was erroneous
Fine of ₱55,000 with subsidiary imprisonment in case of insolvency

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the third issue (the penalty)
source.excerpt: We also agree with petitioner Suelto’s contention that the trial court erred in sentencing him to suffer a straight penalty of one (1) year. This is so because under the third paragraph of Article 365 of the Revised Penal Code, the offender must be sentenced to pay a fine when the execution of the act shall have only resulted in damage to property.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: As explained in Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People, the two kinds of actual or compensatory damages under Article 2199 of the Civil Code are

choices.A: moral damages and exemplary damages.
choices.B: nominal damages and temperate damages.
choices.C: liquidated damages and unliquidated damages.
choices.D: the loss of what a person already possesses (daño emergente) and the failure to receive as a benefit that which would have pertained to him (lucro cesante).

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court said: "There are two kinds of actual or compensatory damages: one is the loss of what a person already possesses (daño emergente), and the other is the failure to receive as a benefit that which would have pertained to him (lucro cesante)." **A, B and C are wrong:** these are other kinds of damages, not the two components of actual damages. **Bar trap:** both components must still be proved.

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the second issue (the two kinds of actual damages)
source.excerpt: There are two kinds of actual or compensatory damages: one is the loss of what a person already possesses (daño emergente), and the other is the failure to receive as a benefit that which would have pertained to him (lucro cesante).

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People, actual or compensatory damages are designed

choices.A: to repair the wrong that has been done, to compensate for the injury inflicted and not to impose a penalty.
choices.B: to punish the wrongdoer as an example to the public.
choices.C: to vindicate a right that has been violated even if no loss was suffered.
choices.D: to compensate for mental anguish and wounded feelings.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court quoted that actual damages "proceed from a sense of natural justice and are designed to repair the wrong that has been done, to compensate for the injury inflicted and not to impose a penalty." **B is wrong:** that describes exemplary damages. **C is wrong:** that describes nominal damages. **D is wrong:** that describes moral damages. **Bar trap:** match each kind of damages to its purpose.

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the second issue (purpose of actual damages)
source.excerpt: Under Article 2199 of the Civil Code, actual or compensatory damages are those awarded in satisfaction of, or in recompense for, loss or injury sustained. They proceed from a sense of natural justice and are designed to repair the wrong that has been done, to compensate for the injury inflicted and not to impose a penalty.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under the rule quoted in Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People, where goods are destroyed by the defendant's wrongful act, the plaintiff is normally entitled to

choices.A: their original purchase price, regardless of their age.
choices.B: twice their market value.
choices.C: their value at the time of destruction, normally the market price of identical or essentially similar goods, plus in a proper case damages for loss of use before replacement.
choices.D: only nominal damages.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court quoted that "where goods are destroyed by the wrongful act of defendant, the plaintiff is entitled to their value at the time of the destruction, that is, normally, the sum of money which he would have to pay in the market for identical or essentially similar goods, plus in a proper case, damages for the loss of the use during the period before replacement." **A, B and D are wrong:** none is the measure stated. **Bar trap:** the reference point is the value at the time of destruction.

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the second issue (destroyed goods)
source.excerpt: The Court further declared that "where goods are destroyed by the wrongful act of defendant, the plaintiff is entitled to their value at the time of the destruction, that is, normally, the sum of money which he would have to pay in the market for identical or essentially similar goods, plus in a proper case, damages for the loss of the use during the period before replacement.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Which provision did the Court apply in Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People to presume the bus driver negligent?

choices.A: Article 2180 of the Civil Code, on the employer's vicarious liability.
choices.B: Article 2185 of the Civil Code, under which a person driving a motor vehicle is presumed negligent if, at the time of the mishap, he was violating any traffic regulation.
choices.C: Article 1733 of the Civil Code, on the extraordinary diligence of common carriers.
choices.D: Article 2176 of the Civil Code, on the definition of quasi-delict.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court cited Article 2185: "unless there is proof to the contrary, it is presumed that a person driving a motor vehicle has been negligent, if at the time of mishap, he was violating any traffic regulation," and found that the driver, by his own admission, violated the Land Transportation and Traffic Code. **A, C and D are wrong:** not the provision applied for this presumption (and the injured party was not a passenger). **Bar trap:** this presumption is rebuttable ("unless there is proof to the contrary").

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (presumption of negligence)
source.excerpt: In relation thereto, Article 2185 of the New Civil Code provides that "unless there is proof to the contrary, it is presumed that a person driving a motor vehicle has been negligent, if at the time of mishap, he was violating any traffic regulation."

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What was the final judgment in Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People?

choices.A: The driver was fined ₱55,000, with subsidiary imprisonment in case of insolvency, and the petitioners were ordered to pay ₱55,000 actual damages and ₱20,000 exemplary damages.
choices.B: The driver was acquitted under the sudden emergency rule.
choices.C: The one-year prison term was affirmed, and actual damages were fixed at ₱100,000.
choices.D: Actual damages of ₱171,088.46 were awarded, as estimated by the owner's engineer.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court ruled that the driver "is sentenced to pay a fine of P55,000.00 with subsidiary imprisonment in case of insolvency" and ordered the petitioners to pay "P55,000.00 by way of actual damages, and P20,000.00 by way of exemplary damages." **B is wrong:** the defense was not proved. **C is wrong:** both were modified. **D is wrong:** the estimate was not proof of actual loss. **Bar trap:** the fine and the actual damages happened to be equal because the fine is measured by the value of the damage.

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, the disposition
source.excerpt: IN LIGHT OF ALL THE FOREGOING, the petition is PARTIALLY GRANTED. The joint decision of the Regional Trial Court of Quezon City is AFFIRMED WITH THE MODIFICATION that petitioner Suelto is sentenced to pay a fine of P55,000.00 with subsidiary imprisonment in case of insolvency. Petitioners are ORDERED to pay to Erlinda V. Valdellon, jointly and severally, the total amount of P55,000.00 by way of actual damages, and P20,000.00 by way of exemplary damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In criminal cases where the imposable penalty is reclusion perpetua to death, what kinds of damages does the Court generally award? Briefly explain the nature of civil indemnity, and why the Court may increase its amount, as discussed in People v. Jugueta.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Generally three: civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages; actual damages or temperate damages may also be awarded in some instances. Civil indemnity ex delicto is equivalent to actual or compensatory damages in civil law, and since it is not a penalty or fine, its amount can be increased by the Court when appropriate.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In People v. Jugueta, the Court explained that civil indemnity ex delicto is the indemnity authorized in criminal law for the offended party, apart from other proven actual damages, and stems from Article 100 of the Revised Penal Code (every person criminally liable is also civilly liable). It is "technically, not a penalty or a fine; hence, it can be increased by the Court when appropriate." Article 2206 of the Civil Code imposes only a minimum (₱3,000) and no ceiling, so the amount may be increased when the present circumstances warrant.
suggestedAnswer.application: Civil indemnity is a kind of monetary restitution to the victim for the damage done by the accused, covering the civil aspect of the crime, in addition to the penalty of imprisonment.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, plus actual or temperate damages in some cases. **Bar trap:** civil indemnity is not a fine, so the rule against increasing penalties does not stop the Court from raising it; Article 2206 sets only a floor.

keyPoints: Generally: civil indemnity, moral damages, exemplary damages; also actual or temperate damages in some instances
Civil indemnity ex delicto = actual or compensatory damages in civil law; from Art. 100 RPC
Not a penalty or fine, so the Court may increase it
Art. 2206: minimum ₱3,000, no ceiling
A monetary restitution to the victim for the civil aspect

source.caseTitle: People v. Jugueta
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (kinds of damages in crimes)
source.excerpt: Anent the award of damages, the Court deems it proper to address the matter in detail as regards criminal cases where the imposable penalty is reclusion perpetua to death. Generally, in these types of criminal cases, there are three kinds of damages awarded by the Court; namely: civil indemnity, moral, and exemplary damages. Likewise, actual damages may be awarded or temperate damages in some instances. First, civil indemnity ex delicto is the indemnity authorized in our criminal law for the offended party, in the amount authorized by the prevailing judicial policy and apart from other proven actual damages, which itself is equivalent to actual or compensatory damages in civil law. This award stems from Article 100 of the RPC which states, "Every person criminally liable for a felony is also civilly liable." It is to be noted that civil indemnity is, technically, not a penalty or a fine; hence, it can be increased by the Court when appropriate. … Also, it is apparent from Article 2206 that the law only imposes a minimum amount for awards of civil indemnity, which is ₱3,000.00. The law did not provide for a ceiling. Thus, although the minimum amount for the award cannot be changed, increasing the amount awarded as civil indemnity can be validly modified and increased when the present circumstance warrants it.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: X was convicted of homicide. During the trial, the prosecution proved that X committed the crime in the dwelling of the victim, but dwelling was not alleged in the Information. X argues that (a) since dwelling was not alleged, it cannot affect his liability at all, and (b) exemplary damages may be awarded only for an ordinary, not a qualifying, aggravating circumstance. Rule on both arguments, citing People v. Jugueta.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Both arguments fail as to the civil liability. An aggravating circumstance not alleged cannot be used to increase the penalty, but if proved at trial it entitles the victim to exemplary damages; and an aggravating circumstance, whether ordinary or qualifying, supports exemplary damages.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In People v. Jugueta, the Court held that aggravating circumstances must be stated in the information so as not to trample on the accused's right to be informed, but "[i]n the civil aspect, the presence of an aggravating circumstance, even if not alleged in the information but proven during trial would entitle the victim to an award of exemplary damages." It also held that the ordinary or qualifying nature of an aggravating circumstance is a distinction that matters only to the criminal, not the civil, liability, so either kind entitles the offended party to exemplary damages under Article 2230. For homicide, ₱50,000 exemplary damages is added if an aggravating circumstance is proved but not alleged.
suggestedAnswer.application: Dwelling cannot raise X's penalty since it was not alleged, but having been proved, it supports an award of exemplary damages in addition to civil indemnity and moral damages.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Exemplary damages may be awarded. **Bar trap:** the requirement to allege aggravating circumstances protects the accused in the criminal aspect only; it does not bar exemplary damages in the civil aspect.

keyPoints: Aggravating circumstances must be alleged to affect the penalty (right to be informed)
In the civil aspect, a proved but unalleged aggravating circumstance supports exemplary damages
Ordinary or qualifying: the distinction matters only to criminal liability
Exemplary damages also for highly reprehensible or outrageous conduct (Art. 2229)
Homicide: ₱50,000 exemplary damages if an aggravating circumstance is proved but not alleged

source.caseTitle: People v. Jugueta
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (exemplary damages)
source.excerpt: Withal, the ordinary or qualifying nature of an aggravating circumstance is a distinction that should only be of consequence to the criminal, rather than to the civil, liability of the offender. In fine, relative to the civil aspect of the case, an aggravating circumstance, whether ordinary or qualifying, should entitle the offended party to an award of exemplary damages within the unbridled meaning of Article 2230 of the Civil Code. The reason is fairly obvious as to why the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure requires aggravating circumstances, whether ordinary or qualifying, to be stated in the complaint or information. It is in order not to trample on the constitutional right of an accused to be informed of the nature of the alleged offense that he or she has committed. A criminal complaint or information should basically contain the elements of the crime, as well as its qualifying and ordinary aggravating circumstances, for the court to effectively determine the proper penalty it should impose. This, however, is not similar in the recovery of civil liability. In the civil aspect, the presence of an aggravating circumstance, even if not alleged in the information but proven during trial would entitle the victim to an award of exemplary damages. … However, an award of ₱50,000.00 exemplary damages in a crime of homicide shall be added if there is an aggravating circumstance present that has been proven but not alleged in the information.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A was convicted of murder qualified by treachery, with the ordinary aggravating circumstance of dwelling, so the penalty would have been death; because of R.A. 9346, he was sentenced to reclusion perpetua. A argues that the damages should follow the penalty actually imposed, reclusion perpetua. The heirs presented no receipts for burial expenses. Following People v. Jugueta, what damages should be awarded to the heirs, and in what amounts?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The damages follow the penalty imposable by law (death), not the penalty actually imposed. The heirs should receive ₱100,000 civil indemnity, ₱100,000 moral damages, ₱100,000 exemplary damages, and ₱50,000 temperate damages, all with 6% interest from finality.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In People v. Jugueta, the Court held that despite R.A. 9346, "the principal consideration for the award of damages ... is 'the penalty provided by law or imposable for the offense because of its heinousness, not the public penalty actually imposed on the offender.'" For crimes where the imposable penalty is death because of an ordinary aggravating circumstance but reclusion perpetua is imposed, the amounts are ₱100,000 civil indemnity, ₱100,000 moral damages and ₱100,000 exemplary damages. When no documentary evidence of burial or funeral expenses is presented, ₱50,000 temperate damages is awarded. In the case, all these awards earn 6% interest from finality.
suggestedAnswer.application: With dwelling, death would have been imposed, so A's case falls under the highest bracket. Had there been no ordinary aggravating circumstance (reclusion perpetua only), the amounts would be ₱75,000 each.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: ₱100,000 each in civil indemnity, moral and exemplary damages, plus ₱50,000 temperate damages. **Bar trap:** do not base the damages on the reduced penalty actually imposed; use the penalty the law prescribes for the crime as committed. Also check later rulings for any change in these amounts.

keyPoints: Basis: the penalty imposable by law, not the penalty actually imposed
Death reduced to reclusion perpetua: ₱100,000 each (civil indemnity, moral, exemplary)
Reclusion perpetua only: ₱75,000 each
No proof of burial expenses: ₱50,000 temperate damages
6% interest from finality on all amounts

source.caseTitle: People v. Jugueta
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (basis and standard amounts)
source.excerpt: As a result, the death penalty can no longer be imposed. Instead, they have to impose reclusion perpetua. Despite this, the principal consideration for the award of damages, following the ruling in People v. Salome and People v. Quiachon, is "the penalty provided by law or imposable for the offense because of its heinousness, not the public penalty actually imposed on the offender." … Again, for crimes where the imposable penalty is death in view of the attendance of an ordinary aggravating circumstance but due to the prohibition to impose the death penalty, the actual penalty imposed is reclusion perpetua, the latest jurisprudence pegs the amount of ₱100,000.00 as civil indemnity and ₱100,0000.00 as moral damages. For the qualifying aggravating circumstance and/or the ordinary aggravating circumstances present, the amount of ₱100,000.00 is awarded as exemplary damages aside from civil indemnity and moral damages. … When the circumstances surrounding the crime call for the imposition of reclusion perpetua only, there being no ordinary aggravating circumstance, the Court rules that the proper amounts should be ₱75,000.00 as civil indemnity, ₱75,000.00 as moral damages and ₱75,000.00 exemplary damages, regardless of the number of qualifying aggravating circumstances present. … VII. In all of the above instances, when no documentary evidence of burial or funeral expenses is presented in court, the amount of ₱50,000.00 as temperate damages shall be awarded.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under the discussion of moral damages in People v. Jugueta, which of the following is imperative for moral damages to be awarded?

choices.A: Proof of pecuniary loss with receipts.
choices.B: That injury was suffered by the claimant, and that such injury sprang from any of the cases in Articles 2219 and 2220 of the Civil Code.
choices.C: That the crime was attended by an aggravating circumstance.
choices.D: That the amount claimed is fixed by law.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** Quoting Del Mundo v. CA, the Court said that although "no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary," it is imperative "that (1) injury must have been suffered by the claimant, and (2) such injury must have sprung from any of the cases expressed in Article 2219 and Article 2220 of the Civil Code." **A is wrong:** no proof of pecuniary loss is needed. **C is wrong:** that is for exemplary damages. **D is wrong:** the amount is left to the court's discretion. **Bar trap:** moral damages are compensatory, not punitive.

source.caseTitle: People v. Jugueta
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (moral damages)
source.excerpt: These damages must be understood to be in the concept of grants, not punitive or corrective in nature, calculated to compensate the claimant for the injury suffered. Although incapable of exactness and no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary in order that moral damages may be awarded, the amount of indemnity being left to the discretion of the court, it is imperative, nevertheless, that (1) injury must have been suffered by the claimant, and (2) such injury must have sprung from any of the cases expressed in Article 2219 and Article 2220 of the Civil Code.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In People v. Jugueta, when are temperate damages of ₱50,000 awarded in murder or homicide cases?

choices.A: When no evidence of burial and funeral expenses is presented, since the heirs undeniably suffered pecuniary loss though its exact amount was not proved.
choices.B: Only when the heirs present official receipts for the burial.
choices.C: In addition to proven actual damages for burial, in every case.
choices.D: Only when the crime is attended by an aggravating circumstance.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said temperate damages are proper "when no evidence of burial and funeral expenses is presented," since under Article 2224 "it cannot be denied that the heirs of the victims suffered pecuniary loss although the exact amount was not proved," and it increased the amount to ₱50,000. **B is wrong:** with receipts, actual damages are awarded instead. **C is wrong:** temperate damages take the place of unproved actual damages. **D is wrong:** no aggravating circumstance is required. **Bar trap:** temperate damages fill the gap when a loss is certain but its amount is not.

source.caseTitle: People v. Jugueta
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (temperate damages)
source.excerpt: Aside from those discussed earlier, the Court also awards temperate damages in certain cases. The award of ₱25,000.00 as temperate damages in homicide or murder cases is proper when no evidence of burial and funeral expenses is presented in the trial court. Under Article 2224 of the Civil Code, temperate damages may be recovered, as it cannot be denied that the heirs of the victims suffered pecuniary loss although the exact amount was not proved. In this case, the Court now increases the amount to be awarded as temperate damages to ₱50,000.00.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under the summary in People v. Jugueta, what damages are awarded to the heirs in a consummated homicide or reckless imprudence resulting in homicide, absent any aggravating circumstance?

choices.A: ₱100,000 civil indemnity, ₱100,000 moral damages and ₱100,000 exemplary damages.
choices.B: ₱75,000 civil indemnity and ₱75,000 moral damages.
choices.C: ₱50,000 civil indemnity, ₱50,000 moral damages and ₱50,000 exemplary damages.
choices.D: ₱50,000 civil indemnity and ₱50,000 moral damages, without exemplary damages.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** For crimes resulting in death with divisible penalties, "like homicide, death under tumultuous affray, reckless imprudence resulting to homicide, the civil indemnity awarded to the heirs of the victim shall be ₱50,000.00 and ₱50,000.00 moral damages without exemplary damages being awarded." **A is the bracket for murder punishable by death reduced to reclusion perpetua. B is wrong:** not the amounts for homicide. **C is wrong:** exemplary damages are added only if an aggravating circumstance is proved. **Bar trap:** the bracket depends on the nature of the penalty (divisible or indivisible).

source.caseTitle: People v. Jugueta
source.part: Decision, summary of the standard amounts (crimes with divisible penalties)
source.excerpt: In other crimes that resulted in the death of a victim and the penalty consists of divisible penalties, like homicide, death under tumultuous affray, reckless imprudence resulting to homicide, the civil indemnity awarded to the heirs of the victim shall be ₱50,000.00 and ₱50,000.00 moral damages without exemplary damages being awarded.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: As explained in People v. Jugueta, exemplary or corrective damages are imposed

choices.A: to compensate the victim for the actual pecuniary loss suffered.
choices.B: to restore the victim's spiritual status quo ante.
choices.C: by way of example or correction for the public good, in addition to the moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages.
choices.D: to vindicate a right where no loss was suffered.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court quoted Article 2229: "Exemplary or corrective damages are imposed, by way of example or correction for the public good, in addition to the moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages," and explained that they serve as a deterrent to serious wrongdoing. **A is wrong:** that is actual damages. **B is wrong:** that is the aim of moral damages. **D is wrong:** that is nominal damages. **Bar trap:** exemplary damages are always in addition to other damages, never awarded alone.

source.caseTitle: People v. Jugueta
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (purpose of exemplary damages)
source.excerpt: ART. 2229. Exemplary or corrective damages are imposed, by way of example or correction for the public good, in addition to the moral, temperate, liquidated or compensatory damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In People v. Jugueta, what did the Court order the accused to pay the heirs of each of the two children killed?

choices.A: ₱75,000 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages.
choices.B: ₱100,000 as civil indemnity, ₱100,000 as moral damages, ₱100,000 as exemplary damages and ₱50,000 as temperate damages, with 6% interest from finality.
choices.C: ₱50,000 as civil indemnity and ₱50,000 as moral damages only.
choices.D: ₱100,000 as civil indemnity and actual damages for burial supported by receipts.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court ordered payment, for each of the two victims, of "(a) ₱100,000.00 as civil indemnity; (b) ₱100,000.00 as moral damages; (c) ₱100,000.00 as exemplary damages; and (d) ₱50,000.00 as temperate damages," with 6% interest from finality. **A is wrong:** dwelling made the imposable penalty death. **C is wrong:** that is the homicide bracket. **D is wrong:** no burial receipts were presented, hence temperate damages. **Bar trap:** the attempted murders carried ₱50,000 each, a different bracket.

source.caseTitle: People v. Jugueta
source.part: Decision, the disposition
source.excerpt: He is ORDERED to PAY the heirs of Mary Grace Divina and Claudine Divina the following amounts for each of the two victims: (a) ₱100,000.00 as civil indemnity; (b) ₱100,000.00 as moral damages; (c) ₱100,000.00 as exemplary damages; and (d) ₱50,000.00 as temperate damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A borrowed ₱1,000,000 from B in 2014 under a promissory note that stipulated no interest. A failed to pay despite B's written demand on March 1, 2015. B sued, won, and the judgment became final on June 1, 2017, but A has not paid. Applying Nacar v. Gallery Frames, what legal interest is due, at what rate, and for which periods?

suggestedAnswer.answer: A owes legal interest of 6% a year on the ₱1,000,000 from the demand on March 1, 2015 (default) until the judgment became final, and 6% a year on the total amount due from June 1, 2017 until full payment. Any interest due itself earns legal interest from judicial demand.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Nacar v. Gallery Frames, the Court applied BSP-MB Circular No. 799, effective July 1, 2013, under which the rate of interest for the loan or forbearance of any money, goods or credits and the rate allowed in judgments, absent an express contract, is 6% a year, no longer 12%. It modified the Eastern Shipping guidelines: for a loan or forbearance with no stipulated rate, interest is 6% from default, i.e., from judicial or extrajudicial demand under Article 1169; the interest due itself earns legal interest from judicial demand; and when a money judgment becomes final and executory, the rate is 6% from such finality until satisfaction, that period being equivalent to a forbearance of credit.
suggestedAnswer.application: The loan was made and the demand made after July 1, 2013, so the 12% rate does not apply to any period. Interest runs at 6% from the demand that put A in default, and at 6% from the finality of the judgment until payment.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: 6% throughout, from demand and then from finality until full payment. **Bar trap:** the 12% rate in Eastern Shipping applies only up to June 30, 2013; the new rate is prospective, so for periods from July 1, 2013 it is 6%.

keyPoints: BSP-MB Circular No. 799, effective July 1, 2013: 6% for loans, forbearance and judgments absent stipulation
Prospective only: 12% only until June 30, 2013
Loan, no stipulation: 6% from default (judicial or extrajudicial demand, Art. 1169)
Interest due earns legal interest from judicial demand
From finality of the judgment: 6% until satisfaction

source.caseTitle: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of legal interest (BSP-MB Circular No. 799)
source.excerpt: Thus, from the foregoing, in the absence of an express stipulation as to the rate of interest that would govern the parties, the rate of legal interest for loans or forbearance of any money, goods or credits and the rate allowed in judgments shall no longer be twelve percent (12%) per annum - as reflected in the case of Eastern Shipping Lines and Subsection X305.1 of the Manual of Regulations for Banks and Sections 4305Q.1, 4305S.3 and 4303P.1 of the Manual of Regulations for Non-Bank Financial Institutions, before its amendment by BSP-MB Circular No. 799 - but will now be six percent (6%) per annum effective July 1, 2013. It should be noted, nonetheless, that the new rate could only be applied prospectively and not retroactively. Consequently, the twelve percent (12%) per annum legal interest shall apply only until June 30, 2013. Come July 1, 2013 the new rate of six percent (6%) per annum shall be the prevailing rate of interest when applicable. … When the obligation is breached, and it consists in the payment of a sum of money, i.e., a loan or forbearance of money, the interest due should be that which may have been stipulated in writing. Furthermore, the interest due shall itself earn legal interest from the time it is judicially demanded. In the absence of stipulation, the rate of interest shall be 6% per annum to be computed from default, i.e., from judicial or extrajudicial demand under and subject to the provisions of Article 1169 of the Civil Code. … When the judgment of the court awarding a sum of money becomes final and executory, the rate of legal interest, whether the case falls under paragraph 1 or paragraph 2, above, shall be 6% per annum from such finality until its satisfaction, this interim period being deemed to be by then an equivalent to a forbearance of credit.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: (a) A judgment for a sum of money became final in 2010 and fixed 12% legal interest from finality until payment; the debtor still has not paid in 2026. May the debtor ask that the rate be reduced to 6% from July 1, 2013? (b) A different judgment became final in 2002 and is executed only now, with no rate fixed in it. What rates apply from its finality? Explain, citing Nacar v. Gallery Frames.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. Judgments that became final and executory before July 1, 2013 are not disturbed and continue to be implemented applying the rate of interest fixed in them. (b) Following the disposition in Nacar, 12% a year from finality until June 30, 2013, and 6% a year from July 1, 2013 until full satisfaction.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Nacar v. Gallery Frames, the Court held that the new 6% rate applies prospectively only, so the 12% rate applies only until June 30, 2013, and "with regard to those judgments that have become final and executory prior to July 1, 2013, said judgments shall not be disturbed and shall continue to be implemented applying the rate of interest fixed therein." In the case itself, whose judgment became final on May 27, 2002, the Court ordered interest of 12% from May 27, 2002 to June 30, 2013 and 6% from July 1, 2013 until full satisfaction.
suggestedAnswer.application: In (a), the rate was fixed in a final judgment before the circular, so it stays at 12%. In (b), no rate was fixed, so the general rule applies: the old rate up to June 30, 2013, and the new rate from July 1, 2013.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) The 12% fixed in the earlier final judgment stays; (b) 12% then 6%. **Bar trap:** distinguish a final judgment that itself fixed the rate (untouched) from the general shift of the legal rate for periods after July 1, 2013.

keyPoints: The 6% rate applies prospectively from July 1, 2013
12% applies only until June 30, 2013
Judgments final before July 1, 2013: not disturbed; the rate fixed in them continues
In Nacar: 12% from May 27, 2002 to June 30, 2013, then 6% from July 1, 2013

source.caseTitle: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of legal interest (transition and judgments already final)
source.excerpt: Nonetheless, with regard to those judgments that have become final and executory prior to July 1, 2013, said judgments shall not be disturbed and shall continue to be implemented applying the rate of interest fixed therein. … (3) interest of twelve percent (12%) per annum of the total monetary awards, computed from May 27, 2002 to June 30, 2013 and six percent (6%) per annum from July 1, 2013 until their full satisfaction.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A Labor Arbiter found an employee illegally dismissed and awarded separation pay and backwages "computed only up to promulgation of this decision." The employer appealed all the way to the Supreme Court and lost four years later. In execution, the employee asks that the awards be recomputed up to the finality of the judgment. The employer invokes the immutability of final judgments. Who is correct? Explain, citing Nacar v. Gallery Frames.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The employee. The recomputation of the monetary consequences of illegal dismissal up to finality does not alter the final judgment, so it does not violate the immutability of judgments.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Nacar v. Gallery Frames, the Court explained (following Session Delights) that such a decision has two parts: the finding of illegality and its monetary consequences, which is final, and the computation of the awards, which is time-bound and can be recomputed. A recomputation is part of the law, Article 279 of the Labor Code, read into the decision; by the nature of an illegal dismissal case, the reliefs continue to add up until full satisfaction. "The illegal dismissal ruling stands; only the computation of monetary consequences of this dismissal is affected, and this is not a violation of the principle of immutability of final judgments." Where separation pay is given in lieu of reinstatement, the finality of the decision is the reckoning point.
suggestedAnswer.application: The employer delayed payment by appealing; the larger amount is the risk it ran when it continued to seek recourse. Backwages and separation pay are computed up to the finality of the decision, with legal interest thereafter.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The awards should be recomputed up to finality. **Bar trap:** the immutability of judgments protects the ruling, not a time-bound computation of its consequences.

keyPoints: Two parts: the finding of illegality and its consequences (final) and the computation (time-bound)
Recomputation is part of the law (Art. 279, Labor Code) read into the decision
Reliefs continue to add up until full satisfaction
Not a violation of the immutability of final judgments
With separation pay in lieu of reinstatement, finality of the decision is the reckoning point

source.caseTitle: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the recomputation of the awards
source.excerpt: Consequently, from the above disquisitions, under the terms of the decision which is sought to be executed by the petitioner, no essential change is made by a recomputation as this step is a necessary consequence that flows from the nature of the illegality of dismissal declared by the Labor Arbiter in that decision. A recomputation (or an original computation, if no previous computation has been made) is a part of the law – specifically, Article 279 of the Labor Code and the established jurisprudence on this provision – that is read into the decision. By the nature of an illegal dismissal case, the reliefs continue to add up until full satisfaction, as expressed under Article 279 of the Labor Code. The recomputation of the consequences of illegal dismissal upon execution of the decision does not constitute an alteration or amendment of the final decision being implemented. The illegal dismissal ruling stands; only the computation of monetary consequences of this dismissal is affected, and this is not a violation of the principle of immutability of final judgments. That the amount respondents shall now pay has greatly increased is a consequence that it cannot avoid as it is the risk that it ran when it continued to seek recourses against the Labor Arbiter's decision.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under BSP-MB Circular No. 799, as applied in Nacar v. Gallery Frames, the rate of interest for the loan or forbearance of any money, goods or credits and the rate allowed in judgments, in the absence of an express contract, is

choices.A: twelve percent (12%) per annum.
choices.B: six percent (6%) per annum, effective July 1, 2013.
choices.C: whatever the court considers reasonable.
choices.D: the prevailing bank lending rate.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** Section 1 of the circular, quoted by the Court, states: "The rate of interest for the loan or forbearance of any money, goods or credits and the rate allowed in judgments, in the absence of an express contract as to such rate of interest, shall be six percent (6%) per annum," effective July 1, 2013. **A is wrong:** 12% applies only until June 30, 2013. **C and D are wrong:** the rate is fixed by the circular. **Bar trap:** the new rate is prospective.

source.caseTitle: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of legal interest (BSP-MB Circular No. 799)
source.excerpt: Section 1. The rate of interest for the loan or forbearance of any money, goods or credits and the rate allowed in judgments, in the absence of an express contract as to such rate of interest, shall be six percent (6%) per annum.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under the guidelines in Nacar v. Gallery Frames, when an obligation not constituting a loan or forbearance of money is breached, and the amount cannot be reasonably established at the time of demand, interest on the damages begins to run

choices.A: from the date the obligation was constituted.
choices.B: from the filing of the complaint, in every case.
choices.C: only from the date the judgment of the court is made, when the quantification of damages may be deemed reasonably ascertained.
choices.D: only from the finality of the judgment.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court restated that "when such certainty cannot be so reasonably established at the time the demand is made, the interest shall begin to run only from the date the judgment of the court is made (at which time the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained)." **A is wrong:** no such rule. **B is wrong:** demand is used only when the amount is then reasonably certain. **D is wrong:** finality starts the separate rule 3. **Bar trap:** Nacar changed the rates, not the reckoning rules of Eastern Shipping.

source.caseTitle: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
source.part: Decision, the modified guidelines (rule 2)
source.excerpt: Accordingly, where the demand is established with reasonable certainty, the interest shall begin to run from the time the claim is made judicially or extrajudicially (Art. 1169, Civil Code), but when such certainty cannot be so reasonably established at the time the demand is made, the interest shall begin to run only from the date the judgment of the court is made (at which time the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained).

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Nacar v. Gallery Frames, how is the new 6% legal interest rate applied?

choices.A: Prospectively only; 12% applies until June 30, 2013, and 6% from July 1, 2013.
choices.B: Retroactively to all unpaid obligations, from their inception.
choices.C: Only to obligations contracted after July 1, 2013.
choices.D: Only to judgments rendered by the Supreme Court.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said "the new rate could only be applied prospectively and not retroactively. Consequently, the twelve percent (12%) per annum legal interest shall apply only until June 30, 2013. Come July 1, 2013 the new rate of six percent (6%) per annum shall be the prevailing rate of interest when applicable." **B is wrong:** no retroactive application. **C is wrong:** older obligations also earn 6% for periods after July 1, 2013 (as in Nacar itself). **D is wrong:** no such limit. **Bar trap:** split the computation at July 1, 2013.

source.caseTitle: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of legal interest (prospective application)
source.excerpt: It should be noted, nonetheless, that the new rate could only be applied prospectively and not retroactively. Consequently, the twelve percent (12%) per annum legal interest shall apply only until June 30, 2013. Come July 1, 2013 the new rate of six percent (6%) per annum shall be the prevailing rate of interest when applicable.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under the guidelines in Nacar v. Gallery Frames, why does legal interest run from the finality of a money judgment until its satisfaction?

choices.A: Because the judgment debtor is presumed to be in bad faith.
choices.B: Because the interim period is deemed to be equivalent to a forbearance of credit.
choices.C: Because it is a penalty for delaying the execution.
choices.D: Because the parties are deemed to have agreed to it.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The guideline states that from finality until satisfaction the rate is 6% a year, "this interim period being deemed to be by then an equivalent to a forbearance of credit." **A, C and D are wrong:** none is the reason given. **Bar trap:** the reason is the same as in Eastern Shipping; only the rate changed from 12% to 6%.

source.caseTitle: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
source.part: Decision, the modified guidelines (rule 3)
source.excerpt: When the judgment of the court awarding a sum of money becomes final and executory, the rate of legal interest, whether the case falls under paragraph 1 or paragraph 2, above, shall be 6% per annum from such finality until its satisfaction, this interim period being deemed to be by then an equivalent to a forbearance of credit.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What did the Court order in Nacar v. Gallery Frames?

choices.A: Payment of the original ₱158,919.92 only, since the Labor Arbiter's decision was final.
choices.B: Backwages and separation pay up to the Labor Arbiter's decision, with 6% interest from 1998.
choices.C: Backwages from dismissal up to May 27, 2002, separation pay up to May 27, 2002, and interest of 12% from May 27, 2002 to June 30, 2013 and 6% from July 1, 2013 until full satisfaction.
choices.D: Reinstatement without backwages.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court ordered payment of "(1) backwages computed from the time petitioner was illegally dismissed on January 24, 1997 up to May 27, 2002 ... (2) separation pay computed from August 1990 up to May 27, 2002 ... and (3) interest of twelve percent (12%) per annum of the total monetary awards, computed from May 27, 2002 to June 30, 2013 and six percent (6%) per annum from July 1, 2013 until their full satisfaction." **A and B are wrong:** the awards were recomputed up to finality. **D is wrong:** separation pay was given in lieu of reinstatement. **Bar trap:** finality (May 27, 2002) is both the end of the computation and the start of interest.

source.caseTitle: Nacar v. Gallery Frames, et al.
source.part: Decision, the disposition
source.excerpt: WHEREFORE, premises considered, the Decision dated September 23, 2008 of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 98591, and the Resolution dated October 9, 2009 are REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Respondents are Ordered to Pay petitioner: (1) backwages computed from the time petitioner was illegally dismissed on January 24, 1997 up to May 27, 2002, when the Resolution of this Court in G.R. No. 151332 became final and executory; (2) separation pay computed from August 1990 up to May 27, 2002 at the rate of one month pay per year of service; and (3) interest of twelve percent (12%) per annum of the total monetary awards, computed from May 27, 2002 to June 30, 2013 and six percent (6%) per annum from July 1, 2013 until their full satisfaction.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A loan agreement stipulated interest of 18% a year. The borrower defaulted, the lender sued, and the court ordered payment of the principal with 18% interest. The borrower argues that from the finality of the judgment until payment, only the legal rate of 6% a year should apply, citing the Eastern Shipping and Nacar guidelines. Is the borrower correct? Explain, citing the 2019 Decision in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The stipulated interest, unless excessive and unconscionable, is the law between the parties and applies until full payment of the obligation, not only until finality of the judgment. The legal rate applies only in the absence of stipulated interest.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Lara's Gifts v. Midtown (2019), the Court held that paragraph 3 of the Eastern Shipping guidelines failed to qualify that, for loans or forbearance of money, the prevailing legal interest applies only in the absence of stipulated interest. Rulings that replaced the stipulated interest with the legal rate from finality contravene Article 2209, which mandates that the indemnity for a debtor's delay is the interest agreed upon. Under Article 1159, contractual obligations have the force of law between the parties; under Article 1956, no interest is due unless expressly stipulated in writing. Unless the stipulated interest is excessive and unconscionable, there is no legal basis to reduce it at any time until full payment.
suggestedAnswer.application: The 18% rate was stipulated and is not claimed to be unconscionable, so it continues to run until the borrower pays in full; the 6% legal rate would apply only if no rate had been agreed.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The borrower is wrong; the 18% stipulated rate runs until full payment. **Bar trap:** the 6% rate from finality under Nacar applies to the legal rate, not to replace a valid stipulated rate. (The Court restated the guidelines on reconsideration in 2022; check that resolution too.)

keyPoints: Stipulated interest is the law between the parties (Art. 1159)
It applies until full payment, unless excessive and unconscionable
Legal interest applies only in the absence of stipulated interest (Art. 2209)
Replacing the stipulated rate with the legal rate from finality contravenes Art. 2209
No interest unless expressly stipulated in writing (Art. 1956)

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
source.part: The Court's Ruling, imposition of legal interest (stipulated interest until full payment)
source.excerpt: Paragraph 3 above failed to qualify that for loans or forbearance of money, the prevailing legal interest should only apply in the absence of stipulated interest. The stipulated interest is the law between the parties and should apply from the time of extrajudicial or judicial demand until full payment. This omission resulted in several rulings of this Court, which imposed the stipulated interest on the adjudged amount until finality of the decision BUT applied the prevailing legal interest in lieu of the stipulated interest from finality of the decision until full payment of the obligation. This is in direct contravention of the law, particularly Article 2209 of the Civil Code, which mandates that when a debtor incurs a delay in obligations to pay a sum of money, the indemnity for damages shall be the payment of the interest agreed upon. Only in the absence of a stipulated interest will the legal interest be applied. To repeat, the stipulated interest is the law between the parties, and should be applied until full payment of the obligation. … Thus, unless the stipulated interest is excessive and unconscionable, there is no legal basis for the reduction of the stipulated interest at any time until full payment of the principal amount. The stipulated interest remains in force until the obligation is satisfied. In the absence of stipulated interest, the prevailing legal interest prescribed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas shall apply.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish the interest under Article 2209 of the Civil Code from the interest under Articles 2210 and 2211, as explained in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales (2019).

suggestedAnswer.answer: Article 2209 applies to obligations consisting in the payment of a sum of money (loans or forbearance of money, goods or credit) where the debtor incurs delay, so there is a debtor-creditor relationship, and the payment of interest is mandatory. Articles 2210 and 2211 apply to other obligations (breach of contract, crimes and quasi-delicts) that do not involve the payment of a sum of money and have no debtor-creditor relationship, and the interest is discretionary on the court.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Lara's Gifts v. Midtown (2019), the Court explained that under Articles 2210 and 2211, when an obligation other than loans or forbearance is breached, the court may in its discretion impose interest on the damages, at the prevailing legal rate prescribed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. In contrast, Article 2209 applies only to loans or forbearance arising from obligations to pay a sum of money where the debtor incurs delay, and the payment of interest there is mandatory, while under Articles 2210 and 2211 it is discretionary.
suggestedAnswer.application: So a borrower in delay must pay interest by law, while a defendant ordered to pay damages for breach of contract or a quasi-delict may be ordered to pay interest only if the court, in its discretion, finds it proper.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Article 2209: sum of money, debtor-creditor, mandatory. Articles 2210-2211: other obligations, discretionary. **Bar trap:** do not treat interest on damages for a tort as a matter of right.

keyPoints: Art. 2209: obligations to pay a sum of money, debtor in delay; debtor-creditor relationship
Art. 2209: payment of interest is mandatory
Arts. 2210-2211: breach of contract, crimes and quasi-delicts; no sum of money or debtor-creditor relationship
Arts. 2210-2211: interest is discretionary on the court
Rate: the prevailing legal interest prescribed by the BSP

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
source.part: The Court's Ruling, Articles 2210 and 2211 apply to obligations other than loans or forbearance
source.excerpt: Under these articles, when the obligation, other than loans or forbearance of money, goods or credits, is breached, the court may in its discretion impose an interest on the damages awarded. The interest imposed in the discretion of the court will be the prevailing legal interest prescribed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. In contrast, Article 2209 of the Civil Code is applicable only to loans or forbearance of money, goods or credit which arise out of "obligations consisting in the payment of a sum of money, and the debtor incurs in delay," and thus where there is a debtor-creditor relationship. Articles 2210 and 2211 refer to obligations that do not involve the payment of a sum of money and there is no debtor-creditor relationship. Moreover, the payment of interest in Article 2209 is mandatory, while the payment of interest in Articles 2210 and 2211 is discretionary on the court.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A seller sues a buyer for the unpaid price of materials, attaching the sales invoices to the complaint. In its answer, the buyer admits the purchases and the existence of the invoices but states that it "does not admit their due execution," without stating any facts and without verifying the denial under oath. At trial, the buyer argues that the invoices have no probative value because their genuineness and due execution were not proved. Is the buyer correct? Explain, citing Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The invoices are actionable documents whose genuineness and due execution are deemed admitted, because the buyer did not specifically deny them under oath and set forth the facts it relies on.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Lara's Gifts v.
