Midtown, the Court applied Sections 7, 8 and 10 of Rule 8 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure: when an action is founded on a written instrument attached to the pleading, its genuineness and due execution are deemed admitted unless the adverse party, under oath, specifically denies them and sets forth what it claims to be the facts. The Rules are no longer satisfied with mere denials, even if specific; they demand that the defendant manifest what it considers the true facts. The buyer's general denial amounted to an admission of the genuineness and due execution of the invoices.
suggestedAnswer.application: The buyer stated no facts and did not deny under oath, so the invoices stand as proof of the transactions; its claim that the goods were substandard, a claim of fraud, had to be proved by it and was not.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The buyer is wrong; the invoices are deemed admitted. **Bar trap:** for an actionable document, a bare denial, even one that says "not admitted," is an admission unless it is under oath and states the facts.

keyPoints: Actionable document attached to the complaint (Rule 8, Sec. 7)
Genuineness and due execution deemed admitted unless specifically denied under oath (Sec. 8)
The denial must set forth the facts relied upon (Sec. 10)
A general denial amounts to an admission
Whoever alleges fraud (substandard goods) must prove it

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
source.part: The Court's Ruling, admissibility of the sales invoices
source.excerpt: In this case, petitioner did not state the facts or substance of the matters relied upon to support its denial of the due execution of the sales invoices. As held in Sy-Quia v. Marsman, "the Rules require that besides specifying the allegations of fact not admitted, the answer should set forth the matters relied upon in support of the denial; so that, in effect, the Rules are no longer satisfied with mere denials, even if specific, but demand that defendant manifest what he considers to be the true facts." The purpose of the specific denial is to compel the defendant to specify the allegations which he or she intends to disprove and disclose the matters relied upon to support such denial, thereby limiting the issues and avoiding unnecessary delays and surprises. Petitioner's general denial amounts to an admission of the genuineness and due execution of the sales invoices.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales (2019), when may interest, whether stipulated or legal, be compounded?

choices.A: Always, once the debtor is in default.
choices.B: Only when the court finds it equitable.
choices.C: Only when compounding is expressly agreed upon in writing by the parties or mandated by law or regulation.
choices.D: Only for loans from banks.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said "there should be no compounding of interest, whether stipulated or legal, unless compounding is expressly agreed upon in writing by the parties or mandated by law or regulation," citing Section 5 of the Usury Law, as amended. **A and B are wrong:** default or equity does not authorize compounding. **D is wrong:** no such limit. **Bar trap:** interest on accrued interest under Article 2212 from judicial demand is a different, legally mandated rule.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
source.part: The Court's Ruling, imposition of legal interest (compounding)
source.excerpt: Moreover, there should be no compounding of interest, whether stipulated or legal, unless compounding is expressly agreed upon in writing by the parties or mandated by law or regulation. Section 5 of the Usury Law, as amended, expressly provides that compounded interest "shall not be reckoned, except by agreement."

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Why did the Court in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales hold the 24% interest stated in the sales invoices binding on the buyer?

choices.A: Because the buyer, doing business since 1990 and buying from the seller since 2004, could not claim to have been misled into agreeing to the rate expressly stated in the invoices, and a 24% rate has been held valid and not unconscionable.
choices.B: Because every interest rate stated in an invoice is binding regardless of its amount.
choices.C: Because the buyer signed a separate loan agreement.
choices.D: Because the legal rate at the time was 24%.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said the buyer, "which has been doing business since 1990 and has been purchasing various materials from respondent since 2004, cannot claim to have been misled into agreeing to the 24% interest rate which was expressly stated in the sales invoices," and that a 24% rate agreed upon is valid and not excessive and unconscionable. **B is wrong:** excessive or unconscionable rates may be reduced. **C is wrong:** the rate was in the invoices. **D is wrong:** the legal rate was 12%, then 6%. **Bar trap:** the parties' experience and the rate's reasonableness both mattered.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
source.part: The Court's Ruling, validity of the 24% interest rate
source.excerpt: In the present case, petitioner, which has been doing business since 1990 and has been purchasing various materials from respondent since 2004, cannot claim to have been misled into agreeing to the 24% interest rate which was expressly stated in the sales invoices. Besides, this Court has already ruled in several cases that an interest rate of 24% per annum agreed upon between the parties is valid and binding and not excessive and unconscionable.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales (2019), the Court held that the legal interest referred to in Article 2209 of the Civil Code is now

choices.A: fixed at 6% a year by the Civil Code and cannot be changed except by Congress.
choices.B: 6% a year or as may be fixed by the Monetary Board of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas pursuant to the Usury Law, as amended by P.D. No. 116.
choices.C: 12% a year in all cases.
choices.D: the rate stipulated by the parties, even if none was agreed.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court held that P.D. No. 116 amended all laws prescribing the legal rate, including Article 2209, so "the legal interest referred to in Article 2209 of the Civil Code is now 6% per annum or as may be fixed by the Monetary Board of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas pursuant to the Usury Law, as amended by PD 116." **A is wrong:** P.D. 116 allowed the Monetary Board to set the rate. **C is wrong:** 12% applied only until June 30, 2013. **D is wrong:** legal interest applies when no rate was agreed. **Bar trap:** the legal rate can change by BSP circular.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
source.part: The Court's Ruling, the legal interest rate in Article 2209 has been amended
source.excerpt: Thus, the legal interest referred to in Article 2209 of the Civil Code is now 6% per annum or as may be fixed by the Monetary Board of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas pursuant to the Usury Law, as amended by PD 116.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales, the buyer claimed the materials delivered were substandard. How did the Court treat this defense?

choices.A: As a claim of fraud that the buyer was bound to substantiate, which it failed to do, since the invoices showed the goods were received in good order.
choices.B: As a valid defense, since the seller did not prove the quality of the goods.
choices.C: As a ground to temper the buyer's liability under Article 1192.
choices.D: As a ground for set-off under Article 1283.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said the buyer was "in effect ... alleging fraud in the transactions, which petitioner is bound to substantiate," and the invoices stated it "RECEIVED MERCHANDISE IN GOOD ORDER & CONDITION." **B is wrong:** the burden was on the buyer. **C and D are wrong:** having failed to prove its claim, the buyer could demand neither a tempering of liability nor an offset. **Bar trap:** whoever alleges fraud or mistake must prove it.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
source.part: The Court's Ruling, default in the contractual obligations
source.excerpt: In effect, petitioner is alleging fraud in the transactions, which petitioner is bound to substantiate. Whoever alleges fraud or mistake affecting a transaction must substantiate his allegation and has the burden of proof.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In its August 28, 2019 Decision in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales, from when did the Court make the 24% stipulated interest run?

choices.A: From the filing of the complaint on February 5, 2008, as the trial court had ruled.
choices.B: From the finality of the decision.
choices.C: From the date of the extrajudicial demand on January 22, 2008, until full payment.
choices.D: From the date of each purchase.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court held that "[s]ince there was an extra judicial demand before the complaint was filed, interest on the amount due begins to run not from the filing of the complaint but from the date of such extrajudicial demand," so the principal "shall earn the stipulated interest of 24% per annum from the date of extrajudicial demand on 22 January 2008 until full payment." **A is the trial court's ruling, which was modified. B and D are wrong:** neither is the reckoning point. **Bar trap:** the 2022 Resolution kept this point but deleted the separate award of legal interest on the 24% interest.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Decision)
source.part: The Court's Ruling, application to the case and the disposition
source.excerpt: Since there was an extra judicial demand before the complaint was filed, interest on the amount due begins to run not from the filing of the complaint but from the date of such extrajudicial demand. Thus, the unpaid principal obligation of ₱1,263,104.22 shall earn the stipulated interest of 24% per annum from the date of extrajudicial demand on 22 January 2008 until full payment.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish conventional interest from compensatory interest, as explained in the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales. Which of the two do the Eastern Shipping and Nacar rules govern?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Conventional interest is the compensation a borrower pays for the use of money in an onerous loan; it is agreed upon by the parties and must be expressly stipulated in writing. Compensatory interest (also called penalty interest, indemnity or moratory interest) is the indemnity for damages arising from the debtor's delay in an obligation to pay a sum of money; it is allowed by law even without a promise to pay interest, and the parties may stipulate it through a penal clause. The Eastern Shipping and Nacar rules govern only compensatory interest.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts v. Midtown, the Court held that conventional interest "is therefore paid not as a consequence of default, nor is it compensatory or a result of a provision of law"; it is the result of the express will of the parties and is allowed only if there is an express stipulation in writing. Compensatory interest "is the indemnity for damages arising from delay on the part of the debtor in an obligation consisting in the payment of a sum of money," allowed by law in the absence of a promise to pay interest. The Eastern Shipping and Nacar rules "govern only compensatory interest, not conventional interest," read with Articles 2209 and 1226.
suggestedAnswer.application: So a borrower not in delay owes only the principal and conventional interest; if the borrower is in delay, compensatory interest accrues as a matter of law in addition to conventional interest.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Conventional = agreed price of money, in writing; compensatory = indemnity for delay, by law or penal clause. **Bar trap:** do not apply the Eastern Shipping/Nacar legal rates to replace the parties' conventional interest.

keyPoints: Conventional interest: price for the use of money; express stipulation in writing required
Compensatory interest: indemnity for delay in paying a sum of money; allowed by law
Compensatory interest may be stipulated through a penal clause
Debtor in delay: compensatory interest accrues in addition to conventional interest
Eastern Shipping and Nacar govern only compensatory interest

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part I (the two kinds of interest)
source.excerpt: Conventional interest is therefore paid not as a consequence of default, nor is it compensatory or a result of a provision of law. It is "rigorously lucrative," and the result of the express will of the parties in a contract. … Compensatory interest, also referred to as penalty interest, indemnity, or moratory interest, is the indemnity for damages arising from delay on the part of the debtor in an obligation consisting in the payment of a sum of money. It is interest allowed by law in the absence of a promise to pay interest as compensation for delay in paying a fixed sum or a delay in assessing and paying damages. … It should be stressed that the Eastern Shipping Lines and Nacar rules govern only compensatory interest, not conventional interest, and should be read in conjunction with the provisions of Articles 2209 and 1226 of the Civil Code.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In 2025, L lent ₱500,000 to B at a stipulated interest of 3% a month (36% a year). B defaults and, when sued, argues that the rate is unconscionable. L argues that since usury ceilings were lifted, the parties are free to agree on any rate. How should the court approach the question, and what happens if the rate is struck down? Explain, citing the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The lifting of the interest ceilings does not give lenders a free hand: a stipulated rate that is unconscionable may be equitably reduced. Since 36% is more than twice the prevailing legal rate (6%), it is suspect, and L must prove that the rate is required by prevailing market conditions and that the parties were on equal footing. If the rate is struck down, only the rate is nullified; the agreement to pay interest remains, and the legal rate prevailing when the agreement was made applies.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts v. Midtown, the Court held that stipulated rates are subject to the unconscionability standard, determined by the context of each case. "The legal rate of interest is the presumptive reasonable compensation for borrowed money ... in cases where stipulated interest is more than twice the prevailing legal rate of interest, it is for the creditor to prove that this rate is required by prevailing market conditions"; the creditor must also show the parties were on an equal footing. Where the monetary interest rate is found unconscionable, "only the rate is nullified and deemed not written into the contract; the parties' agreement on the payment of interest remains," and the legal rate prevailing at the time of the agreement applies.
suggestedAnswer.application: L bears the burden of justifying 36%. Without proof of market conditions and equal bargaining positions, the court may strike the rate and apply the legal rate in effect in 2025.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The rate is suspect; if unjustified, it is replaced by the legal rate, but interest remains due. **Bar trap:** striking down an unconscionable rate does not erase the obligation to pay interest.

keyPoints: Lifting of usury ceilings is not a carte blanche for lenders
Unconscionability depends on the context of each case
Legal rate = presumptive reasonable compensation; more than twice the legal rate is suspect
Creditor must prove market conditions and equal footing
Only the rate is nullified; the legal rate at the time of the agreement applies

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part II(B) (unconscionability of stipulated interest)
source.excerpt: The legal rate of interest is the presumptive reasonable compensation for borrowed money. While parties are free to deviate from this, any deviation must be reasonable and fair. Any deviation that is far-removed is suspect. Thus, in cases where stipulated interest is more than twice the prevailing legal rate of interest, it is for the creditor to prove that this rate is required by prevailing market conditions. (Emphasis supplied) Conformable to the foregoing pronouncements, "[t]he maximum interest rate that will not cross the line of conscionability is 'not more than twice the prevailing legal rate of interest.' If the stipulated interest exceeds this standard, the creditor must show that the rate is necessary under current market conditions." The creditor must also show that the parties were on an equal footing when they stipulated on the interest rate. Furthermore, where the monetary interest rate is found to be unconscionable, only the rate is nullified and deemed not written into the contract; the parties' agreement on the payment of interest remains. In such instance, "the legal rate of interest prevailing at the time the agreement was entered into" is applied by the courts.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A seller sold goods on a 60-day credit term, with 24% interest a year on overdue accounts. The trial court awarded the seller the price plus 24% interest from judicial demand. Only the buyer appealed. On appeal, the Supreme Court added legal interest on the accrued 24% interest under Article 2212. On reconsideration, how did the Court characterize the transaction and the 24% interest, and what did it do with the added award? Explain, citing the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court held that the contract was not a loan or forbearance of money, goods or credit but a sale of goods on credit, and that the 24% was compensatory interest imposed as indemnity for the delay in paying the price under Article 2209. Although Article 2212 could in principle apply to that accrued interest, the added award was deleted because the seller did not appeal, so granting it on the buyer's appeal was ultra vires.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In the 2022 Resolution, the Court modified its 2019 Decision and held "that the contract involved is not a loan or forbearance of money, goods, or credit, but a sale of goods on credit." The 24% would run only upon the buyer's failure to pay on the due date, so it was a compensatory interest under Article 2209, and by Article 2212 the accrued compensatory interest may earn interest on interest. However, the trial court's award "became final and executory as to Midtown Industrial Sales as it did not appeal. Thus, the additional award of legal interest on the 24% interest, in an appeal brought by Lara's Gifts, is ultra vires." The Court also noted that the unconscionability standards cannot apply to interest on interest under Article 2212, which is fixed by law.
suggestedAnswer.application: The buyer still pays the principal with 24% interest from the extrajudicial demand until full payment, and the attorney's fees, but not the legal interest on the 24% interest.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Sale on credit; 24% compensatory; the extra award deleted. **Bar trap:** an appellee who did not appeal cannot obtain affirmative relief beyond what the judgment gave it.

keyPoints: Sale of goods on credit, not a loan or forbearance
The 24% ran only upon default: compensatory interest under Art. 2209
Art. 2212 interest on interest could apply, and it is fixed by law (no unconscionability test)
The seller did not appeal: the judgment was final as to it
Adding relief on the buyer's appeal was ultra vires; the award was deleted

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part III (application to the case)
source.excerpt: Now to this case, we modify our earlier Decision and hold that the contract involved is not a loan or forbearance of money, goods, or credit, but a sale of goods on credit. From January to December 2007, petitioner Lara's Gifts purchased from respondent Midtown various industrial and construction materials totaling ₱1,263,104.22. The purchases were on a 60-day credit term, with the condition that a 24% interest rate per annum would be charged on all accounts overdue. This means that the 24% interest rate per annum would run only upon petitioner's failure to pay on the due date. Thus, the 24% interest rate is a compensatory interest, imposed as indemnity for damages caused by the delay in the payment of the raw materials' purchase price, pursuant to Article 2209. By the express provision of Article 2212, the 24% compensatory interest, which have accrued at the time of judicial demand, may be subject to "interest on interest." However, as Justice Amy C. Lazaro-Javier pointed out, the Regional Trial Court adjudged in favor of Midtown Industrial Sales only P1,263,104.22 plus interest at 24% per annum, computed from February 5, 2008 until fully paid; and P50,000.00 as attorney's fees. This judgment award became final and executory as to Midtown Industrial Sales as it did not appeal. Thus, the additional award of legal interest on the 24% interest, in an appeal brought by Lara's Gifts, is ultra vires.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales, payment of conventional interest is allowed only if

choices.A: the debtor is in delay.
choices.B: there is an express stipulation for the payment of interest, and the stipulation is in writing.
choices.C: the court finds it equitable.
choices.D: the loan is from a bank.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court said payment of conventional interest is allowed only if "1) There is an express stipulation for the payment of interest, and 2) The stipulation for the payment of interest is in writing." **A is wrong:** delay gives rise to compensatory, not conventional, interest. **C and D are wrong:** neither is a condition. **Bar trap:** conventional interest is paid not as a consequence of default.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part I(A) (conditions for conventional interest)
source.excerpt: However, payment of conventional interest is allowed only if the following conditions concur: 1) There is an express stipulation for the payment of interest, and 2) The stipulation for the payment of interest is in writing.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales, if a contract for the payment of a sum of money has no penal clause but stipulates conventional interest, what compensatory interest applies upon the debtor's delay?

choices.A: The legal interest rate, always.
choices.B: No interest at all.
choices.C: The stipulated penalty, which is presumed.
choices.D: The conventional or monetary interest.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court laid down: "(1) If there is a penal clause that stipulates the penalty or indemnity, then the stipulated penalty or indemnity shall be applicable. (2) If there is no penal clause, but there is a stipulation on conventional or monetary interest, then the conventional or monetary interest shall be applicable. (3) If there is no stipulation on the penalty or on conventional interest, then the legal interest rate shall be applicable." **A is wrong:** legal interest is the last resort. **B is wrong:** delay always gives rise to compensatory interest. **C is wrong:** there was no penal clause. **Bar trap:** follow the order: penalty, then conventional, then legal rate.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part I(B) (which compensatory interest applies)
source.excerpt: (1) If there is a penal clause that stipulates the penalty or indemnity, then the stipulated penalty or indemnity shall be applicable. (2) If there is no penal clause, but there is a stipulation on conventional or monetary interest, then the conventional or monetary interest shall be applicable. (3) If there is no stipulation on the penalty or on conventional interest, then the legal interest rate shall be applicable. In contracts of simple loan of money, the legal interest rate is currently 6%.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales, why can the standards of unconscionability not apply to interest on interest under Article 2212?

choices.A: Because interest on interest is fixed by law and, absent a stipulated rate, the legal rate applies by operation of law, not subject to the court's discretion.
choices.B: Because interest on interest is always lower than the stipulated rate.
choices.C: Because Article 2212 applies only to bank loans.
choices.D: Because interest on interest is a form of moral damages.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court, adopting Justice Caguioa's view, said "'interest on interest' is fixed by law. In the absence of a contractual stipulation between the parties on the rate of interest on accrued interest, the legal rate shall apply by operation of law. Its imposition is not subject to the court's discretionary power." **B, C and D are wrong:** none is the reason given. **Bar trap:** Article 2212 is deemed written into every contract with stipulated interest.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part II(C) (interest on interest)
source.excerpt: However, the standards of unconscionability cannot apply to interest on interest under Article 2212 of the Civil Code, viz: … As Justice Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa elucidated, "interest on interest" is fixed by law. In the absence of a contractual stipulation between the parties on the rate of interest on accrued interest, the legal rate shall apply by operation of law. Its imposition is not subject to the court's discretionary power.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales, may a stipulated compensatory (penalty) interest be reduced by the courts?

choices.A: No, only conventional interest may be reduced.
choices.B: Yes, when found unconscionable, since the reduction depends not on the type of interest but on whether the rate is unconscionable.
choices.C: No, because a penal clause is always binding as written.
choices.D: Yes, but only if the debtor has paid at least half of the principal.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court said: "The reduction of interest rates is not limited to monetary interest. It is not dependent on the type of interest imposed on the party, but on whether the interest rate was unconscionable or not. Thus, compensatory interest, when found to be unconscionable, may also be reduced," citing Articles 1229 and 2227. **A and C are wrong:** penalties may be equitably reduced. **D is wrong:** no such condition. **Bar trap:** partial or irregular performance is one ground for reducing a penalty, but not the only one.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, Part II (who may be reduced)
source.excerpt: The reduction of interest rates is not limited to monetary interest. It is not dependent on the type of interest imposed on the party, but on whether the interest rate was unconscionable or not. Thus, compensatory interest, when found to be unconscionable, may also be reduced.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What did the 2022 Resolution in Lara's Gifts & Decors v. Midtown Industrial Sales order?

choices.A: It reversed the 2019 Decision and dismissed the complaint.
choices.B: It reduced the 24% interest to 12% as unconscionable.
choices.C: It partially granted reconsideration and deleted the award of legal interest on the 24% compensatory interest, leaving the principal with 24% interest from the extrajudicial demand and the attorney's fees.
choices.D: It denied the motion for reconsideration in full.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court ruled: "the Motion for Reconsideration is PARTIALLY GRANTED. This Court's August 28, 2019 Decision is MODIFIED in that the award of legal interest on the 24% per annum compensatory interest is hereby DELETED," ordering payment of the principal "plus stipulated interest at 24% per annum to be computed from January 22, 2008, the date of extrajudicial demand, until full payment" and ₱50,000 attorney's fees. **A, B and D are wrong:** the Court upheld the 24% rate and modified only that award. **Bar trap:** read the 2019 Decision together with this Resolution.

source.caseTitle: Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, the disposition
source.excerpt: ACCORDINGLY, the Motion for Reconsideration is PARTIALLY GRANTED. This Court's August 28, 2019 Decision is MODIFIED in that the award of legal interest on the 24% per annum compensatory interest is hereby DELETED. Petitioner Lara's Gifts & Decors, Inc. is ordered to PAY respondent Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. the following: (1) ONE MILLION TWO HUNDRED SIXTY-THREE THOUSAND ONE HUNDRED FOUR PESOS and 22/100 (P1,263,104.22) representing the principal amount plus stipulated interest at 24% per annum to be computed from January 22, 2008, the date of extrajudicial demand, until full payment;

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: X Corp., an exporter, sues its bank for moral damages after the bank's error caused several of X Corp.'s checks to bounce, leading suppliers to cancel its credit line and hold its orders. The bank argues that a corporation, not being a natural person, can never recover moral damages. Is the bank correct? Explain, citing Simex International v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Not entirely. As a rule a corporation is not entitled to moral damages, but there is an exception where the corporation has a good reputation that is debased, resulting in its social humiliation; X Corp. falls within it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Simex v. CA, the Court held that "a corporation is not as a rule entitled to moral damages because, not being a natural person, it cannot experience physical suffering or such sentiments as wounded feelings, serious anxiety, mental anguish and moral shock. The only exception to this rule is where the corporation has a good reputation that is debased, resulting in its social humiliation." The bouncing checks impaired the corporation's prestige and diminished confidence in it as a reliable debtor.
suggestedAnswer.application: X Corp.'s credit line was canceled and its orders were held because its checks bounced, so its good name in the business community was damaged by the bank's fault. One past collection suit does not show it had no good reputation to protect.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: X Corp. may recover moral damages under the exception. **Bar trap:** the rule (no moral damages for corporations) has an exception for a debased good reputation; know both.

keyPoints: General rule: a corporation cannot recover moral damages (it cannot feel suffering or anguish)
Exception: its good reputation is debased, resulting in social humiliation
Bouncing checks impaired its prestige and its standing as a reliable debtor
Credit line canceled, orders held, business declined
A single past collection case did not show it had no good name

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral damages (corporations)
source.excerpt: Moreover, a corporation is not as a rule entitled to moral damages because, not being a natural person, it cannot experience physical suffering or such sentiments as wounded feelings, serious anxiety, mental anguish and moral shock. The only exception to this rule is where the corporation has a good reputation that is debased, resulting in its social humiliation. We shall recognize that the petitioner did suffer injury because of the private respondent's negligence that caused the dishonor of the checks issued by it. The immediate consequence was that its prestige was impaired because of the bouncing checks and confidence in it as a reliable debtor was diminished.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The trial court found that a bank negligently failed to credit a depositor's deposit, causing its checks to bounce and its business to suffer. Since the depositor could not prove the exact peso amount of its losses, the court awarded only ₱20,000 as nominal damages. Was the award proper? Explain the purpose of moral damages and of nominal damages, citing Simex International v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Since the depositor proved it suffered loss, the proper award is moral damages, not nominal damages; the lack of proof of the exact amount does not bar moral damages.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Simex v. CA, the Court held that moral damages "are not awarded to penalize the defendant but to compensate the plaintiff for the injuries he may have suffered." Their amount need not be established with exactitude, because "[m]oral damages are not susceptible of pecuniary estimation"; Article 2216 provides that no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary for moral, nominal, temperate, liquidated or exemplary damages, and the amount is left to the court's discretion. Under Article 2221, nominal damages are adjudicated to vindicate or recognize a violated right, "and not for the purpose of indemnifying the plaintiff for any loss suffered by him."
suggestedAnswer.application: Because the depositor proved a real loss (canceled credit line, held orders, declined business, tarnished reputation), nominal damages were the wrong remedy. In the case, the Court replaced the ₱20,000 nominal damages with ₱20,000 moral damages, and added ₱50,000 exemplary damages.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Moral damages, not nominal damages, should be awarded. **Bar trap:** nominal damages are for a violated right without proven loss; once a loss is shown, they are not the proper relief.

keyPoints: Moral damages compensate, they do not penalize
Not susceptible of pecuniary estimation; no proof of pecuniary loss needed (Art. 2216)
Amount left to the court's discretion
Nominal damages (Art. 2221): vindicate a right, not indemnify a loss
Loss proved: moral damages in lieu of nominal damages

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral damages (purpose and proof) and nominal damages
source.excerpt: We agree that moral damages are not awarded to penalize the defendant but to compensate the plaintiff for the injuries he may have suffered. In the case at bar, the petitioner is seeking such damages for the prejudice sustained by it as a result of the private respondent's fault. The respondent court said that the claimed losses are purely speculative and are not supported by substantial evidence, but if failed to consider that the amount of such losses need not be established with exactitude precisely because of their nature. Moral damages are not susceptible of pecuniary estimation. Article 2216 of the Civil Code specifically provides that "no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary in order that moral, nominal, temperate, liquidated or exemplary damages may be adjudicated." … Under Article 2221 of the Civil Code, "nominal damages are adjudicated in order that a right of the plaintiff, which has been violated or invaded by the defendant, may be vindicated or recognized, and not for the purpose of indemnifying the plaintiff for any loss suffered by him." As we have found that the petitioner has indeed incurred loss through the fault of the private respondent, the proper remedy is the award to it of moral damages, which we impose, in our discretion, in the same amount of P20,000.00.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A bank failed to credit a deposit, causing a depositor's checks to bounce. When told of the error, it took a week to correct it and never explained why it happened. The bank argues that exemplary damages are improper because it eventually corrected its records and the checks were paid. Rule on the bank's argument, citing Simex International v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The argument fails. Given a bank's fiduciary duty to treat its depositors' accounts with meticulous care, its unexplained error and its delay in correcting it were wanton, warranting exemplary damages.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Simex v. CA, the Court held that, "as a business affected with public interest and because of the nature of its functions, the bank is under obligation to treat the accounts of its depositors with meticulous care, always having in mind the fiduciary nature of their relationship." Having been informed of its error, the bank corrected it only a week later, 23 days after the deposit, with no satisfactory explanation; "[s]uch ineptness comes under the concept of the wanton manner contemplated in the Civil Code that calls for the imposition of exemplary damages" (Art. 2232).
suggestedAnswer.application: Correcting the error late does not excuse it: the error should not have been made at all, and the checks should have been paid on presentment. The bank's lackadaisical attitude was gross negligence. The Court imposed ₱50,000 exemplary damages as a deterrent.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Exemplary damages are proper. **Bar trap:** a later correction does not erase a bank's breach of its high duty of care; the standard for banks is meticulous care, given the fiduciary nature of the relationship.

keyPoints: Banks are businesses affected with public interest
Duty to treat depositors' accounts with meticulous care; fiduciary relationship
Unexplained error and a week's delay in correcting it after notice
Such ineptness is "wanton" under Art. 2232: exemplary damages
₱50,000 exemplary damages as a warning and deterrent

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of exemplary damages (duty of banks)
source.excerpt: The point is that as a business affected with public interest and because of the nature of its functions, the bank is under obligation to treat the accounts of its depositors with meticulous care, always having in mind the fiduciary nature of their relationship. In the case at bar, it is obvious that the respondent bank was remiss in that duty and violated that relationship. What is especially deplorable is that, having been informed of its error in not crediting the deposit in question to the petitioner, the respondent bank did not immediately correct it but did so only one week later or twenty-three days after the deposit was made. It bears repeating that the record does not contain any satisfactory explanation of why the error was made in the first place and why it was not corrected immediately after its discovery. Such ineptness comes under the concept of the wanton manner contemplated in the Civil Code that calls for the imposition of exemplary damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Simex International v. Court of Appeals, moral damages are awarded

choices.A: to penalize the defendant for its wrongdoing.
choices.B: to compensate the plaintiff for the injuries it may have suffered.
choices.C: to vindicate a right without regard to loss.
choices.D: to set an example for the public good.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court said "moral damages are not awarded to penalize the defendant but to compensate the plaintiff for the injuries he may have suffered." **A is wrong:** they are not punitive. **C is wrong:** that is nominal damages (Art. 2221). **D is wrong:** that is exemplary damages (Art. 2229). **Bar trap:** know the distinct purpose of each kind of damages.

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral damages (purpose)
source.excerpt: We agree that moral damages are not awarded to penalize the defendant but to compensate the plaintiff for the injuries he may have suffered.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under Article 2216 of the Civil Code, as applied in Simex International v. Court of Appeals, no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary for an award of

choices.A: actual or compensatory damages only.
choices.B: loss of earning capacity.
choices.C: attorney's fees.
choices.D: moral, nominal, temperate, liquidated or exemplary damages.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court quoted Article 2216: "no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary in order that moral, nominal, temperate, liquidated or exemplary damages may be adjudicated," so the amount (except liquidated damages) is left to the court's discretion. **A and B are wrong:** actual damages, including loss of earning capacity, must be proved. **C is wrong:** attorney's fees need a basis under Article 2208. **Bar trap:** "no proof of pecuniary loss" does not mean no proof of injury at all.

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral damages (proof)
source.excerpt: Article 2216 of the Civil Code specifically provides that "no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary in order that moral, nominal, temperate, liquidated or exemplary damages may be adjudicated." That is why the determination of the amount to be awarded (except liquidated damages) is left to the sound discretion of the court, according to "the circumstances of each case."

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Simex International v. Court of Appeals, which provision did the Court cite for the rule that actual damages may be recovered for injury to the plaintiff's business standing or commercial credit?

choices.A: Article 2205 of the Civil Code.
choices.B: Article 2219 of the Civil Code.
choices.C: Article 2208 of the Civil Code.
choices.D: Article 2221 of the Civil Code.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said: "Article 2205 of the Civil Code provides that actual or compensatory damages may be received '(2) for injury to the plaintiff s business standing or commercial credit,'" and that once the loss is established, absolute certainty as to its amount is not required. **B is wrong:** Article 2219 lists cases for moral damages. **C is wrong:** Article 2208 is on attorney's fees. **D is wrong:** Article 2221 is on nominal damages. **Bar trap:** this injury also bolstered the claim for moral damages.

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral damages (injury to business standing)
source.excerpt: Article 2205 of the Civil Code provides that actual or compensatory damages may be received "(2) for injury to the plaintiff s business standing or commercial credit." There is no question that the petitioner did sustain actual injury as a result of the dishonored checks and that the existence of the loss having been established "absolute certainty as to its amount is not required."

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Simex International claimed ₱1,000,000 in moral damages. How did the Court treat that claim?

choices.A: It awarded the full amount since moral damages need no proof.
choices.B: It found the claim "nothing short of preposterous" for a business of its size and awarded ₱20,000 in moral damages in place of nominal damages.
choices.C: It denied any moral damages since a corporation can never recover them.
choices.D: It remanded the case to fix the amount.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court said the ₱1,000,000 claim was "nothing short of preposterous. Its business certainly is not that big, or its name that prestigious," and it imposed moral damages of ₱20,000 in lieu of nominal damages. **A is wrong:** the amount is still left to the court's sound discretion. **C is wrong:** the exception for a debased reputation applied. **D is wrong:** the Court fixed the amount itself. **Bar trap:** discretion over the amount means the court may grant much less than claimed.

source.caseTitle: Simex International (Manila), Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral damages (the amount claimed)
source.excerpt: From every viewpoint except that of the petitioner's, its claim of moral damages in the amount of P1,000,000.00 is nothing short of preposterous. Its business certainly is not that big, or its name that prestigious, to sustain such an extravagant pretense.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What did the Court order in Simex International v. Court of Appeals?

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of moral damages? How should a court fix their amount? Explain, citing Makabali v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Moral damages are not intended to enrich the complainant at the defendant's expense. They are awarded to enable the injured party to obtain means, diversions or amusements that will alleviate the moral suffering caused by the defendant's culpable act, that is, to restore within the limits of the possible the spiritual status quo ante. Their amount must be proportionate to the suffering inflicted and depends on the circumstances of each case.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Makabali v. CA, the Court held that there is no hard and fast rule in determining a fair amount of moral damages, since each case is governed by its own circumstances. Under Article 2217, moral damages, which include physical suffering, mental anguish, fright, serious anxiety, besmirched reputation, wounded feelings, moral shock, social humiliation and similar injury, are incapable of pecuniary estimation. "[T]he award of moral damages is aimed at a restoration within the limits of the possible, of the spiritual status quo ante; and therefore it must be proportionate to the suffering inflicted."
suggestedAnswer.application: In the case, the Court considered the petitioners' social standing, their embarrassment and humiliation, and their anxiety on their first trip abroad with meager funds, and found ₱5,000 minimal.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Moral damages compensate, proportionately, and do not enrich. **Bar trap:** "incapable of pecuniary estimation" does not mean the amount is arbitrary; it must be proportionate to the proven suffering.

keyPoints: No hard and fast rule; each case on its own circumstances
Art. 2217: the kinds of moral injury; incapable of pecuniary estimation
Not to enrich the complainant
To restore the spiritual status quo ante within the limits of the possible
Proportionate to the suffering inflicted

source.caseTitle: Makabali, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of moral damages (purpose and amount)
source.excerpt: To begin with, there is no hard and fast rule in the determination of what would be a fair amount of moral damages, since each case must be governed by its own peculiar circumstances. Article 2217 of the Civil Code recognizes that moral damages which include physical suffering, mental anguish, fright, serious anxiety, besmirched reputation, wounded feelings, moral shock, social humiliation and similar injury, are incapable of pecuniary estimation. … It must be emphasized that moral damages are not intended to enrich the complainant at the expense of a defendant. They are awarded only to enable the injured parties to obtain means, diversions or amusements that will serve to alleviate the moral sufferings the injured parties have undergone by reason of defendant's culpable action. In other words, the award of moral damages is aimed at a restoration within the limits of the possible, of the spiritual status quo ante; and therefore it must be proportionate to the suffering inflicted.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A trial court awarded a plaintiff a lump sum of ₱5,000 "as moral and exemplary damages." The defendant argues that exemplary damages could not be awarded at all because the plaintiff did not prove them. Is the defendant correct? Is a single lump-sum award proper? Explain, citing Makabali v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The defendant is not correct: exemplary damages need not be proved, though they are not a matter of right and the plaintiff must first show entitlement to moral, temperate or compensatory damages. Moral and exemplary damages should be awarded separately, because their nature and purposes differ.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Makabali v. CA, the Court held that "[w]hile exemplary damages cannot be recovered as a matter of right, they need not be proved, although plaintiff must show that he is entitled to moral, temperate or compensatory damages before the court may consider the question of whether or not exemplary damages should be awarded." It noted that it gave separate awards for moral and exemplary damages, "because the nature and purposes of said damages are different. While moral damages have to do with injury personal to the awardee, such as physical suffering and the like, exemplary damages are imposed by way of example or correction for the public good."
suggestedAnswer.application: If the plaintiff shows entitlement to moral damages, the court may then consider exemplary damages without separate proof of their amount; but it should state each award separately.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Exemplary damages need no proof but presuppose other damages; separate awards are proper. **Bar trap:** exemplary damages cannot stand alone; first establish moral, temperate or compensatory damages. (In Makabali itself the Court still fixed a combined sum, capped by the complaint's prayer.)

keyPoints: Exemplary damages: not a matter of right, but need not be proved
Plaintiff must first show entitlement to moral, temperate or compensatory damages
Moral damages: injury personal to the awardee
Exemplary damages: by way of example or correction for the public good
Different natures and purposes: separate awards are proper

source.caseTitle: Makabali, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of exemplary damages and of separate awards
source.excerpt: As to exemplary damages, Article 2229 of the Civil Code provides that such damages may be imposed by way of example or correction for the public good. While exemplary damages cannot be recovered as a matter of right, they need not be proved, although plaintiff must show that he is entitled to moral, temperate or compensatory damages before the court may consider the question of whether or not exemplary damages should be awarded. … It will thus be noted that We have awarded moral and exemplary damages depending upon the facts attendant to each case. It will also be noted that We gave separate awards for moral and exemplary damages. This is as it should be because the nature and purposes of said damages are different. While moral damages have to do with injury personal to the awardee, such as physical suffering and the like, exemplary damages are imposed by way of example or correction for the public good.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Two sisters sued a travel agency that left them stranded on a package tour abroad, praying for a total of ₱35,000 in moral and exemplary damages. On appeal, the Supreme Court found that they deserved far more than the ₱5,000 awarded below. May the Court award them more than ₱35,000? What must a claimant prove to recover moral damages? Explain, citing Makabali v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The award should not exceed the ₱35,000 the claimants prayed for in their complaint. To recover moral damages, the claimant must satisfactorily prove at the trial the factual basis of the damages and its causal connection to the defendant's acts, and must specifically pray for them in the complaint.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Makabali v. CA, the Court held that "the claimant must have satisfactorily proven during the trial the existence of the factual basis of the damages and its causal connection to defendant's acts," because moral damages, though incapable of pecuniary estimation, are designed to compensate for actual injury, not to penalize, and "are allowable only when specifically prayed for in the complaint." Since the petitioners limited their claim for moral and exemplary damages to a total of ₱35,000, the award "should not exceed the said amount."
suggestedAnswer.application: The findings below that the sisters suffered anguish, embarrassment and mental suffering because of the agency's failure, which acted in wanton disregard of their rights, supplied the factual basis and causal connection. The Court raised the award to ₱35,000 and the attorney's fees to ₱5,000.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: ₱35,000 at most. **Bar trap:** however strong the case, moral damages cannot exceed what was prayed for in the complaint.

keyPoints: Prove the factual basis of the damages at trial
Prove the causal connection to the defendant's acts
Moral damages compensate actual injury; they do not penalize
Allowable only when specifically prayed for in the complaint
The award may not exceed the amount prayed for (₱35,000)

source.caseTitle: Makabali, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the requisites and the limit of the award
source.excerpt: It is essential however, in the award of damages that the claimant must have satisfactorily proven during the trial the existence of the factual basis of the damages and its causal connection to defendant's acts. This is so because moral damages, though incapable of pecuniary estimation, are in the category of an award designed to compensate the claimant for actual injury suffered and not to impose a penalty on the wrongdoer, and are allowable only when specifically prayed for in the complaint. … We note however that petitioners limited their claim for moral and exemplary damages in their complaint filed with the Court of First Instance to a total of P35,000.00 plus attorney's fees and costs. We feel that Our award should not exceed the said amount.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Parents sued for damages for the death of their child, run over by a truck, alleging ₱10,000 actual damages and moral damages "in an amount to be fixed by the court." In their answer, the defendants denied negligence and alleged that they had no knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to the damages claimed. The trial court rendered judgment on the pleadings and awarded the damages as alleged. Was this proper? Explain, citing Raagas v. Traya.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The answer tendered a valid issue on the damages, so judgment on the pleadings was improper and a trial on the merits is required.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Raagas v. Traya, the Court held that the defendants' averment that they "have no knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to the truth of the allegations" as to the damages, together with their claim that the death was due to an unforeseen event or the fault of the child or his parents, "has the effect of tendering a valid issue." It added that even if the allegations regarding the amount of damages are not specifically denied, such damages are not deemed admitted, and actual damages must be proved, not based on speculation, conjecture or guesswork.
suggestedAnswer.application: The damages, and the issue of fault, had to be proved by evidence. Since nothing had been proved, the trial court could not award any amount on the pleadings alone.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The judgment should be set aside and the case tried on the merits. **Bar trap:** failure to deny the amount of damages specifically does not admit them; damages must still be proved.

keyPoints: Lack of knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief tenders a valid issue
Damages are not deemed admitted even if their amounts are not specifically denied
Actual damages must be proved; no speculation, conjecture or guesswork
Moral damages: prove the factual basis and causal relation
Judgment on the pleadings set aside; trial on the merits required

source.caseTitle: Raagas, et al. v. Traya, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of whether the answer tendered an issue on damages
source.excerpt: The plaintiffs' claim for actual, moral, nominal and corrective damages, was controverted by the averment in the answer to the effect that the defendants "have no knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief as to the truth of the allegations" as to such damages, "the truth of the matter being that the death of Regino Raagas was occasioned by an unforeseen event and/or by the fault of the small boy Regino Raagas or his parents." Such averment has the effect of tendering a valid issue. … In Abubakar Tan vs. Tian Ho, L-18820, December 29, 1962 and Lim Giok vs. Bataan Cigar and Cigarette Factory, L-15861, April 16, 1960, we held that even if the allegations regarding the amount of damages in the complaint are not specifically denied in the answer, such damages are not deemed admitted.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What must be proved to recover (a) actual damages and (b) moral damages? Is an allegation of moral damages in the complaint enough? Explain, citing Raagas v. Traya.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) For actual damages, the claimant must present actual proof that damage was suffered and evidence of its actual amount; the court cannot rely on speculation, conjecture or guesswork. (b) For moral damages, an allegation is not even necessary, but it is essential that the claimant satisfactorily prove the existence of the factual basis of the damage and its causal relation to the defendant's acts; an allegation alone is not enough.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Raagas v. Traya, the Court declared "in no uncertain terms that actual damages must be proved, and that a court cannot rely on 'speculation, conjecture or guesswork' as to the fact and amount of damages, but must depend on actual proof that damage had been suffered and on evidence of the actual amount." It reaffirmed that "although an allegation is not necessary in order that moral damages may be awarded, 'it is, nevertheless, essential that the claimant satisfactorily prove the existence of the factual basis of the damage and its causal relation to defendant's acts.'"
suggestedAnswer.application: So even in a death case, the parents had to prove their losses and the suffering and its link to the defendants' acts at a trial, rather than obtain an award on the pleadings.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Both require proof at trial: actual damages as to fact and amount; moral damages as to factual basis and causation. **Bar trap:** "no proof of pecuniary loss" for moral damages does not dispense with proof of the injury and its cause.

keyPoints: Actual damages: actual proof of the damage and evidence of its amount
No speculation, conjecture or guesswork
Moral damages: an allegation is not necessary
But the factual basis and its causal relation to the defendant's acts must be satisfactorily proved
An allegation alone is never enough

source.caseTitle: Raagas, et al. v. Traya, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the proof required for actual and moral damages
source.excerpt: In Tomassi vs. Villa-Abrille, L-7047, August 21, 1968, Suntay Tanjangco vs. Jovellanos, et al., L-12332, June 30, 1960, and Delfin vs. Court of Agrarian Relations, et al., L-23348, March 14, 1967, 1967 A PHILD 453, we declared in no uncertain terms that actual damages must be proved, and that a court cannot rely on "speculation, conjecture or guesswork" as to the fact and amount of damages, but must depend on actual proof that damage had been suffered and on evidence of the actual amount. Finally, in Malonzo vs. Galang et. al., L-13851, July 27, 1960, we reaffirmed the rule that although an allegation is not necessary in order that moral damages may be awarded, "it is, nevertheless, essential that the claimant satisfactorily prove the existence of the factual basis of the damage and its causal relation to defendant's acts."

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Raagas v. Traya, the trial court reasoned that, since the defendants did not deny that their truck had no current registration plate, they were presumed negligent, and it rendered judgment on the pleadings for damages. What did the Supreme Court decide, and why?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Supreme Court set aside the judgment on the pleadings and remanded the case for trial on the merits, because the answer tendered valid issues on the damages and on fault, which required evidence.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Raagas v. Traya, the trial court relied on Article 2185 (a driver violating a traffic regulation is presumed negligent) and treated the unanswered allegation on the registration plate as an admission. The Supreme Court held that the trial court erred: the answer's averments tendered a valid issue, damages are not deemed admitted, and actual and moral damages must be proved. This "points up the inescapable need of a full-blown trial on the merits at which the parties will be afforded every opportunity to present evidence in support of their respective contentions and defenses."
suggestedAnswer.application: Even if a presumption of negligence might arise, the presumption is rebuttable ("unless there is proof to the contrary"), and the damages themselves still had to be proved, so the parties had to be heard at trial.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Remanded for trial. **Bar trap:** a presumption of negligence does not prove damages; judgment on the pleadings is proper only when the answer tenders no issue.

keyPoints: Trial court: presumption of negligence (Art. 2185) from the unanswered plate allegation
Supreme Court: the answer tendered valid issues
Damages not deemed admitted; must be proved
Need for a full-blown trial on the merits
Judgment set aside; case remanded

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A city treasurer, sued in his personal capacity by a company whose trucks he seized for unpaid taxes, counterclaimed for ₱40,000 moral damages, alleging shock, fright, wounded feelings and social humiliation suffered by him and his family because of the suit. He presented no evidence on these. The trial court, finding the company's suit baseless, awarded him ₱2,000 in damages. Was the award proper? Explain, citing San Miguel Brewery v. Magno.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Moral damages require pleading and proof of the moral suffering; since the treasurer presented no evidence, no moral damages could be awarded.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In San Miguel Brewery v. Magno, the Court held that "[i]n order that moral damages may be awarded, there must be pleading and proof of moral suffering, mental anguish, fright and the like." While no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary, the amount being left to the court's discretion (Art. 2216), "it is, nevertheless, essential that the claimant should satisfactorily prove the existence of the factual basis of the damages (Article 2217) and its causal connection to defendant's acts," because moral damages are designed to compensate actual injury, not to penalize.
suggestedAnswer.application: The treasurer only alleged his suffering in his counterclaim and offered no evidence of it or of its link to the suit, so the ₱2,000 award had no basis and was set aside.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The award was improper. **Bar trap:** an allegation of mental anguish in a pleading is not proof; moral damages need evidence of the factual basis and causation.

keyPoints: Pleading and proof of moral suffering, mental anguish, fright and the like are required
No proof of pecuniary loss needed; amount left to the court (Art. 2216)
But the factual basis (Art. 2217) and causal connection must be satisfactorily proved
Moral damages compensate actual injury, not penalize

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A city treasurer, acting under a city ordinance authorizing distraint, seized a taxpayer's trucks for unpaid taxes. The taxpayer sued him in his personal capacity for the cost of renting replacement trucks, which the treasurer admitted it had spent. Is the treasurer personally liable for those damages? Explain, citing San Miguel Brewery v. Magno.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Since he acted in his official capacity under an ordinance empowering him to issue the warrant, and was not shown to have acted in bad faith, he cannot be made to answer personally for damages.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In San Miguel Brewery v. Magno, the Court held that the claim for the ₱2,160 rental of replacement trucks "erroneously assumes that the defendant is personally liable for damages," disregarding that he issued the warrant as City Treasurer, empowered by law to do so. "[N]ot having been shown that the defendant, either as a private citizen or as City Treasurer of Butuan, had acted in bad faith, there can be no question that appellee Francisco Magno, who was merely performing a duty enjoined by law to be performed when he issued the warrant of distraint and levy, cannot be made to answer personally for damages."
suggestedAnswer.application: The stipulation that the taxpayer incurred the rental costs did not make the treasurer personally liable, because he acted within his legal authority and in good faith. The ordinance's validity could not be attacked collaterally in a suit against him personally.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Not personally liable. **Bar trap:** proof that the plaintiff suffered a loss is not enough; the defendant must be the one legally answerable for it.

No showing of bad faith
A public officer merely performing a duty enjoined by law is not personally liable

An ordinance cannot be attacked collaterally

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A columnist was convicted of libel for falsely accusing a customs official of corruption. The trial court awarded the official ₱800,000 actual damages and ₱1,000,000 moral damages, although the official presented no evidence of any pecuniary loss. The columnist argues that, since no actual damages were proved, no moral damages can be awarded either. Rule on the awards and the argument, citing Tulfo v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The actual damages must be deleted because no pecuniary loss was proved, but the moral damages may stand: libel is a case where moral damages may be recovered, and they can be awarded even in the absence of actual damages.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Tulfo v. People, the Court held under Article 2199 that one is entitled to compensation "only for such pecuniary loss suffered by him as he has duly proved"; without proof of actual loss that can be measured, the award of actual damages cannot stand. Moral damages compensate injuries such as besmirched reputation and wounded feelings; no proof of pecuniary loss is needed, but the injury must have been suffered and must have sprung from a case in Articles 2219 or 2220. "Justification for the award of moral damages is found in Art. 2219(7) of the Civil Code, which states that moral damages may be recovered in cases of libel, slander, or any other form of defamation." "Moral damages can be awarded even in the absence of actual or compensatory damages."
suggestedAnswer.application: The libelous articles caused injury to the official; the criminal cases of libel fall squarely within Article 2219(7). The lack of proven actual damages does not affect his right to moral damages.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Delete the actual damages; keep the moral damages. **Bar trap:** moral damages do not depend on an award of actual damages; they depend on an injury from a case listed in Articles 2219 or 2220.

keyPoints: Actual damages: only for pecuniary loss duly proved (Art. 2199); none shown, so deleted
Moral damages: injury suffered, from a case in Arts. 2219 or 2220, with causal relation
Libel, slander or other defamation: Art. 2219(7)
Moral damages may be awarded even without actual damages
The ₱1,000,000 moral damages stood

source.caseTitle: Tulfo v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (actual and moral damages)
source.excerpt: The award of damages by the lower court must be modified. Art. 2199 of the Civil Code provides, "Except as provided by law or by stipulation, one is entitled to an adequate compensation only for such pecuniary loss suffered by him as he has duly proved. Such compensation is referred to as actual or compensatory damages." There was no showing of any pecuniary loss suffered by the complainant Atty. So. Without proof of actual loss that can be measured, the award of actual damages cannot stand. … It was the articles of Tulfo that caused injury to Atty. So, and for that Atty. So deserves the award of moral damages. Justification for the award of moral damages is found in Art. 2219(7) of the Civil Code, which states that moral damages may be recovered in cases of libel, slander, or any other form of defamation. As the cases involved are criminal cases of libel, they fall squarely within the ambit of Art. 2219(7). Moral damages can be awarded even in the absence of actual or compensatory damages. The fact that no actual or compensatory damage was proven before the trial court does not adversely affect the offended party’s right to recover moral damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What are the requisites for an award of moral damages, and what kind of causal relation must exist? Explain, citing the rule quoted in Tulfo v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Although no proof of pecuniary loss is needed, it is imperative that (1) injury was suffered by the claimant, and (2) such injury sprang from any of the cases expressed in Articles 2219 and 2220 of the Civil Code. A causal relation must exist: the act or omission must be the proximate cause, and the injury its direct consequence.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Tulfo v. People, the Court quoted Del Mundo v. CA: moral damages "may be awarded to compensate one for manifold injuries such as physical suffering, mental anguish, serious anxiety, besmirched reputation, wounded feelings and social humiliation," in the concept of grants, "not punitive or corrective in nature." It is imperative "that (1) injury must have been suffered by the claimant, and (2) such injury must have sprung from any of the cases expressed in Article 2219 and Article 2220 of the Civil Code. A causal relation, in fine, must exist between the act or omission ... and the resulting injury ... i.e. the first must be the proximate cause and the latter the direct consequence thereof."
suggestedAnswer.application: In Tulfo, the libelous articles were the proximate cause of the injury to the official's reputation and feelings, and libel is a case under Article 2219(7).
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Injury, a case under Arts. 2219 or 2220, and proximate causation. **Bar trap:** moral damages are compensatory grants, not punitive; the amount is discretionary, but the requisites are not.

keyPoints: Moral damages compensate physical suffering, mental anguish, anxiety, besmirched reputation, wounded feelings, social humiliation
Grants, not punitive or corrective
Requisite 1: injury suffered by the claimant
Requisite 2: the injury sprang from a case in Arts. 2219 or 2220
The act must be the proximate cause; the injury its direct consequence

source.caseTitle: Tulfo v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (requisites of moral damages, quoting Del Mundo)
source.excerpt: Moral damages, upon the other hand, may be awarded to compensate one for manifold injuries such as physical suffering, mental anguish, serious anxiety, besmirched reputation, wounded feelings and social humiliation. These damages must be understood to be in the concept of grants, not punitive or corrective in nature, calculated to compensate the claimant for the injury suffered. Although incapable of exactness and no proof of pecuniary loss is necessary in order that moral damages may be awarded, the amount of indemnity being left to the sound discretion of the court, it is imperative, nevertheless, that (1) injury must have been suffered by the claimant, and (2) such injury must have sprung from any of the cases expressed in Article 2219 and Article 2220 of the Civil Code. A causal relation, in fine, must exist between the act or omission referred to in the Code which underlies, or gives rise to, the case or proceeding on the one hand, and the resulting injury, on the other hand; i.e. the first must be the proximate cause and the latter the direct consequence thereof.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a libel case, the trial court awarded the offended public official ₱500,000 exemplary damages on top of moral damages, noting that the false accusations of corruption also distressed his children. No aggravating circumstance was alleged or proved. (a) Should the exemplary damages stand? (b) How may the effect on the family be considered? Explain, citing Tulfo v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. In criminal offenses, exemplary damages may be imposed only when the crime was committed with one or more aggravating circumstances; there being none, they must be deleted. (b) The effect on the family adds an imperative dimension to the award of moral damages to the defamed person.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Tulfo v. People, the Court held that under Article 2230, "[i]n criminal offenses, exemplary damages as a part of the civil liability may be imposed when the crime was committed with one or more aggravating circumstances." Since "[n]o aggravating circumstances accompanied the commission of the libelous acts," no exemplary damages could be awarded. On moral damages, the Court took judicial notice that the sense of kinship runs deeply in a Filipino family, so an attempt to besmirch the name of the head of the family "invariably puts the other members in a state of disrepute, distress, or anxiety," which "adds an imperative dimension to the award of moral damages to the defamed party."
suggestedAnswer.application: The ₱500,000 exemplary damages were deleted, while the ₱1,000,000 moral damages to the official were kept.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: No exemplary damages without an aggravating circumstance; the family's distress supports the moral damages to the defamed party. **Bar trap:** a grave or shameful crime does not by itself justify exemplary damages under Article 2230; look for an aggravating circumstance.

keyPoints: Art. 2230: exemplary damages in crimes need one or more aggravating circumstances
No aggravating circumstance: exemplary damages deleted
Kinship in the Filipino family: the family shares the distress
This adds an imperative dimension to the moral damages of the defamed party
Exemplary damages are separate and distinct from fines

source.caseTitle: Tulfo v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of damages (exemplary damages) and the effect on the family
source.excerpt: The Court can perhaps take judicial notice that the sense of kinship runs deeply in a typical Filipino family, such that the whole family usually suffers or rejoices at the misfortune or good fortune, as the case may be, of any of its member. Accordingly, any attempt to dishonor or besmirch the name and reputation of the head of the family, as here, invariably puts the other members in a state of disrepute, distress, or anxiety. This reality adds an imperative dimension to the award of moral damages to the defamed party. The award of exemplary damages, however, cannot be justified. Under Art. 2230 of the Civil Code, "In criminal offenses, exemplary damages as a part of the civil liability may be imposed when the crime was committed with one or more aggravating circumstances. Such damages are separate and distinct from fines and shall be paid to the offended party." No aggravating circumstances accompanied the commission of the libelous acts; thus, no exemplary damages can be awarded.
