source.excerpt: He executed it as an employee, a salesman of the St. Joseph Lumber from whom Espiritu made his purchases of construction materials and who, therefore, had personal knowledge of the transaction. Although the prosecution of Espiritu for estafa did not prosper, the unsuccessful prosecution may not be labelled as malicious. "Sound principles of justice and public policy dictate that persons shall have free resort to the courts for redress of wrongs and vindication of their rights without later having to stand trial for instituting prosecutions in good faith" (Buenaventura vs. Sto. Domingo, 103 Phil. 239).

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: An employee and his employer were sued together and represented by a lawyer the employer hired. The lawyer focused only on the employer, never told the employee about the pre-trial, missed the pre-trial, and let the default judgment become final because the employer's business was insolvent anyway. The creditor then levied on the employee's car. What relief, if any, does the employee have? Explain, citing Lao v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The judgment against the employee may be set aside as a nullity, because he was deprived of his day in court by the gross negligence of the counsel hired to defend him, and he had a valid defense besides. Its execution against him cannot proceed.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Lao v. CA, the Court found that the lawyer "neglected to defend Lao. He concentrated on the defense of the company and completely forgot his duty to defend Lao as well. He never informed Lao about the pre-trial conferences." He allowed the judgment to become final, so the creditor levied on Lao's car. "In view of the foregoing circumstances, the judgment against Lao was a nullity and should be set aside. Its execution against the petitioner cannot be allowed to proceed." Moreover, as an agent, Lao was not personally liable to the party with whom he contracted (Art. 1897).
suggestedAnswer.application: The Court partially set aside the Court of Appeals' decision insofar as it held Lao solidarily liable and absolved him of any liability from the unsuccessful estafa prosecution.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The employee is absolved. **Bar trap:** a client is generally bound by his counsel's mistakes, but not where gross negligence deprives him of his day in court.

keyPoints: Counsel concentrated on the employer and forgot the employee
He never informed the employee of the pre-trial
Gross negligence deprived the employee of his day in court
The judgment against the employee was a nullity; no execution against him
An agent is not personally liable to the party with whom he contracted (Art. 1897)

source.caseTitle: Lao v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the employee's day in court and the disposition
source.excerpt: There is merit in petitioner's contention that he was deprived of his day in court in the damage suit filed by Espiritu, due to the gross ignorance, negligence, and dereliction of duty of Attorney Manuel Querubin whom his employer had hired to act as counsel for him and the St. Joseph Lumber. However, Attorney Querubin neglected to defend Lao. He concentrated on the defense of the company and completely forgot his duty to defend Lao as well. He never informed Lao about the pre-trial conferences. … In view of the foregoing circumstances, the judgment against Lao was a nullity and should be set aside. Its execution against the petitioner cannot be allowed to proceed.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
Ana and Ben were passengers of a provincial bus. While the bus was running too fast, a tire burst and the bus fell into a ravine. Ana died; Ben suffered a fractured arm. Nothing shows that the bus company or its driver acted with fraud, malice or bad faith; it was simply the driver's carelessness.

(a) Ana's parents sue the bus company for breach of contract of carriage and ask for moral damages for their mental anguish. Will their claim prosper? Explain.

(b) Ben also sues the bus company for breach of contract of carriage and asks for moral damages for his pain and suffering. Will his claim prosper? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Yes. When a passenger dies, her ascendants may demand moral damages for mental anguish by reason of her death, and once they prove they are entitled to them, the court must award them. (b) No. A passenger who is only injured cannot recover moral damages in a suit for breach of contract of carriage unless he proves that the carrier acted with fraud or bad faith, and the driver's mere carelessness is not bad faith.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Article 1764 of the Civil Code makes Article 2206 apply to the death of a passenger caused by a common carrier's breach of contract, and Article 2206(3) allows the spouse, legitimate and illegitimate descendants and ascendants of the deceased to demand moral damages for mental anguish. Once these heirs claim and prove their entitlement, "it becomes the duty of the court to award moral damages to the claimant in an amount commensurate with the mental anguish suffered by them." But this is the exception: "where the injured passenger does not die, moral damages are not recoverable unless it is proved that the carrier was guilty of malice or bad faith," and "the mere carelessness of the carrier's driver does not per se constitute or justify an inference of malice or bad faith on the part of the carrier" (Art. 2220).
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Ana died because of the carrier's breach of the contract of carriage, so her parents, as ascendants, fall under Articles 1764 and 2206(3); they need not prove bad faith. (b) Ben survived, so the exception does not apply. His suit rests on the contract, and the only fault shown is the driver's carelessness in running too fast, which is not malice or bad faith.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) Ana's parents may recover moral damages; (b) Ben may not. **Bar trap:** the same accident gives opposite answers. The death of a passenger is the exception that allows moral damages without proof of bad faith; for an injured passenger suing on the contract, bad faith or fraud must be proved.

keyPoints: Art. 1764 makes Art. 2206 apply to the death of a passenger
Art. 2206(3): ascendants may demand moral damages for mental anguish
Once claimed and proved, the court must award them
Injured passenger who survives: moral damages only if the carrier acted with malice or bad faith (Art. 2220)
The driver's mere carelessness is not bad faith

source.caseTitle: Mercado, et al. v. Lira, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of Articles 1764 and 2206 and of G.R. No. L-13358 (death vs. injury of a passenger)
source.excerpt: Article 2206 states further that "In addition" to the amount of at least P3,000.00 to be awarded for the death of a passenger, the spouse, legitimate and illegitimate descendants and ascendants of the deceased may demand moral damages as a consequence of the death of their deceased kin, which simply means that once the above-mentioned heirs of the deceased claim compensation for moral damages and are able to prove that they are entitled to such award, it becomes the duty of the court to award moral damages to the claimant in an amount commensurate with the mental anguish suffered by them. … The exception to the basic rule of damages now under consideration is a mishap resulting in the death of a passenger, in which case Art. 1764 makes the common carrier expressly subject to the rule of Art. 2206, that entitles the spouse, descendants and ascendants of the deceased passenger to 'demand moral damages for mental anguish by reason of the death of the deceased' (Necesito v. Paras, G.R. No. L-10605, Resolution on motion to reconsider, Sept. 11, 1958). But the exceptional rule of Art. 1764 makes it all the more evident that where the injured passenger does not die, moral damages are not recoverable unless it is proved that the carrier was guilty of malice or bad faith. We think it is clear that the mere carelessness of the carrier's driver does not per se constitute or justify an inference of malice or bad faith on the part of the carrier

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
Carla was riding a jeepney as a paying passenger when its driver carelessly swerved and hit a lamp post. Carla's leg was broken. Dino, who was walking on the sidewalk and had no dealings with the jeepney, was also hit and injured. No fraud or bad faith of the jeepney operator was shown.

(a) Carla sues the operator for breach of contract of carriage. Her lawyer argues that she may recover moral damages because her case is "analogous" to a quasi-delict causing physical injuries under Article 2219(2) of the Civil Code. Is the lawyer correct? Explain.

(b) Dino sues the operator and the driver for his injuries. May he invoke Article 2219(2) as a basis for moral damages? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. A passenger injured through the carrier's negligence in breach of the contract of carriage is not within the "analogous cases" of Article 2219; for breaches of contract, Article 2220 governs and requires fraud or bad faith. (b) Yes. Dino had no pre-existing contract with the operator, so his case is a quasi-delict, and Article 2219(2) lists quasi-delicts causing physical injuries among the cases where moral damages may be recovered.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Article 2219 lists "(1) A criminal offense resulting in physical injuries; (2) Quasi-delicts causing physical injuries" among the cases for moral damages, while Article 2220 provides that the same rule (moral damages) "applies to breaches of contract where the defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith." Contrasting the two, "a breach of contract can not be considered included in the descriptive term 'analogous cases' used in Art. 2219; not only because Art. 2220 specifically provides for the damages that are caused by contractual breach, but because the definition of quasi-delict in Art. 2176 of the Code expressly excludes the cases where there is a 'preexisting contractual relation between the parties.'"
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Carla had a contract of carriage with the operator, so her suit is on the contract; with no fraud or bad faith shown, she cannot get moral damages by calling her case "analogous" to a quasi-delict. (b) Dino was a stranger to the operator; the fault that injured him, with no pre-existing contract, is a quasi-delict causing physical injuries, a case expressly listed in Article 2219(2).
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) The lawyer is wrong; (b) Dino may invoke Article 2219(2). **Bar trap:** the same careless act can be a breach of contract as to the passenger and a quasi-delict as to the pedestrian; the existence of a pre-existing contract decides which rule on moral damages applies.

keyPoints: Art. 2219(2): quasi-delicts causing physical injuries
Art. 2220: moral damages for breach of contract only with fraud or bad faith
A breach of contract is not an "analogous case" under Art. 2219
Art. 2176: a quasi-delict excludes a pre-existing contractual relation
Passenger: contract (needs bad faith); pedestrian with no contract: quasi-delict

source.caseTitle: Mercado, et al. v. Lira, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of G.R. No. L-13358 (Articles 2219, 2220 and 2176)
source.excerpt: "Art. 2219. Moral damages may be recovered in the following and analogous cases: (1) A criminal offense resulting in physical injuries; (2) Quasi-delicts causing physical injuries; … "Art. 2220. Willful injury to property may be a legal ground for awarding moral damages if the court should find that, under the circumstances, such damages are justly due. The same rule applies to breaches of contract where the defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith." By contrasting the provisions of these two articles it immediately becomes apparent that: (a) In cases of breach of contract (including one transportation) proof of bad faith or fraud (dolus), i.e., wanton or deliberately injurious conduct, is essential to justify an award of moral damages; and (b) That a breach of contract can not be considered included in the descriptive term 'analogous cases used in Art. 2219; not only because Art. 2220 specifically provides for the damages that are caused by contractual breach, but because the definition of quasi-delict in Art. 2176 of the Code expressly excludes the cases where there is a 'preexisting contractual relation between the parties.'

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
Elena, a bus passenger, was injured when the bus she was riding crashed. She sues the bus company for breach of contract of carriage and asks for moral damages.

(a) Elena's only evidence is that she was injured during the trip. She argues that since a common carrier is presumed at fault when a passenger is injured, the carrier must also be presumed to have acted in bad faith, so moral damages follow. Is she correct? Explain.

(b) Suppose instead that Elena presents evidence that the carrier's negligence was so gross as to amount to malice. Could that support moral damages? Explain briefly.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. The law presumes a common carrier negligent, not malicious, when a passenger is injured; bad faith is not to be lightly inferred from a breach through negligence. (b) It could. Negligence may occasionally be so gross as to amount to malice, but that fact must be shown in evidence; if proved, it can supply the bad faith that Article 2220 requires.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Treating every breach of the duty of safe carriage as bad faith "is untenable, for under it the carrier would always be deemed in bad faith, in every case its obligation to the passenger is infringed, and it would never be accountable for simple negligence; while under the law (Art. 1756), the presumption is that common carriers acted negligently (and not maliciously)." "It is true that negligence may be occasionally so gross as to amount to malice; but that fact must be shown in evidence, and a carrier's bad faith is not to be lightly inferred from a mere finding that the contract was breached through negligence of the carrier's employees."
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Elena's proof of injury raises only the presumption of negligence under Article 1756; it does not prove fraud or bad faith, so she cannot recover moral damages on that alone. (b) If her evidence actually shows negligence so gross as to amount to malice, she would have the showing of bad faith that a passenger suing on the contract needs; but the court cannot assume it from the mere breach.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) Incorrect; (b) possibly, but only on evidence. **Bar trap:** the presumption against carriers is a presumption of negligence; do not convert it into a presumption of bad faith. Gross negligence amounting to malice must be proved, not presumed.

keyPoints: Art. 1756 presumes carriers negligent, not malicious
If every breach were bad faith, carriers would never be liable for simple negligence
Bad faith is not lightly inferred from a breach through negligence
Negligence may be so gross as to amount to malice
But that must be shown in evidence

source.caseTitle: Mercado, et al. v. Lira, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of G.R. No. L-13358 (presumed negligence is not bad faith; gross negligence)
source.excerpt: This theory is untenable, for under it the carrier would always be deemed in bad faith, in every case its obligation to the passenger is infringed, and it would never be accountable for simple negligence; while under the law (Art. 1756), the presumption is that common carriers acted negligently (and not maliciously), and Art. 1762 speaks of negligence of the common carrier. … It is true that negligence may be occasionally so gross as to amount to malice; but that fact must be shown in evidence, and a carrier's bad faith is not to be lightly inferred from a mere finding that the contract was breached through negligence of the carrier's employees.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
Ana and Ben are members of a private beach club. Ana deliberately ignored the club's booking rules and shouted insults at the staff member who stopped her. The board sent her a written notice, received her written explanation, and suspended her for two months, as the club's by-laws allow. Ben, who joined her in breaking the rules, was suspended in the same way.

(a) Ana sues the club for moral and exemplary damages, saying the suspension embarrassed her before her friends. Will her suit prosper? Explain.

(b) Ben's only evidence is his own testimony that some friends stopped doing business with him after the suspension; he admits they never told him the suspension was the reason. Is that enough? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. The club merely exercised its legal right under its by-laws after giving notice and a chance to explain; any damage that results is damnum absque injuria, and the embarrassment was brought on by Ana herself. (b) No. Bare, self-serving testimony, with no other evidence and no proof that the suspension caused the loss, does not prove damage by preponderance of evidence.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: "One who makes use of his own legal right does no injury. Qui jure suo utitur nullum damnum facit. If damage results from a person's exercising his legal rights, it is damnum absque injuria." The suspended members must prove by preponderance of evidence that there is fault or negligence on the club's part; membership in a club is a privilege, subject to its rules, and mental anguish caused by deliberately violating those rules is brought upon oneself. Mere "self-serving declarations," with neither testimonial nor documentary evidence to bolster them, do not prove the damage claimed.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Ana broke the rules on purpose and was suspended in the manner the by-laws provide, so the club committed no legal wrong. (b) Ben offers only his own word, and even admits his friends gave no reason linking their conduct to his suspension.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Neither Ana nor Ben may recover. **Bar trap:** feeling embarrassed or losing business is damage, but without a legal wrong (injury) it is not compensable; and a claimant's own testimony alone is weak proof.

keyPoints: One who uses his own legal right does no injury (qui jure suo utitur nullum damnum facit)
Damage from the exercise of a legal right is damnum absque injuria
The claimant must prove fault or negligence by preponderance of evidence
Anguish from one's own deliberate violation of the rules is self-inflicted
Self-serving declarations without other evidence do not prove damage

source.caseTitle: The Orchard Golf & Country Club, Inc., et al. v. Yu and Yuhico
source.part: Decision, the claim for moral and exemplary damages
source.excerpt: With regard to the purported damages they incurred, respondents testified during the trial to support their respective allegations. … Apart from these self-serving declarations, respondents presented neither testimonial nor documentary evidence to bolster their claims. Worse, Yu even admitted that Freddy Lim and Atty. Benjie did not tell him that his suspension was the reason why they did not want to transact with him. … "One who makes use of his own legal right does no injury. Qui jure suo utitur nullum damnum facit. If damage results from a person's exercising his legal rights, it is damnum absque injuria." In this case, respondents failed to prove by preponderance of evidence that there is fault or negligence on the part of petitioners in order to oblige them to pay for the alleged damage sustained as a result of their suspension as Club members. Certainly, membership in the Club is a privilege. Regular members are entitled to use all the facilities and privileges of the Club, subject to its rules and regulations. As correctly pointed out by petitioners, the mental anguish respondents experienced, assuming to be true, was brought upon them by themselves for deliberately and consciously violating the rules and regulations of the Club.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Carla lost a profitable deal after her homeowners' association lawfully suspended her privileges, in accordance with its rules, for repeated violations. She sues the association, arguing: "I suffered a real loss because of what the association did, so I am entitled to damages." Is her argument correct? In your answer, distinguish injury, damage and damages.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The mere fact that she suffered a loss does not give her a right to damages. There must be both a legal wrong inflicted by the defendant (injury) and damage resulting from it; a loss that does not result from a violation of a legal duty is damnum absque injuria.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: "[T]he mere fact that the plaintiff suffered losses does not give rise to a right to recover damages. To warrant the recovery of damages, there must be both a right of action for a legal wrong inflicted by the defendant, and damage resulting to the plaintiff therefrom. Wrong without damage, or damage without wrong, does not constitute a cause of action." "Injury is the illegal invasion of a legal right; damage is the loss, hurt, or harm which results from the injury; and damages are the recompense or compensation awarded for the damage suffered. Thus, there can be damage without injury in those instances in which the loss or harm was not the result of a violation of a legal duty."
suggestedAnswer.application: Carla suffered damage (the lost deal), but the association acted under its rules and did not violate any legal duty owed to her, so there is no injury in the legal sense, and no damages are due.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Her argument is wrong; this is damage without injury. **Bar trap:** do not confuse damage (the loss) with injury (the legal wrong); both are needed before damages (the compensation) can be awarded.

keyPoints: A loss alone does not give a right to damages
Need both a legal wrong by the defendant and resulting damage
Injury: illegal invasion of a legal right
Damage: the loss, hurt or harm; damages: the compensation
Damage without injury (damnum absque injuria) is not compensable

source.caseTitle: The Orchard Golf & Country Club, Inc., et al. v. Yu and Yuhico
source.part: Decision, damages, damage and injury (quoting Spouses Custodio v. CA)
source.excerpt: x x x [T]he mere fact that the plaintiff suffered losses does not give rise to a right to recover damages. To warrant the recovery of damages, there must be both a right of action for a legal wrong inflicted by the defendant, and damage resulting to the plaintiff therefrom. Wrong without damage, or damage without wrong, does not constitute a cause of action, since damages are merely part of the remedy allowed for the injury caused by a breach or wrong. There is a material distinction between damages and injury. Injury is the illegal invasion of a legal right; damage is the loss, hurt, or harm which results from the injury; and damages are the recompense or compensation awarded for the damage suffered. Thus, there can be damage without injury in those instances in which the loss or harm was not the result of a violation of a legal duty. These situations are often called damnum absque injuria.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
Dela Corp. lost an intra-corporate case in the Regional Trial Court. Its lawyer filed a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review under Rule 43. Seven days after the 15-day period lapsed, the lawyer candidly admitted the mistake and asked the Court of Appeals for time to file the petition; the appeal appeared meritorious, and the other side suffered no material prejudice.

(a) May the Court of Appeals allow the petition? Explain.

(b) Would the answer be the same if, instead, Dela Corp. had filed months late, without any explanation, and with no showing that its appeal had merit? Reason briefly.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Yes. Although the periods for appeal are generally inviolable, they may be relaxed to serve substantial justice where the appeal appears meritorious or there are compelling reasons; a short, candidly explained delay with no prejudice, under a rule that itself allows extensions, justifies relaxation. (b) No. The general rule would apply: perfecting an appeal within the period is mandatory and jurisdictional, and nothing would justify relaxing it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: "In general, procedural rules setting the period for perfecting an appeal or filing a petition for review are inviolable considering that appeal is not a constitutional right but merely a statutory privilege and that perfection of an appeal in the manner and within the period permitted by law is not only mandatory but jurisdictional. However, procedural rules may be waived or dispensed with in order to serve and achieve substantial justice. Relaxation of the rules may be had when the appeal, on its face, appears to be absolutely meritorious or when there are persuasive or compelling reasons." Under A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC, the Court of Appeals may grant an additional 15 days and a further extension for the most compelling reasons, so the period "is neither an impregnable nor an unyielding rule."
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Dela Corp.'s delay was only seven days, it admitted its mistake, its appeal looked meritorious, and the rule itself contemplates extensions. (b) Without any reason, merit or candor, there is nothing to take the case out of the general rule.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) The petition may be allowed; (b) not. **Bar trap:** relaxation is the exception; it needs a meritorious appeal or compelling reasons, not just a request.

keyPoints: Periods to appeal are generally inviolable; appeal is a statutory privilege
Perfection within the period is mandatory and jurisdictional
Rules may be relaxed to serve substantial justice
When the appeal appears meritorious or there are compelling reasons
A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC itself allows extensions

source.caseTitle: The Orchard Golf & Country Club, Inc., et al. v. Yu and Yuhico
source.part: Decision, relaxation of the rules on the period to appeal
source.excerpt: Unlike LBP and Atty. Abrenica, petitioners in this case committed an excusable delay of merely seven (7) days. … In general, procedural rules setting the period for perfecting an appeal or filing a petition for review are inviolable considering that appeal is not a constitutional right but merely a statutory privilege and that perfection of an appeal in the manner and within the period permitted by law is not only mandatory but jurisdictional. However, procedural rules may be waived or dispensed with in order to serve and achieve substantial justice. Relaxation of the rules may be had when the appeal, on its face, appears to be absolutely meritorious or when there are persuasive or compelling reasons to relieve a litigant of an injustice not commensurate with the degree of thoughtlessness in not complying with the prescribed procedure. Notably, under A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC (Re: Mode of Appeal in Cases Formerly Cognizable by the Securities and Exchange Commission), while the petition for review under Rule 43 of the Rules should be filed within fifteen (15) days from notice of the decision or final order of the RTC, the CA may actually grant an additional period of fifteen (15) days within which to file the petition and a further extension of time not exceeding fifteen (15) days for the most compelling reasons. This implies that the reglementary period is neither an impregnable nor an unyielding rule.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
In two separate murder cases, the heirs claim damages for the victim's loss of earning capacity, but neither presents any documents (no payslips, no tax records).

(a) Ana's victim, her son, was a daily wage farm worker earning less than the minimum wage; Ana testifies to how much he earned. May the court award loss of earning capacity? Explain.

(b) Ben's victim, his brother, was a salaried office manager; Ben testifies to his salary but presents no document. May the court award loss of earning capacity on that testimony alone? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Yes. Documentary evidence is the rule, but oral testimony suffices when the victim was a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage. (b) No, not under the exception. A salaried manager is not a self-employed person or a daily wage worker earning below the minimum wage, so the general rule requiring documentary evidence applies.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Following People v. Dizon: "As a rule, documentary evidence should be presented to substantiate the claim for loss of earning capacity." To claim it "despite the nonavailability of documentary evidence, there must be oral testimony that: (a) the victim was self-employed earning less than the minimum wage under the current labor laws and judicial notice was taken of the fact that in the victim's line of work, no documentary evidence is available; (b) the victim was employed as a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage under current labor laws."
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Ana's son fits the second exception, so her testimony is enough. (b) Ben's brother fits neither exception; without documents, the claim fails under the general rule.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) Award proper; (b) not on testimony alone. **Bar trap:** the testimony-only exception is narrow; it covers low-income self-employed or daily wage earners, not every victim whose papers are missing.

keyPoints: General rule: documentary evidence of lost earnings
Exception 1: self-employed earning less than the minimum wage, where no documents exist in that line of work
Exception 2: daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage
Then oral testimony suffices
A salaried manager falls under neither exception

source.caseTitle: People v. Muyco
source.part: Decision, award for loss of earning capacity (proof required, citing People v. Dizon)
source.excerpt: On the other hand, this Court notes that the trial court failed to award damages for loss of earning capacity despite the testimony of Leticia Boteja to this effect. In People v. Dizon this Court discussed the requisites for such award — As a rule, documentary evidence should be presented to substantiate the claim for loss of earning capacity. … To be able to claim damages for loss of earning capacity despite the nonavailability of documentary evidence, there must be oral testimony that: (a) the victim was self-employed earning less than the minimum wage under the current labor laws and judicial notice was taken of the fact that in the victim's line of work, no documentary evidence is available; (b) the victim was employed as a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage under current labor laws. . .

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Carla, 20 years old, was killed. She worked as a daily wage farm laborer earning ₱2,000 a month, below the minimum wage, as her father credibly testified. Using the formula 2/3 × (80 − age at death) × (gross annual income − 80% of gross annual income), compute the award for her loss of earning capacity. Show the computation.

suggestedAnswer.answer: ₱160,000. Life expectancy = 2/3 × (80 − 20) = 40 years. Gross annual income = ₱2,000 × 12 = ₱24,000. Less living expenses of 80% (₱19,200) = ₱4,800. Award = 40 × ₱4,800 = ₱160,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The formula applied was: "2/3 (80 - ATD [age at time of death]) x (GAI [gross annual income]) - 80% GAI." For the 19-year-old victim earning ₱1,600 a month, the Court computed 2/3 (61) × [₱19,200 − ₱15,360] = 40.67 × ₱3,840 = ₱156,172.80. Since Carla was a daily wage worker earning below the minimum wage, her father's testimony suffices to prove her income.
suggestedAnswer.application: Applying the same steps to Carla's age (20) and income (₱2,000 a month) gives 40 × ₱4,800 = ₱160,000.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: ₱160,000. **Bar trap:** deduct the living expenses from the gross annual income before multiplying by the life expectancy; and note that this formula deducts 80% of gross income, while other decisions deduct a different share for living expenses (for example, 50%), so apply the formula the facts and the decision call for.

keyPoints: Life expectancy: 2/3 × (80 − age at death) = 40
Gross annual income: ₱2,000 × 12 = ₱24,000
Less 80% for living expenses: ₱24,000 − ₱19,200 = ₱4,800
Testimony suffices for a daily wage worker below the minimum wage

source.caseTitle: People v. Muyco
source.part: Decision, award for loss of earning capacity (the formula)
source.excerpt: In the instant case, the victim was nineteen (19) years old at the time of his death and earning P1,600.00 monthly as a farm laborer. Thus, his heirs are entitled to receive an award for lost earnings in accordance with the following formula: 2/3 (80 - ATD [age at time of death]) x (GAI [gross annual income]) - 80% GAI. Thus — 2/3 (80-19) x (P1,600 x 12) - 80% (P1,600.00 x 12) 2/3 (61) x P19,200 - 80% (P19,200) 40.67 x [P19,200 - P15,360] 40.67 x P3,840 = P156,172.80 ==========

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
Dan was charged with murder for stabbing Eli during a drinking session. The only eyewitness, Eli's uncle, testified that he stood frozen and did nothing while the stabbing happened a meter away; he also said the wound was on the neck, while the autopsy placed it just below the collarbone. Dan, whom the uncle positively identified, testified that he was in another town about 50 kilometers away, but offered no evidence that it was impossible for him to travel to the scene that night.

(a) Does the uncle's failure to act, or his mistake about the wound's location, destroy his credibility? Explain.

(b) Will Dan's alibi prosper? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. People react differently to startling events, so freezing does not make a witness unworthy of belief, and discrepancies on minor details strengthen rather than weaken credibility. (b) No. Alibi is weak against positive identification, and it fails all the more when the accused does not show that it was physically impossible for him to be at the scene.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: "Different people react differently to a given type of situation. There is no standard form of human behavioral response when one is confronted with a strange, startling or frightful experience. … A witness' inability to move, help or even to run away when the incident occurs is not a ground to label his testimony as doubtful." "Inconsistencies and discrepancies in the testimony of a witness on minor details only serve to strengthen the credibility of the witness." Alibi becomes "all the more ineffectual when he failed to demonstrate that it was physically impossible for him to be at the crime scene."
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) The uncle's shock is a natural reaction, and the wound's exact location is a minor detail. (b) A town 50 kilometers away is not shown to be beyond reach that night, and Dan was positively identified.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) Credibility stands; (b) the alibi fails. **Bar trap:** for alibi, mere distance is not enough; the accused must show physical impossibility of being at the scene.

keyPoints: No standard human reaction to a startling event
A witness's inability to move or help does not make him unworthy of belief
Minor discrepancies strengthen credibility
Alibi is weak against positive identification
Alibi requires physical impossibility of being at the scene

source.caseTitle: People v. Muyco
source.part: Decision, credibility of the eyewitness and the defense of alibi
source.excerpt: We disagree. Different people react differently to a given type of situation. There is no standard form of human behavioral response when one is confronted with a strange, startling or frightful experience. … A witness' inability to move, help or even to run away when the incident occurs is not a ground to label his testimony as doubtful and unworthy of belief. … Inconsistencies and discrepancies in the testimony of a witness on minor details only serve to strengthen the credibility of the witness. … Weak as it was, accused-appellant's alibi became all the more ineffectual when he failed to demonstrate that it was physically impossible for him to be at the crime scene at the time it was committed. He testified being in Passi, Iloilo, during the stabbing incident. Passi, Iloilo is only fifty (50) kilometers from Cabatuan, Iloilo, the place where the crime was committed. He did not offer any evidence to prove impossibility of access between the two (2) places when the crime transpired.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
Ana, a 40-year-old government accountant, died when the bus she was riding fell into a ravine because it was running too fast. In the suit against the bus company, her husband Ben testified on her salary, but no payslips, tax records or other documents of her income were presented. It is clear, though, that the family lost the income she used to earn.

(a) May the court award damages for Ana's loss of earning capacity? Explain.

(b) If not, may the court award any other damages for the family's lost income? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. Loss of earning capacity must, as a rule, be proved by documentary evidence; testimony alone suffices only if the deceased was self-employed or a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage, and a salaried government accountant is neither. (b) Yes, temperate damages, since some pecuniary loss was suffered but its amount cannot be proved with certainty (Art. 2224).
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Article 1764 in relation to Article 2206, a common carrier whose breach results in a passenger's death is liable for indemnity for death, indemnity for loss of earning capacity and moral damages. But "[a]s a rule, documentary evidence should be presented to substantiate the claim for damages for loss of earning capacity," except when the deceased is self-employed earning less than the minimum wage (where no documents are available in that line of work) or a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage. Where the earnings do not fall within the exceptions but "the fact of loss [has] been established, temperate damages" may be awarded, since under Article 2224 temperate damages "may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount can not, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty."
suggestedAnswer.application: Ana's income was not proved by documents and she does not fall within the exceptions, so no award for loss of earning capacity can be made. But the family's loss of her income is certain, so temperate damages are proper.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) No award for loss of earning capacity; (b) temperate damages instead. **Bar trap:** a failed claim for lost earnings does not leave the heirs with nothing; when the fact of loss is clear but its amount is unproved, temperate damages fill the gap.

keyPoints: Arts. 1764 and 2206: death indemnity, loss of earning capacity, moral damages
Loss of earning capacity needs documentary evidence, as a rule
Exceptions: self-employed or daily wage workers earning below the minimum wage
A salaried employee is not within the exceptions
Temperate damages when loss is shown but its amount cannot be proved (Art. 2224)

source.caseTitle: Victory Liner, Inc. v. Gammad, et al.
source.part: Decision, damages for the death of a passenger and temperate damages
source.excerpt: Article 1764 in relation to Article 2206 of the Civil Code, holds the common carrier in breach of its contract of carriage that results in the death of a passenger liable to pay the following: (1) indemnity for death, (2) indemnity for loss of earning capacity, and (3) moral damages. … The award of compensatory damages for the loss of the deceased’s earning capacity should be deleted for lack of basis. As a rule, documentary evidence should be presented to substantiate the claim for damages for loss of earning capacity. By way of exception, damages for loss of earning capacity may be awarded despite the absence of documentary evidence when (1) the deceased is self-employed earning less than the minimum wage under current labor laws, and judicial notice may be taken of the fact that in the deceased’s line of work no documentary evidence is available; or (2) the deceased is employed as a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage under current labor laws. … The award is clearly erroneous because the deceased’s earnings does not fall within the exceptions. However, the fact of loss having been established, temperate damages in the amount of P500,000.00 should be awarded to respondents. Under Article 2224 of the Civil Code, temperate or moderate damages, which are more than nominal but less than compensatory damages, may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount can not, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
In a suit for the death of a bus passenger, Carla, the passenger's widow, proved the funeral expenses with (1) official receipts totaling ₱80,000, (2) her own handwritten list of other wake expenses, and (3) a contract for building the tomb. The trial court awarded all three as actual damages, and also awarded ₱400,000 "as moral and exemplary damages" in one lump sum.

(a) Which of Carla's proofs support actual damages? Explain.

(b) Is the lump-sum award of moral and exemplary damages proper? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Only the official receipts. A handwritten list of expenses and a contract for the tomb are not competent proof and cannot replace official receipts. (b) No. Moral and exemplary damages rest on different jural foundations and must be determined separately.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: "[O]nly substantiated and proven expenses or those that appear to have been genuinely incurred in connection with the death, wake or burial of the victim will be recognized. A list of expenses ... and the contract/receipt for the construction of the tomb ... cannot be considered competent proof and cannot replace the official receipts necessary to justify the award." Moral damages "cannot be lumped with exemplary damages because they are based on different jural foundations. These damages are different in nature and require separate determination." Moral damages may be awarded when a passenger's death results from a breach of carriage (Art. 1764 in relation to Art. 2206), while exemplary damages may be recovered in contracts if the defendant acted in a wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive or malevolent manner.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Carla's actual damages should be limited to the ₱80,000 in official receipts. (b) The court must fix moral damages (for her anguish over her husband's death) and, if the carrier's conduct warrants it, exemplary damages, each on its own basis.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) Receipts only; (b) the awards must be separated. **Bar trap:** do not treat a party's own list of expenses as proof; and never lump moral and exemplary damages together.

keyPoints: Actual damages: only substantiated and proven expenses
A handwritten list or a tomb contract cannot replace official receipts
Moral and exemplary damages have different jural foundations
They must be determined separately
Exemplary damages in contracts: wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive or malevolent conduct

source.caseTitle: Victory Liner, Inc. v. Gammad, et al.
source.part: Decision, moral, exemplary and actual damages
source.excerpt: Anent the award of moral damages, the same cannot be lumped with exemplary damages because they are based on different jural foundations. These damages are different in nature and require separate determination. In culpa contractual or breach of contract, moral damages may be recovered when the defendant acted in bad faith or was guilty of gross negligence (amounting to bad faith) or in wanton disregard of contractual obligations and, as in this case, when the act of breach of contract itself constitutes the tort that results in physical injuries. By special rule in Article 1764 in relation to Article 2206 of the Civil Code, moral damages may also be awarded in case the death of a passenger results from a breach of carriage. On the other hand, exemplary damages, which are awarded by way of example or correction for the public good may be recovered in contractual obligations if the defendant acted in wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive, or malevolent manner. … The actual damages awarded by the trial court reduced by the Court of Appeals should be further reduced. In People v. Duban, it was held that only substantiated and proven expenses or those that appear to have been genuinely incurred in connection with the death, wake or burial of the victim will be recognized. A list of expenses (Exhibit "J"), and the contract/receipt for the construction of the tomb (Exhibit "F") in this case, cannot be considered competent proof and cannot replace the official receipts necessary to justify the award.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
A bus company was sued for the death of a passenger, Dina. Its lawyer filed an answer, a pre-trial brief and a timely appeal, but missed several hearings, so the company was deemed to have waived cross-examination and its evidence. The company itself never checked on the case. It loses.

(a) May the company escape the judgment by claiming its lawyer's negligence denied it due process? Explain.

(b) On the merits, the company argues that the heirs never proved that its driver was negligent. Is that a defense? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. The negligence of counsel binds the client; the exception for reckless or gross negligence that deprives the client of due process does not apply where counsel actively took part in the case and the client itself was negligent. (b) No. When a passenger dies, the carrier is presumed at fault; the heirs need not prove negligence, and the presumption is overcome only by proof of extraordinary diligence.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: "It is settled that the negligence of counsel binds the client," since counsel's acts within the scope of his authority are the client's acts, subject to exceptions "where reckless or gross negligence of counsel deprives the client of due process of law, or when its application will result in outright deprivation of the client's liberty or property or where the interests of justice so require." "In a contract of carriage, it is presumed that the common carrier was at fault or was negligent when a passenger dies or is injured. Unless the presumption is rebutted, the court need not even make an express finding of fault or negligence ... This statutory presumption may only be overcome by evidence that the carrier exercised extraordinary diligence."
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) The lawyer filed the key pleadings and an appeal, and the company did not monitor its case, so there was no deprivation of due process. (b) The company presented no evidence of extraordinary diligence, so the presumption of fault stands.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) Bound by counsel; (b) presumption of fault stands. **Bar trap:** the burden in carriage is reversed; the passenger's heirs do not have to prove negligence.

keyPoints: The negligence of counsel binds the client
Exception: reckless or gross negligence depriving the client of due process
Not where counsel took part in the case and the client was itself negligent
A carrier is presumed at fault when a passenger dies or is injured
Overcome only by proof of extraordinary diligence

source.caseTitle: Victory Liner, Inc. v. Gammad, et al.
source.part: Decision, negligence of counsel and breach of contract of carriage
source.excerpt: It is settled that the negligence of counsel binds the client. This is based on the rule that any act performed by a counsel within the scope of his general or implied authority is regarded as an act of his client. Consequently, the mistake or negligence of counsel may result in the rendition of an unfavorable judgment against the client. However, the application of the general rule to a given case should be looked into and adopted according to the surrounding circumstances obtaining. Thus, exceptions to the foregoing have been recognized by the court in cases where reckless or gross negligence of counsel deprives the client of due process of law, or when its application will result in outright deprivation of the client’s liberty or property or where the interests of justice so require, and accord relief to the client who suffered by reason of the lawyer’s gross or palpable mistake or negligence. … Anent the second issue, petitioner was correctly found liable for breach of contract of carriage. A common carrier is bound to carry its passengers safely as far as human care and foresight can provide, using the utmost diligence of very cautious persons, with due regard to all the circumstances. In a contract of carriage, it is presumed that the common carrier was at fault or was negligent when a passenger dies or is injured. Unless the presumption is rebutted, the court need not even make an express finding of fault or negligence on the part of the common carrier. This statutory presumption may only be overcome by evidence that the carrier exercised extraordinary diligence.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
Ana and her husband were riding a motorcycle on the left side of a provincial highway. A delivery truck driven by Ben, coming from behind on the right lane, saw them ahead but did not slow down; it veered to the left and hit them. Ben's employer, Fast Freight Inc., proves that before hiring Ben it checked his NBI clearance and gave him a driving test and a physical examination. It did not know that Ben had been involved in earlier sideswiping incidents, and it gave him no training on discipline and road behavior.

(a) Was Ben negligent? Explain.

(b) Is Fast Freight Inc. liable with Ben? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Yes. Under the test of foreseeability, a reasonable driver who saw the motorcycle ahead would have slowed down; Ben drove on and veered left into it. (b) Yes. When an employee's negligence causes damage, the employer is presumed to have failed in the selection or supervision of the employee; tests limited to driving ability and fitness, without knowledge of the driver's past incidents or instilling discipline on the road, do not overcome the presumption.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: "Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence. To be negligent, a defendant must have acted or failed to act in such a way that an ordinary reasonable man would have realized that certain interests of certain persons were unreasonably subjected to a general but definite class of risks." "Whenever an employee's negligence causes damage or injury to another, there instantly arises a presumption that the employer failed to exercise the due diligence of a good father of the family in the selection or supervision of its employees," which the employer must overcome by convincing proof. Tests "concentrated on the ability to drive and physical fitness to do so," without knowing the driver's previous sideswiping incidents or inculcating discipline and correct behavior on the road, were insufficient.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Ben saw the danger and did not take the precaution of slowing down. (b) Fast Freight's screening is the same kind held insufficient; it did not supervise Ben's road behavior or know his record.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) Ben was negligent; (b) Fast Freight is liable. **Bar trap:** passing hiring tests is not enough; the employer must prove diligence in both selection and supervision.

keyPoints: Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence
Seeing the danger and not slowing down is negligent
Employee's negligence raises a presumption of the employer's negligence
Overcome only by convincing proof of diligence in selection and supervision
Tests on driving skill and fitness alone are not enough

source.caseTitle: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
source.part: Decision, negligence of the driver and liability of the employer
source.excerpt: Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence. To be negligent, a defendant must have acted or failed to act in such a way that an ordinary reasonable man would have realized that certain interests of certain persons were unreasonably subjected to a general but definite class of risks. In this case, the bus driver, who was driving on the right side of the road, already saw the motorcycle on the left side of the road before the collision. However, he did not take the necessary precaution to slow down, but drove on and bumped the motorcycle, and also the passenger jeep parked on the left side of the road, showing that the bus was negligent in veering to the left lane, causing it to hit the motorcycle and the passenger jeep. Whenever an employee’s negligence causes damage or injury to another, there instantly arises a presumption that the employer failed to exercise the due diligence of a good father of the family in the selection or supervision of its employees. To avoid liability for a quasi-delict committed by his employee, an employer must overcome the presumption by presenting convincing proof that he exercised the care and diligence of a good father of a family in the selection and supervision of his employee. The Court upholds the finding of the trial court and the Court of Appeals that petitioner is liable to respondent, since it failed to exercise the diligence of a good father of the family in the selection and supervision of its bus driver, Margarito Avila, for having failed to sufficiently inculcate in him discipline and correct behavior on the road. Indeed, petitioner’s tests were concentrated on the ability to drive and physical fitness to do so. It also did not know that Avila had been previously involved in sideswiping incidents.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Carlo, 50 years old, owned and ran a small hardware store. He was killed when a negligent truck driver hit him. His heirs proved, through his income tax documents, that the store's gross annual income was ₱400,000, but presented no evidence of the store's operating expenses or of Carlo's living expenses. Using the method that pegs necessary business expenses at 80% of gross income and living expenses at 50% of the net income, compute the award for loss of earning capacity. Show the computation.

suggestedAnswer.answer: ₱800,000. Life expectancy = 2/3 × (80 − 50) = 20 years. Gross annual income ₱400,000 less necessary expenses of 80% (₱320,000) = ₱80,000. Less living expenses of 50% of that (₱40,000) = ₱40,000 net. Award = 20 × ₱40,000 = ₱800,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Indemnity for loss of earning capacity under Article 2206 "is awarded not for loss of earnings, but for loss of capacity to earn money," and "only net earnings, not gross earnings, are to be considered; that is, the total of the earnings less expenses necessary for the creation of such earnings or income, less living and other incidental expenses. In the absence of documentary evidence, it is reasonable to peg necessary expenses ... at 80 percent of the gross income, and peg living expenses at 50 percent of the net income (gross income less necessary expenses)."
suggestedAnswer.application: Carlo ran a business, so its necessary expenses must first be deducted from his gross income; with no evidence of expenses, they are pegged at 80%, and living expenses at 50% of what remains.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: ₱800,000. **Bar trap:** for a business owner, deduct the business's necessary expenses first, then the living expenses; never multiply the gross income.

keyPoints: Art. 2206 indemnity is for loss of capacity to earn
Only net earnings count
Without documents: necessary expenses at 80% of gross, living expenses at 50% of net
Life expectancy: 2/3 × (80 − 50) = 20

source.caseTitle: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
source.part: Decision, computation of loss of earning capacity (net earnings)
source.excerpt: The indemnity for loss of earning capacity of the deceased is provided for by Article 2206 of the Civil Code. Compensation of this nature is awarded not for loss of earnings, but for loss of capacity to earn money. … In the computation of loss of earning capacity, only net earnings, not gross earnings, are to be considered; that is, the total of the earnings less expenses necessary for the creation of such earnings or income, less living and other incidental expenses. In the absence of documentary evidence, it is reasonable to peg necessary expenses for the lease and operation of the gasoline station at 80 percent of the gross income, and peg living expenses at 50 percent of the net income (gross income less necessary expenses).

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt:
In the same accident, Carlo's wife, Dina, who was riding with him, suffered a broken leg, and their motorcycle was wrecked. To prove the motorcycle's damage, Dina presented only a repair shop's job estimate of ₱18,000; she presented no receipts.

(a) May Dina recover the ₱18,000 as actual damages? If not, what may she recover for the motorcycle? Explain.

(b) May Dina recover moral damages for her own injuries from the negligent driver and his employer? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) No. A job estimate is not competent proof of the actual damage; but since some loss to the motorcycle was clearly suffered, temperate damages may be awarded. (b) Yes. Moral damages may be recovered in quasi-delicts causing physical injuries (Art. 2219).
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: "Under Art. 2224 of the Civil Code, temperate damages 'may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty.'" Where the evidence of a motorcycle's repair "was merely a job estimate," temperate damages were awarded. "Under Art. 2219 of the Civil Code, moral damages may be recovered in quasi-delicts causing physical injuries."
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) The motorcycle was undeniably damaged through the driver's negligence, but the estimate does not prove the actual cost, so temperate damages, not actual damages, are proper. (b) Dina's broken leg is a physical injury caused by a quasi-delict, which is one of the cases listed in Article 2219.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: (a) Temperate damages, not the estimate as actual damages; (b) moral damages may be awarded. **Bar trap:** unlike a passenger suing on a contract of carriage, a victim of a quasi-delict causing physical injuries need not prove bad faith to recover moral damages.

keyPoints: A job estimate is not proof of actual damage
Temperate damages when loss is certain but its amount is not proved (Art. 2224)
Moral damages in quasi-delicts causing physical injuries (Art. 2219)
The appellate court may review matters not assigned as errors if needed for a just decision

source.caseTitle: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
source.part: Decision, damages awarded on appeal though not assigned as errors
source.excerpt: In addition, the Court of Appeals correctly awarded temperate damages in the amount of ₱10,000.00 for the damage caused on respondent’s motorcycle. Under Art. 2224 of the Civil Code, temperate damages "may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty." The cost of the repair of the motorcycle was prayed for by respondent in her Complaint. However, the evidence presented was merely a job estimate of the cost of the motorcycle’s repair amounting to ₱17, 829.00. … The Court of Appeals also correctly awarded respondent moral damages for the physical injuries she sustained due to the vehicular accident. Under Art. 2219 of the Civil Code, moral damages may be recovered in quasi-delicts causing physical injuries.
